Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007

BBC News Tue, 17 Nov 2026 13:15:38 GMT

He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?

Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.

The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.

"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast.

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.

Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."

Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".

Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast.

"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire.

"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."

Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."

So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?

Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.

"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.

"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.

"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a. k. a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote.

"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".

Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.

"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.

However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.

Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.

"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.

"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."

Collider's Collier Jennings named The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.

"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.

"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.

"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.

"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."

Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on suspected paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.

It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen not as a villain but equally not as a hero.

"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."

Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.

The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time before the Bond casting was announced.

"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."

Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?

BBC News Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:35:53 GMT

If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.

Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.

But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out.

Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.

The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.

It used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.

According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.

Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.

Some people live in one area and work in another, but the analysis did not account for this.

Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.

The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.

The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.

Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.

Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.

Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.

Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.

Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.

While it can be hard for anyone looking for their first job, the situation is also tough for older jobseekers.

Across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.

The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.

Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.

Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.

In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.

The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012.

How Met failed to stop rape-unit detective who abused women

BBC News Tue, 17 Nov 2026 06:02:28 GMT

Contains upsetting scenes.

Warning: Contains details of violence, coercion and sexual abuse - and strong language

The Metropolitan Police repeatedly missed opportunities to stop a predatory detective inspector from sexually exploiting women whose cases he investigated, including one who married him and later died in unexplained circumstances, BBC Panorama can reveal.

Warren Arter used his position - running a unit investigating sexual assaults in south-east London - to target women it was his job to protect.

Two women, speaking out for the first time, have told Panorama how Arter groomed them. One says he raped her.

In the case of his wife, Rebekah, he filmed her being sexually abused and distributed the footage. She died in Barbados two years ago, while on holiday with him. On Sunday, the BBC revealed how he lied about what happened on the Caribbean island.

There were multiple investigations into Arter while he was employed by the Met. Now the former detective who led one of them has told the BBC that senior bosses tried to interfere with his inquiries, despite him having found potential victims.

While Arter was suspended as a result of that investigation, he remained on full pay for seven years - before being sacked in 2023 for drug offences.

The following year, the Met - having learned of his wife's death in Barbados - arrested him on his return to the UK for sexual offences alleged by another woman.

Arter took his own life days later in HMP Wandsworth. Despite the evidence against him, the Met has not reviewed all the cases he handled.

In response to our investigation, the Metropolitan Police has for the first time publicly apologised to the women he abused. It said it was now working to examine Arter's electronic devices to identify if there are further victims and that it encouraged other women to come forward.

Panorama has uncovered several opportunities to stop Arter that were missed by the Met:

This last missed opportunity came after the Casey Review's conclusion that the Met was "institutionally misogynistic", as well as the convictions of rapist and murderer Wayne Couzens, and rapist David Carrick - both Met officers - and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley's promise to "lift the stone" and "tackle everything underneath it".

Panorama can now reveal that 21 potential victims of Arter were identified in an investigation by the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). The Met has not contacted all the women whose cases he investigated during his 20 years as a serving officer.

The upskirting image that was sent in March 2024 to a woman we are calling Layla should have led to Arter's arrest.

Bail conditions or custody would have prevented him from taking his wife, Rebekah, to Barbados.

On 28 June, Arter rang Rebekah's relatives from the island to tell them she had died.

Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship in 2006 when the Met put then-Det Sgt Warren Arter in charge of investigating her former partner.

Arter pursued Rebekah, they began a relationship and he quickly moved in with her.

Her now-adult son, Elliot, says Arter initially made his mum feel "safer" but that his behaviour soon changed.

"He'd say to her: 'Get in the kitchen, make my dinner you slag. Make me a tea you [expletive] bitch,'" Elliot recalls.

Arter would openly watch pornography on his tablet while he was in the living room with her, Elliot says.

He also collected urine from Elliot, claiming he was testing it at the police lab to help the boy's promising football career - but Elliot now suspects it was an effort to hide Arter's drug use.

The inquest into Rebekah's death heard evidence that use of sedatives had become so routine in the home she shared with Arter, that a daily smart-speaker reminder announced "G o'clock" - a reference to the date-rape drug GHB.

In the years before she died, Arter had filmed and distributed videos of his wife being sexually abused. The BBC has seen some of them.

Many show her unconscious or otherwise incapacitated while Arter insults her.

"You should get raped," he says, in one video.

In another, Arter can be heard speaking to a man behind the camera, asking him to be quiet and saying "they go mad otherwise" - suggesting the video was being made for a wider audience.

His crimes were so brazen that he sent abuse videos of Rebekah unsolicited to at least four women he knew.

Two were women whose cases he had investigated - one of them was Layla.

She had met Arter in 2010 after she reported being raped. His exploitation of her continued for more than a decade, up until she reported the upskirting image - which she had deleted - to staff from the IOPC.

Both Layla, and her adult daughter who was with her when she spoke to the IOPC, say she identified the woman in the photo as Rebekah - whom she recognised from previous videos.

The IOPC says the staff member has no record or recollection of being told the identity of the woman in the photo - and it did not have the authority to investigate as Arter was no longer a police officer.

It did, however, tell the Metropolitan Police about the upskirting allegation.

Arter's abuse could have been stopped more than a decade earlier - soon after he had met Rebekah.

He claimed their relationship had begun after a chance meeting on a night out, an account she corroborated, when he was questioned by the IOPC during an investigation started in 2017.

However, Panorama has learned Rebekah was bombarded with more than nine hours of calls from Met phone numbers in the three months following the conclusion of her case in 2006. We also know that Arter searched her name on Met computer systems without any obvious justification.

Officers have faced misconduct proceedings, even prison, for relationships which began in similar circumstances, but at that time Arter was not disciplined.

It is not clear when his bosses found out about the relationship, but some of his colleagues appear to have known early on.

The BBC understands that four officers told the IOPC investigation they believed Arter had met Rebekah on a case. One said they knew Rebekah had been a victim of domestic abuse, but they refused to sign a statement.

The Met told Panorama that the IOPC's subsequent report had found that Arter's colleagues knew of his relationship with Rebekah, but did not know he had met her in the course of his duties, therefore he was not subject to any misconduct proceedings.

None of the various investigations into Arter led to criminal charges before he was arrested in 2024. On one occasion, he even received a payout after being arrested for harassment.

The IOPC has now told the BBC that of 21 possible Arter victims it had identified by 2020, it assessed he had inappropriate contact or relationships with eight of them, including Layla and Rebekah.

Panorama has, however, learned of at least one more alleged victim who says she was groomed and sexually exploited over 12 years.

Former Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Dame Vera Baird, is calling for an investigation by an outside force into all the cases Arter handled throughout his career.

"If a doctor had been found to abuse one person, they would look at all his list from start to finish.

"It's quite outrageous - there will be women living now with trauma imposed by him on them."

When Det Insp Jaysen Veeren tried to investigate Arter a decade ago, he says senior Met bosses tried to interfere with his work.

Veeren was a fast-rising officer in the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards (DPS) - which investigates police misconduct - and says he was warned he would be a "fool" to join the team because of its reputation within the force.

"The DPS is referred to as 'the rats' - you eat your own," he says.

But when, in 2016, he intercepted a Crimestoppers tip complaining about Arter's conduct with victims, he recalls telling his boss: "This is the case that I joined for."

Initially, his investigation was well resourced and he travelled to Australia to interview a woman who said Arter had sex with her after she reported being sexually assaulted as a tourist in London.

Veeren then cold-called other cases.

"We had one victim and, all of a sudden, you've got a second, third," he recalls. "It was quite obvious you're dealing with a predator."

Arter had been able to visit many of the women alone. One woman told Veeren: "He may as well have walked into my house with his [penis] out".

Veeren eventually arrested Arter and suspended him in December 2016 but Arter's phone had been wiped.

He then designed a plan to contact all the women whose cases Arter had investigated, but says he was prevented from doing so and his team encountered "interference" from senior officers outside of the DPS.

Emails seen by the BBC reveal his investigation was likened to a "witch hunt" by a detective chief inspector, who questioned its justification with the Met "haemorrhaging talent". A chief superintendent told Veeren's boss that staff felt the case was a "fishing expedition".

The two senior officers - who have since left the force - told the BBC this was not interference and said they were acting on concerns of colleagues about how the investigation was being carried out.

Veeren says he felt unable to widen his investigation and examine all of Arter's cases.

He referred his case into Arter to the IOPC in the expectation it would do so, and later reported his concerns to the watchdog as part of a wider whistleblowing complaint - alleging corruption within the DPS.

He resigned from the force in 2019 when he discovered none of his allegations would be upheld. The Met says his complaints to the IOPC had either been disproven or not corroborated.

Layla says Arter's abuse has "ruined her life" and she still struggles to leave the house.

Fourteen years before she told the IOPC about Arter's upskirting image, Layla reported being raped in a hotel room by a member of staff.

Arter was put in charge of her case, as the rape unit lead. He immediately began to target her.

Within hours of their first meeting, Arter asked Layla to put her head in his lap and then he stroked her hair, while a PC drove them to a sexual assault referral centre.

There, Arter was found by staff alone in the toilets with her.

A doctor was so alarmed by his behaviour that she reported concerns to the Met about his intimacy with Layla.

Layla has told us that Arter remained present while she had an internal medical examination.

The Met failed to investigate or monitor the detective's ongoing contact with Layla, who at the time was a vulnerable alcoholic.

Arter visited Layla dozens of times over the next few months, she tells us, sexually exploiting her during what he described as "therapy time".

Panorama has learned that Arter told colleagues that Layla was becoming too attached to him.

He was commended for victim care in her case - just as he had been in the domestic abuse case of his future wife, Rebekah.

Even after Arter informed Layla that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) had declined to authorise charges in July 2010, he continued to contact her - helping her with a successful compensation claim under a government-funded scheme.

After Veeren referred his investigation to the IOPC, the watchdog described Layla as having been "groomed" by Arter.

Layla says Arter, who by this time had been suspended, was telling her what to tell investigators. She did not provide them with a statement.

Despite Layla's known vulnerability, and the evidence against Arter, it took three years for a file of evidence about his sexual misconduct to be sent to the CPS, which then declined to pursue criminal charges in 2020.

It was a further three years before Arter appeared at a misconduct hearing - and only then for drug offences.

He was finally dismissed from the Met in 2023 - have received at least £300,000 in pay while suspended. He kept his pension.

However, despite having left the force, a decision to review Arter's alleged sexual misconduct was then made.

In March 2024, IOPC staff visited Layla at home. She revealed Arter had sent her the upskirting image. By this point, she says she had begun to "wake up" to Arter's exploitation of her.

The watchdog told the Met about the illegal image - but the force failed to arrest him.

The Met told Panorama this was because of human error when using a new crime recording system.

On 28 June 2024, Rebekah died in a hotel room in Barbados while on holiday with Arter.

Disturbed by the lies Arter was telling them - his account of what had happened kept changing - her son Elliot and daughter-in-law Lacey went to the couple's house in south-east London.

They say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up.

They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent.

On 2 July, Elliot and Lacey drove to Bexleyheath Police Station - the same station where Arter had worked.

Staff were initially uninterested in Rebekah's death thousands of miles away, say the couple - and it was only when they mentioned Arter's name that officers became interested. "It was like chaos," Lacey says.

The family say they were told the Met was considering sending officers out to Barbados to help the investigation.

However, the BBC has been told that a senior Met boss from its Gold Command group was briefed that evening about the incident, in light of Arter's alleged offending, and a decision was taken not to send officers to the Caribbean island.

The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made.

Later that week, the Met visited Layla and interviewed her about Arter, where she disclosed he had raped her on one occasion and sexually assaulted her on another.

Arter flew back to London from Barbados on 9 July and was arrested at Heathrow Airport, accused of rape, voyeurism and coercive control. He took his own life in prison three days later.

Neither the Met nor the IOPC has ever released their investigation reports into Arter's sexual misconduct - despite Freedom of Information requests by the BBC.

Arter was seen as the star detective in a unit lauded for its results investigating rape and sexual assault.

But the Met has never investigated that unit's "sanction detection rates" - the proportion of reported crimes for which action was taken against suspects.

In 2009, Conservative politician James Cleverly, then a Member of the London Assembly, said the unit had achieved rates of 96%.

This is despite the figure being three times the London average and at a time when some officers were known to be systemically manipulating the recording of offences. The Met says it does not recognise the 96% figure.

Dame Vera says there seems to be many missed opportunities to stop Arter, spanning from 2006 to 2024: "There must have been other people who knew exactly what was going on."

Rebekah's family say the Met should investigate whether other men helped Arter abuse her.

When she died the Met seized electronic devices from the house she had shared with Arter. Elliot says some of those devices have not been analysed in two years.

His solicitor says a public inquiry is needed to reveal the full extent of Arter's offending.

"It's a disgrace for the Metropolitan Police, and it's also a dirty secret - one they want to keep hidden," says Sophie Naftalin.

The Met told Panorama that Arter could have been arrested sooner and it was "deeply sorry" for the harm caused to victims by his repeated exploitation of his position for sexual purposes.

It acknowledged progress with Arter's devices had been slow but said it was now being prioritised, and it encouraged anyone else who believes they were targeted to come forward.

It added that the recording of rape cases was examined nationally in 2014 - and there have been significant changes to the scrutiny of crime figures.

The IOPC says it regretted that its investigation took three years but it was a complex case involving delays out of its control. It added that the allegations were treated "extremely seriously" and resulted in referrals to the CPS.

The CPS says it thoroughly reviewed this evidence but concluded there was no realistic prospect of conviction at that time.

It says it did charge Arter with misconduct in public office before his death in 2024.

In September 2025, the UK coroner in Rebekah's case issued what is known as a prevention of future deaths report.

It said there was a risk that further deaths could occur unless action was taken.

In response, the Met said it had already taken action to improve vetting and to tackle police officers abusing their powers.

The IOPC said information had not been made available to it at the time of a specific risk to Rebekah, and that it had since strengthened its safeguarding procedures.

Elliot says he has spent the past two years trying to get answers.

"I don't think I've grieved yet", he says.

"I don't know what will happen when that day will come."

We now know how radiation destroys electronics devices

New Scientist November 17, 2026

Researchers are gaining a new understanding of exactly how radiation destroys electronics devices. The work is a step towards building more resilient electronics for use in nuclear fusion experiments or in space.

Cristyan Quiñones at North Carolina State University stayed up for nearly three days so he could watch a beam of heavy ions destroy an array of electronics devices. It was a high-stakes experiment: few labs around the world operate heavy ion beams and securing access to run experiments is difficult. But it is only with experiments like this that researchers can systematically study the dangers that electronics devices would encounter on board a satellite or near a nuclear reactor.

In those challenging high-radiation environments, electronics devices can dramatically and rapidly fail during what is called “single-event burnout” (SEB). Thanks to their experiments, Quiñones and his colleagues have now zeroed in on exactly how SEB happens.

Advertisement

Moon bases will need to be 3 metres underground to avoid radiation

The researchers focused on electronics components called diodes that they built from aluminium nitride, a semiconductor made from aluminium and nitrogen. Similar diodes are used to help power electronics devices, and aluminium nitride has been put forward as a promising foundation for the next generation of such power components.

Researchers have also theorised that aluminium nitride is resilient to radiation exposure, which would make it a good choice for use in high-radiation environments such as space. But this idea has not been thoroughly investigated in experiments, says team member Ramón Collazo, also at North Carolina State University.

In the new experiment, which also involved researchers from NASA, energetic ions of silver, gold or the rare earth metal praseodymium hit and entered each aluminium nitride diode, and the researchers tracked how much electric voltage the diode could then sustain before SEB destroyed it.

Through data analysis and computer simulations, they found that each ion caused a disturbance within the diode, which, combined with the voltage, created a localised electric field. At some threshold voltage, that field became strong enough for nearby electrons to flock towards it, and this avalanche of electrons onto the small area led to a miniature explosion.

Microscope images from the experiment clearly showed tiny, melted craters in the aluminium nitride diode where SEB happened in this way. Additionally, comparing aluminium nitride to similar semiconductors, the team determined that it could withstand higher electrical fields before exploding, but relatively low voltages. Such a systematic and careful comparison had not been done before, but will inform how the material is used going forward.

A storm as powerful as the Carrington event of 1859 might cause some issues, says a reader, but modern planes have a lot of safeguards built in. You should be more worried about “superflares”

Understanding SEB is important because it is among the biggest challenges for making electronics reliable in space, says Ronald Schrimpf at Vanderbilt University in Tennessee, who wasn’t involved with the experiment. He says that power systems are often the most vulnerable part of an overall spacecraft, with phenomena like SEB occurring even when there are physical shields to protect electronics, so studying proposed power device materials that are potentially more resilient, like aluminium nitride, is timely. “If your power supply goes down, nothing works, right?” says Schrimpf.

While radiation-resilient electronics are important in nuclear engineering and a variety of other settings, including the technology used in radiation therapy for cancers, they have recently gained more attention because of proposals to put data centres into space. But Schrimpf says that making electronics ready for space is a complex scientific problem that also involves logistical challenges because the facilities for testing electronics materials, such as the ion beam in the new experiment, are scarce. For Collazo, uncovering physical processes such as the electron avalanche in aluminium nitride is key for innovation in this area.

“Cristyan is telling us the physics of what is happening. You can now design the device around it because you know what is actually causing the problem,” he says. The researchers are now working on developing design principles based on what they have learned about SEB so far, says Collazo.

IEEE Transactions on Nuclear Science DOI: 10.1109/TNS.2026.3750781

“The gut microbiome will become part of every person’s medical record”

New Scientist November 17, 2026

For New Scientist’s 70th birthday, I attempted to forecast what the world will be like another 70 years in the future, in the year 2096. I interviewed dozens of experts to inform what I wrote, though of course they did not always agree with me or each other – and the vision of the future I produced is mine alone. Nevertheless, I thought it would be interesting for readers to hear directly from some of the biggest names in science about their hopes and dreams for the end of the century. Here they are in their own words.

“I’d be very excited if we could get to a place where it’s possible to use CRISPR in a preventive fashion. Rather than treating disease after it’s happened, thinking about ways to protect people from Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s or similar diseases. Eliminating or even reducing incidents of these age-associated degenerative disorders would have an enormous impact. It would mean that people are able to continue doing the kind of work that they want to do, and contributing to the economy, to their families, in ways that currently can be limited. As I get older, it sounds very appealing to be able to turn the page and have another chapter that maybe wouldn’t have been possible otherwise.”

“The divide between rich and poor is likely to be ever wider, and the poor will have the problems of lack of water, lack of access to healthcare, lack of access to good food and maybe lack of access to effective vaccines. As we go forward, how has community lasted? How has education lasted? And how has trust lasted? And how does populism and social media play into what you believe? I think we’re going to see dreadful divergences. And with that, of course, you get social unrest and war.”

Advertisement

“When people moved out of manual labour into desk-based jobs, physical activity levels dropped, and we realised that is bad for us – we have to move, we have to exercise for longevity, for our mental health, for lowered risk for a whole bunch of diseases. People brought that into their leisure time. They started going to gyms, they started going to yoga and doing triathlons. I wonder now, if we’re replacing so much of thinking with AI, will we realise the mental consequences of not thinking? What will it do to our levels of happiness, our levels of dementia, our ability to be human? Are we now going to have places people go to use their brain as a muscle?”

“Food will be recognised as biological information, not just fuel. The gut microbiome will become part of every person’s medical record. Maintaining microbial diversity will be considered as important as monitoring blood pressure or cholesterol once was. ⁠Personalised nutrition will replace generic dietary advice, with food recommendations tailored to each person’s microbiome, genetics, metabolism, immune system and lifestyle, and AI acting as a personal nutrition coach. ⁠Most long-term conditions will be prevented or controlled through personalised nutrition and early biological monitoring. ⁠The greatest medical breakthrough is prevention. Instead of asking, ‘How do we treat disease?’, doctors will ask, ‘How do we maintain the biological ecosystem that keeps people healthy?'”

“One of the big questions we haven’t answered is this: what is the minimum gravity required for a child to grow and develop normally? If we discover that we can’t raise children on the moon, then it will always just be a temporary outpost for adults, like Antarctica. And hopefully we’ll have something like the Antarctic Treaty System for the moon, so that, despite our eternally imperfect human greed and short-term thinking and insecurity and selfishness, we can still manage to find a way to settle the moon that is beneficial with long-term human presence.”

Just nine countries back pledge to tackle AI’s environmental footprint

New Scientist November 17, 2026

Only nine countries have signed an international pledge to make AI greener, despite warnings at the COP31 climate summit that the technology’s growing energy demands threaten climate goals.

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge was launched on 16 November at the summit in Turkey. Developed by the summit’s presidency and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), it intends to make AI more sustainable by encouraging cleaner energy use, more efficient data centres and greater transparency about the technology’s environmental footprint.

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

“AI and other frontier technologies are a double-edged sword,” said Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, at a press conference on 16 November. “The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones and put these technologies responsibly to work.”

Advertisement

But Ketan Joshi, an independent analyst researching AI’s climate impacts, questions that analogy. He says it conflates traditional machine learning, already used in applications such as weather forecasting, with energy-intensive generative AI. “You don’t need to have a giant, energy-hungry generative AI chatbot if you want to have better wind forecasting for a wind power developer,” he says.

The initiative comes as AI’s rapid expansion is placing growing pressure on electricity grids. According to the International Energy Agency, electricity consumption from AI-focused data centres increased by 50 per cent in 2025.

Free newsletter

Joshi says there is little evidence that technology companies are building enough renewable energy capacity to meet this growing demand. Even companies that have invested heavily in renewables, such as Amazon and Google, are increasingly turning to fossil fuels to support their rapid expansion, he says.

The only countries to have endorsed the pledge so far are Andorra, Brazil, Colombia, Luxembourg, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Korea, Turkey and Uganda.

The pledge is voluntary, with no binding targets for cutting emissions or reducing energy consumption. It sets out four areas for action, including increasing the use of low- and zero-emission energy to power AI infrastructure, improving energy and water efficiency, and measuring the environmental impacts of AI systems. It also calls for greater financial and technical support to help developing countries use AI to tackle climate change.

However, the agreement leaves considerable room for interpretation. The call for using “low- and zero-emission energy”, for example, allows continued reliance on fossil gas rather than committing to renewable electricity.

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

Countries can also choose additional commitments, such as requiring AI companies to disclose their energy consumption and environmental impacts, or introducing sustainability requirements for data centres.

“I’m surprised that more countries haven’t signed up, given the pledge’s limited demands,” says Joshi. “It’s not a pledge that really strikes at the heart of the problem.” He argues that voluntary promises are unlikely to be sufficient without restrictions on the expansion of data centres and stronger AI regulation.

COP31 President Murat Kurum defended the initiative, saying the rapid growth of AI must be “powered and deployed responsibly, and used for the benefit of climate actions”. The ITU says progress on the pledge will be reviewed at annual UN climate summits until 2030, starting at COP32 next year.

Joshi fears the pledge could provide cover for continued expansion via fossil fuel sources. “I think we’re going to be going into an era of a return to greenwashing, a return to sort of empty promises,” he says. “What we really need is stronger and stricter regulation.”

Plans to rely on carbon removal tech spark debate at COP31

New Scientist November 17, 2026

The world is certain to overshoot 1.5°C of global warming. The question now being discussed at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is whether we can bring temperatures back down again – and what it would take to do so.

If we remove more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than we emit, global temperatures should eventually begin to fall. The draft negotiating text welcomes efforts to accelerate the development and deployment of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) and carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) technologies. It calls for global carbon capture to be scaled up to at least 500 million tonnes of CO₂ by 2035, with a higher ambition of 1.3 to 2.5 gigatonnes annually, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors.

Can we really reverse global warming after overshooting 1.5°C?

But these technologies have never been deployed at anything approaching that scale, and many environmentalists are concerned that promoting them will undermine efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

Advertisement

CDR approaches range from planting trees to extracting CO₂ directly from the air and burying it underground. Some involve growing crops that absorb carbon, burning them to produce energy and capturing the resulting emissions. Others aim to increase the amount of CO₂ absorbed by the oceans. CCUS involves technologies that capture CO₂ emissions from industrial facilities and power plants, which can either be used in industrial processes or products or stored underground.

Aakaluk Adrienne Blatchford, an Iñupiaq and Yupik advocate from Alaska and an observer at COP31, says fossil fuel companies have long promoted carbon removal technologies at COP summits as a way of addressing climate change while continuing to extract oil and gas.

Free newsletter

There is evidence that the fossil fuel industry has helped shape the scientific discussion around these technologies. An investigation by ProPublica and Drilled found that oil and gas companies have funded climate research at prestigious US universities for over 30 years, supporting work on technologies that could allow continued fossil fuel use. Representatives from these industries have found ways to participate in climate negotiations at COP meetings.

At this year’s summit, Blatchford has noticed a particularly visible presence of carbon brokers. “When you walk around the pavilions and you see the amount of carbon brokers, it becomes clear how much commercial interest surrounds the proposed solutions,” she says.

An analysis released on 16 November by the Center for International Environmental Law reveals that a record 700 CCUS lobbyists are at COP31, including 45 who are part of national delegations, potentially granting them privileged access to the talks. The CCS lobbyist presence at the talks has never been higher: it exceeds the combined total of delegates from the smallest 50 national delegations, according to the analysis.

Whether references to these technologies will survive negotiations over the final COP31 agreement remains uncertain. According to Blatchford, Brazil, Denmark, the EU, Saudi Arabia and the UK are the key players pushing for CDR. Small island developing states, Germany, Kenya and Mexico seem to object to relying on these technologies, she says. Her main concern is that the promise to remove carbon later could undermine efforts to stop emitting it now. “CDR is just another way for them to keep doing business as usual and put us on the back burner,” she says.

One of Earth’s most vital carbon sinks is faltering. Can we save it?

The scientific evidence supporting CDR technologies is growing but not yet robust. “Questions remain about how much additional atmospheric CO₂ might be removed and stored durably, and what ecological harms might arise,” says James Kerry, a marine biologist at conservation group OceanCare.

“We need to recognise that some proposed approaches may face scientific and practical limitations that field research cannot overcome,” says Kerry. For example, a recent study on ocean fertilisation argues that even large experiments won’t resolve the uncertainties surrounding the net atmospheric carbon removal and downstream ecological impacts associated with this technology. “This is precisely why a precautionary approach is so important. Further research does not necessarily mean that fundamental uncertainties will be resolved, nor that a proposed intervention will ultimately prove feasible or desirable,” says Kerry.

Climate scenarios assessed by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change envisage storing up to 6 gigatonnes of CO₂ underground each year by the middle of the century. But the amount of CO₂ we can currently remove from the atmosphere and permanently store is less than the amount a single, large fossil fuel power plant emits in a year.

Spreading crushed rock on farms could absorb 1 billion tonnes of CO2

Kwami Dodzi Kpondzo, a climate campaigner based in Togo and an observer at COP31, is particularly concerned about bioenergy with carbon capture and storage. This involves growing plants, burning them for energy and capturing the CO₂ for underground storage. To remove substantial amounts of carbon, vast areas could be needed to grow the biomass. “They need a huge amount of land,” says Kpondzo. “It means community displacement, forest grabs and livelihood destruction.”

Converting agricultural land into biomass plantations, he says, could reduce food security, while irrigation and fertiliser used to grow the biomass could put further pressure on water supplies and ecosystems, and lead to biodiversity loss.

Blatchford raises similar concerns about the potential impact on Indigenous peoples, particularly where carbon removal projects compete for land and water. “We still practise our way of life and we still steward our homelands in a way that we always have,” she says. None of this means reversing global warming is physically impossible. But it does mean that the amount of warming we could eventually reverse depends heavily on how quickly emissions fall in the first place. “There are a lot of things that we could stop doing to drop emissions,” says Blatchford. “First and foremost, stop burning fossil fuels.”

How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096

New Scientist November 16, 2026

How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist, I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct.

I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek.

I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections, which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece.

Advertisement

The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now, so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, published by the Financial Times under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today.

I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to consider how climate change will interact with the diseases and medical conditions we face. Meanwhile, many of the people I spoke to hadn’t deeply considered how AI would affect the evolution of their chosen discipline.

We’ve loved sci-fi at New Scientist for the past 70 years, but which novels got the future right? From Neuromancer to The Handmaid’s Tale, Emily H. Wilson picks the most prescient reads of the past seven decades

In weaving all this together, one of the most surprising things I arrived at was the idea of expanding the legal concept of personhood. Looking at how our attitudes towards both animals and artificial intelligence are changing today, it seemed to me that this was a possibility, so I created the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood. Its existence in the story had a number of interesting downstream effects, and I kept finding different ways for non-human people to influence the world. Again, this is a big bet, but I think not an unreasonable one.

One thing I couldn’t escape from in writing this piece is the idea that I and probably all of the people I interviewed won’t be around to see what comes to pass. I would be 110 years old in 2096 – not impossible, especially given the advances in medicine I describe in the piece, but still unlikely. In some ways, 70 years from now is the perfect amount of time to forecast the future, being just outside most adults’ expected lifespan. We can never know what will really happen – we can only imagine.

Nuclear bomb in space would disable 98 per cent of satellites within a week

New Scientist November 16, 2026

A single nuclear explosion in space would wipe out 98 per cent of satellites within a week, sending vital technology around the world into disarray from which it would take years to recover, warn experts.

Zachary Petersen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and his colleagues modelled the effect of a 1 megaton explosion 500 kilometres above the South Atlantic. They found that an initial spike of X-rays from the blast was damaging, but it wasn’t the most disruptive part: electrons released by radioactive fission would become trapped in Earth’s magnetic field, exposing satellites to a kind of artificial radiation belt, over and over again.

This level of exposure would take out 98 per cent of satellites within one week. And while many spacecraft use specialised computer chips that are more resistant to radiation, the researchers found that even when they altered their simulations to assume that satellites were three times more resilient to radiation damage, the effects were still disastrous, with 97 per cent still failing within two weeks.

Advertisement

UK military taps up astronomers to spot snooping foreign satellites

Worryingly, such explosions aren’t without precedent. The US detonated a 1.4 megaton nuclear bomb at an altitude of 400 km in 1962. Satellites were disrupted by the blast, but Earth was orbited by only a relatively small number of devices at the time – humans have now launched around 25,000 objects into space, many of which still orbit the planet. Global navigation systems like GPS, internet connections and weather forecasts rely on these satellites and the data they provide.

A nuclear explosion in space would probably have long-lasting repercussions, not only because satellites would need to be replaced, but because there would be an estimated 20 collisions within two years as broken satellites drifted aimlessly. Those collisions present a risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical scenario in which debris hits other satellites, creating more debris and a chain reaction of destruction that would make orbit lethal to future launches for decades, or even longer.

The Outer Space Treaty now bans the launch of nuclear weapons into space, and all major spacefaring nations are party to it. But tensions remain. In 2024 a vote was raised at the UN to reaffirm commitment to the rule, which Russia vetoed. Earlier that year, the US had warned that Russia plans to launch a space weapon with possible nuclear capabilities.

Free newsletter

Petersen and his colleagues didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, but Craig Underwood at the University of Surrey, UK, says the consequences of losing so many of our satellites would be catastrophic for society because we are so dependent on space technology.

“The recent low-Earth orbit mega constellations [like Starlink] would be particularly affected,” says Underwood. “During the Cold War, much thought was given to protecting critical space systems and our societies were much less dependent on electronic technology. I suspect that since the 1990s, less attention has been paid to the prospect of having to survive a nuclear conflict. Our civil defence infrastructure has been dismantled, and society is much more vulnerable.”

“While individual satellites can, in principle, be replaced relatively quickly, recovery would not be straightforward. New satellites would have to be launched into an environment still affected by elevated radiation levels and increased debris, potentially limiting their operational lifetime and effectiveness. As a result, restoring orbital infrastructure could take years,” says Chantal Cappelletti at the University of Nottingham, UK. “The result would not be an immediate collapse of modern society, but rather a prolonged degradation of many services that we now take for granted. Recovery would likely require years of rebuilding orbital infrastructure while managing elevated radiation and debris hazards.”

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2611.09827

New Scientist November 16, 2026

The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University.

But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information.

Advertisement

SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike

Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says.

The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington.

This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants.

The findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao, a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.”

Free newsletter

But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns.

Yury Dvorkin at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland adds that the analysis is relatively “coarse”, not accounting for factors such as how network constraints impact grid power emissions. “They ignore a lot of nuance,” he says.

“There are definitely a lot of assumptions baked in [to the study],” says Dominici. She wants to see data centre developers and operators be more transparent about the environmental impacts and energy use of their facilities. “My frustration is that as we are moving forward, this narrative is not informed by rigorous scientific data, and data-driven decision making,” she says.

Public resistance to data centres has increased sharply in the US over the past year, with a recent poll suggesting 76 per cent of Americans would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.

At the same time, the industry is developing rapidly, with many new facilities now reliant on private gas power generation rather than grid electricity, which increases their climate impact.

Hundreds of millions of people live close enough to data centres used to power AI to feel warmer average temperatures in their local area

Hyperscale data centres reduce the cost of computing power to companies by harnessing economies of scale to run their servers as efficiently as possible. But the larger the data centre, the greater the impact on local communities.

Alongside high levels of power demand, hyperscale data centres also require large volumes of water to cool their servers, and take up a lot of land. In Utah, a plan to build a data centre that would cover land twice the size of Manhattan and almost double the state’s annual peak electricity demand has triggered fierce backlash from residents.

“People might notice increasing land prices, electricity prices, water prices,” says de Vries-Gao. “They might notice an increase in air pollution, waste pollution. This is why people are ultimately protesting. The hyperscale data centres are probably the most painful type of facility simply because of the sheer size of them.”
