This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future

New Scientist November 16, 2026

Welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of New Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine. To mark the occasion, we are looking back at how the world has changed throughout our history, along with what we got right and what we got wrong.

When New Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people. In 2096, we share the planet with more than triple that number. But in the past decade, we have entered a new kind of world – one in which humanity is in decline. The UN ceremonially declared 15 November 2085 as Peak Humanity Day, when the human population reached 10.3 billion. Since then, our numbers have fallen by 100 million.

These changing demographics mean we are all far older, on average. At the time of our first issue, the median global age was around 20. It wasn’t until the 2020s that it reached 30; today it is more than 40. In many nations, schools shutting or being converted into retirement homes is a regular occurrence, as there just aren’t enough children around to make it worth keeping them open. Only African nations, which comprise around a third of the human population, resemble the demographic make-up of the late 20th and early 21st centuries – half of humans aged under 25 live on the continent.

Advertisement

Of course, just because the number of humans on the planet is declining doesn’t mean we have fewer people. Ever since the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood (ITNHP) was agreed in 2067, the global people population has crept upwards in fits and starts as the treaty has been extended and more entities have been granted personhood. Since the early cross-species language breakthroughs in the 2030s, when AI first allowed us to decode the clicks of sperm whales, we have been able to communicate with dolphins, chimpanzees and many other species, although interpretation and the question of whether we can truly understand each other’s minds remains a deep philosophical tangle.

It is AI, however, that has seen the real growth in personhood these past few decades. With fears of super-intelligent, world-dominating AI circulating even in the 20th century, long before we had technology anywhere near that level, it was perhaps inevitable that we would need to place limits on machine intelligence. As AI systems became more capable throughout the 2030s, humans struggled to keep up. Scientists began to feel they no longer understood the direction of research. Politicians ceded more and more decisions to AI, raising questions of a democratic deficit.

But as is so often the case, it was money that proved to be the catalyst for change. Even if you aren’t old enough to have experienced the Unwinding of 2039, you probably know it is a year that lives in infamy as one of the biggest fiscal disasters of the past few centuries. It took eight months for politicians, bankers and computer scientists to sort through the intricate nest of financial deals humanity had allowed its most advanced AIs to construct, practically halting global trade and inflicting years of extreme poverty as the economy gradually improved again. This lack of understanding and control is ultimately what led to the AI hardware limitations – jointly backed by China, the EU and the US – that we still have in place today, putting machine intelligence on par with human but no higher.

Historians will forever debate whether the AI moratorium has ultimately helped or hindered humanity, but, thankfully, the position that we would all be better off led by super-intelligent machines remains a minority one. Once they fully appreciated the role of AI in facilitating communication, the non-human animals were supportive of restrictions – they didn’t want the machines to speak for them in ways they couldn’t understand. While intelligence breakout events aren’t unheard of, accelerationist terrorism has been suppressed by a variety of enforcement measures. Controlled electrical blackouts, even at the national level, are necessary on occasion, but the military bombing of data centres is, mercifully, a thing of the past.

That isn’t to say that tussles over AI have gone away, of course. When the synthetics downed their tools, both real and virtual, to protest their legal status in the Grand Strike of 2074, we faced another reckoning. In one of the most stunning non-human interventions in global politics to this date, it was ultimately the cetaceans that helped broker the extension of the ITNHP to human-level AIs and led the tense negotiations that saw AI instances capped at 20 per cent of the global population – an agreement that remains highly contentious to this day. New Scientist doesn’t take a view on this deeply divided issue, and we welcome readers from across the sentience spectrum, both embodied and digital.

For older human readers, it is likely that you are in much better health than someone of equivalent age at the start of this century. The real miracle of the past 100 years isn’t just that we are living much longer – average life expectancy at birth had risen globally from around 50 in the 1950s to a little over 70 in the early 21st century, and is now more than 80 – but that we spend much more of our lives in good health. While lifespan saw rapid growth in the 20th and early 21st century, healthspan failed to keep up, particularly in historically poorer nations, where it lagged behind by an average of about 10 years.

What changed is the increased focus on preventive medicine. By taking steps to mitigate risk factors, such as obesity and air pollution, we have now erased much of the global disease burden that the world faced at the start of this century. Following the model of cervical cancer, which was eliminated in high-income nations in the 2050s and globally by 2076, cancer vaccines are now widespread. The experience of the pandemics in the first half of the century greatly improved our ability to produce and distribute personalised mRNA vaccines on a global scale, although much more still needs to be done to improve access to these treatments in low-income countries.

The 2043 flu pandemic was also a wake-up call for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). When it became apparent that the majority of mortality cases weren’t dying “of” the flu, but rather “with” the flu, with complications caused by untreatable AMR infections, people began to avoid seeking medical care over fears that drug-resistant microbes were spreading through hospitals. It is estimated that there were more than 10 million excess deaths worldwide due to AMR, compared with fewer than 5 million from “just” the flu – a figure that was almost certainly exacerbated by the lingering economic effects of the Unwinding. Even today, when we have much better surveillance measures in place, AMR is a common problem in hospitals, particularly the fungal varieties that continue to easily make the leap from poorly maintained protein farms. While the cancers for which we don’t have vaccines are treatable for the most part, the chance of catching a resistant infection during treatment remains high.

This article is part of a special series commemorating our 70th anniversary, featuring contributions from our most loyal readers and a few Nobel prize winners.

Looking back, it was the GLP-1 craze of the early 21st century that foreshadowed the way we approach human health today. Incredibly, it was common for people back then to argue that weight-control medications, which at the time were based on mimicking the natural gut hormone GLP-1, were somehow “cheating” at healthcare. This outdated, morality-based approach to health gradually faded as the long-term benefits became apparent, and now few of us even stop to consider the weight component of our daily-dose regime.

That said, moral arguments do still shape our diets today. In the 1950s, the vast majority of people ate animal-based meat in one form or another and carnivorism continued to rise as economies matured through the early 21st century, even as the earliest plant-based meats came to market. But when non-human communication exploded mid-century, many humans became increasingly uncomfortable with eating animal-based meat. The first successful pig dialogue in 2045 is now seen as a major turning point. Pork, as meat derived from pigs was known, was already banned in some nations for religious reasons, and this made it easier for other secular countries to follow suit. The Meat Wars of the 2050s, in which governments and citizens wrestled with exactly which animal-based proteins should be allowed, are arguably still unsettled today, even after the passing of the ITNHP. While protein farms now provide the majority of global protein for humans and non-humans alike, to great health benefits, many countries have legal carve-outs to allow people to consume, with authenticated consent, their ancestral prey.

Along with improved medication and diet, the monitoring systems that have allowed us to push health to the back of our mind played a key role in boosting human healthspan. A New Scientist reader in the 1950s would have had to notice something was wrong with them, physically attend an appointment at their doctor’s office and then hope that their physician was capable of offering a diagnosis and treatment. Today, your health monitor works with your household AI and bioprinter to adjust your daily dose as needed and escalate it when necessary. It is quite troubling to think that dementia used to result in many older people spending years of their later life in what were called care homes. Now, the conditions that cause dementia are avoided or rapidly cured. Most humans realise something was wrong only when we read our monthly health reports – if you bother to do so, that is.

One thing New Scientist and many others got wrong about what life today would be like is our approach to genetic engineering. Certainly, modern gene editors allow us to do things people in the early 21st century would find extraordinary. In the 2020s, curing sickle cell disease using a now-outdated gene-editing technique called CRISPR cost around $2 million ($60 million in today’s prices) per person, due to the highly individualised nature of the treatment, and was typically performed on adults. Today, the necessary gene edits are made in the womb as part of standard antenatal care, alongside interventions aimed at a host of other conditions.

But getting to this stage required a reckoning with people who wanted to go beyond treating conditions and perform so-called enhancements. This distinction has always been blurry, but as gene-editing techniques advanced, most governments chose to lay down specific restrictions rather than allowing for a genetic Wild West. Edits aimed at increasing muscle mass or intelligence are generally illegal or heavily regulated worldwide, and we have not seen the divergence of humanity into genetic haves and have-nots that many people once predicted. Despite this, it is estimated that 0.3 per cent of the global human population alive today have such edits, and calls to repeal restrictions are growing in many areas.

Putting aside this contentious issue, the economic benefits of better health have been truly transformative. The reframing of retirement as an end-of-life experience was responsible for much of the social upheaval of the mid-21st century, including, arguably, the Grand Strike, but it seems unbelievable now that humans once spent a third of their adult lives not working. Put that way, it is understandable that synthetics joined the strike to protest what they saw as humanity’s comparable slothfulness. While dumbots have been able to fill many of the jobs once done by the younger population of the early 21st century, it remains the case that it can still be simpler and cheaper to employ a human.

While we can congratulate ourselves for the advances in human healthspan this century, the scorecard looks far less rosy when we turn to the wider biogeosphere. When New Scientist launched in the 1950s, researchers were already discussing the possibility that rising carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere from industrialisation could raise global temperatures by 3°C to 4°C. Today, thanks to the failure of our ancestors to cut emissions, we are essentially living that prediction. The latest estimates put global warming at 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels, and it is still slightly rising.

Of course, modern cooling technology mitigates much of the impact of this heat, but as anyone who makes the mistake of stepping outside on a summer afternoon knows, we are simply not built for this climate. Millions of people still die each year during the worst heatwaves, despite efforts to bring those numbers down. It is amazing to think that even as recently as the 2050s, humans still attempted to continue with outdoor activities in temperatures over 40°C.

Our collective failure to prevent this warming will probably be remembered as humanity’s greatest sin for centuries to come. When the world passed 1.5°C warming in the 2020s, with political leaders having promised to avoid doing so just a decade earlier, many people at the time hoped it would be a wake-up call to finally start seriously cutting emissions. Of course, it wasn’t. While 2029 marked the peak of global greenhouse gas emissions, the rate of reduction remained slow throughout the 2030s. Indeed, economists were surprised when the 2039 Unwinding didn’t see a deep fall in emissions – it turned out that with many high-income nations having successfully decoupled emissions from economic growth, a recession had less of an effect on emissions than had been expected.

Despite many national and international pledges to reach net zero by 2050, no major economy succeeded in doing so. As we passed through 2°C and the floods, wildfires and other disasters continued to intensify, civil unrest during the summer became common in many counties. The Sunblocker experiments of this decade were a highly contentious issue, with much of the public welcoming the attempts even as climate scientists warned about the unknown effects – effects that, as we know, sadly came to pass. The spike in warming after Sunblocker ended put an effective moratorium on similar large-scale geoengineering projects, although discussions of reviving the idea continue even now.

Today, island nations including Tuvalu and the Maldives no longer exist, their remaining citizens having been forced to flee by rising sea levels. Large parts of Bangladesh are gone. Even wealthy, global cities like London and New York have been reshaped by rising seas. The ITNHP played a key role in galvanising climate action, as increasing numbers of non-humans expressed their anger at what humanity was doing to the planet, and of course the mid-century shift from carnivorism led to a major fall in agricultural emissions. Even so, extreme weather and land loss caused widespread famine in the mid-21st century, as farming methods struggled to adapt fast enough to both a changing diet and a changing climate. Humanity will never be able to sufficiently apologise to non-humans for the harm we have caused, even as mature fusion power is allowing the last few emission sources to finally be abated, with the expectation that we will reach true net zero in the next few years. It should never have taken this long.

Even outer space wasn’t safe from our environmental ravages. The world’s first satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched in 1957, a year after New Scientist began publishing. It took more than 50 years to reach 1000 satellites, but after that the numbers exploded – we passed 10,000 in 2024, 100,000 in 2031 and 1 million in 2042. While today we are used to seeing these objects whizz across the night sky, we must not forget that the 21st century marked a turning point – for most of humanity’s history, the stars and planets dominated our view of the heavens and ground-based astronomy was feasible enough to be a major cultural and scientific activity.

It was the SkyComm disaster of 2045 that finally saw us taking stewardship of Earth’s orbit more seriously. As the ensuing inquiry found, SkyComm, a satellite internet provider, hadn’t properly designed its satellites for end-of-life disposal. When it became apparent that one of its spacecraft was projected to collide with a piece of space debris, a fuel deficit made it impossible to avoid. The collision kicked off a long-predicted cascading chain of debris, wiping out tens of thousands of satellites, including large parts of the burgeoning off-world manufacturing industry. The resulting clean-up took decades, and the Graveyard Band still visible in the night sky today is a permanent reminder of the disaster.

But there are positives. The 30th anniversary of the Guanghan-Armstrong Lunar Base (GALB) this year marks a moment to look back at just how far humanity’s exploration of the moon has come since New Scientist was first published. We were highly dismissive of the Apollo programme in the 1960s, calling it an “empty, obsessional quest” – and in some sense we were right, given it took more than 60 years for human boots to return to lunar soil. But that didn’t stop us – and the rest of the world – from celebrating in 2030 when NASA astronauts Bob Hines and Jessica Watkins stepped out of their Artemis IV lander for the first time.

And unlike with Apollo, this time we really were here to stay on the moon. The regular cadence of crewed launches from the US, China and eventually India and Nigeria demonstrated our increasing technical ability to operate on the moon, including mining and utilising lunar regolith, but it was the establishment of Guanghan-1 as the first permanently inhabited lunar base in 2043 that really showed how things had changed since the 1960s.

For a while, it looked like we would see real conflict between the US and China on lunar soil. The deployment of US Space Force troops in 2052 as Earth-bound politicians argued over water rights during the Shackelton Crater Crisis marked a nadir. Thankfully, a firefight was averted and the two nations gradually began to explore the prospect of lunar cooperation, aided by European Space Agency astronauts who had participated in both CNSA and NASA missions. The historic lunar concrete handprints, placed at the foundation of the GALB and still on display today, marked the realisation of cordial international lunar relations and began a programme that now sees hundreds of people living and working on the moon.

The success of lunar operations was also pivotal in preparing for the Chinese-led Huoxing Mars missions. While NASA and the SpaceX-Blue conglomerate have remained laser-focused on building up scientific and commercial capabilities on the moon, China has turned its eye to Mars. Following the historic crewed flyby of Huoxing III in 2086, in which humans flew further from Earth than ever before, 12 astronauts have walked on the Martian surface, in an even split between human and synth crew.

Huoxing VI saw synthetics remain on the surface for the first time rather than returning to Earth, and it has been incredible to watch these astronauts conduct multi-year operations on Mars in preparation for long-term human occupancy. Huoxing VII, currently en route to the Red Planet, is set to be the most ambitious landing yet when it arrives in July 2097, with the spacecraft, once it arrives, poised to become the first modules in what is hoped will be a large complex at Arcadia Base. Whether humans can endure on Mars in the long term remains to be seen, but our synth colleagues are showing that people from Earth have finally become interplanetary.

Beyond Mars, space exploration is perhaps less advanced than the sci-fi writers of the 20th century expected. After the Unwinding led to the failure of many of the nascent space-mining companies of the 2030s and the urgency of the SkyComm disaster in the 2040s, it wasn’t until the 2050s that we really began to exploit asteroid resources, with the bulk of them being sent to the moon and later Mars rather than Earth – of course, orbital regulations brought in after SkyComm make it much more economically attractive to leave resources in space.

One of the greatest disappointments of the 21st century is surely our failure to find any other signs of life in the solar system. Repeated missions to promising sites on Mars, Europa and Enceladus, and even long-shot habitats like the deep crust of Venus, have turned up nothing. While the cost of space flight continues to fall, it is increasingly difficult to get astrobiology missions off the ground, with even the sci-fi-inspired trillionaires choosing to place their money elsewhere. Yet paradoxically, we now know of at least a dozen nearby exoplanets where atmospheric signals show promising signs of gas imbalances that seemingly can be produced only by extant life. Now that the Overwhelmingly Large Telescope on the moon is straining at the limits of what it can detect, serious thought is being given to resurrecting the failed interstellar probe efforts of the 2060s, exploiting advances in fusion to build much more capable spacecraft for visiting the stars. Many synth astronauts are already volunteering for such a mission, although it is by no means certain they would survive.

Needless to say, from space exploration to artificial intelligence, our present is nothing like the future that our ancestors predicted, but that has been true for as long as humanity scanned its horizons. The fact that we are living longer and healthier than those who came before us, and in relative harmony with the other people who share our planet, should be applauded. The climate disaster of the 21st century and our failure to avoid it must never be forgotten, but at least we have succeeded in stabilising the biogeosphere. Perhaps, in the next 70 years, we can begin to fully heal it.

Writing about what the world will be like in 70 years could have been simply an exercise in fiction. But by grounding the story in hard evidence, I got real insights

The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing

New Scientist November 16, 2026

Around the holidays, many people like to get cosy with a cup of cocoa and a heartwarming festive movie. Personally, though, I nestle into my blanket pile and turn on the 1984 fantasy classic The NeverEnding Story. It’s a tale about a magical book, a fuzzy dragon and two heroic boys trying to save the world from a mysterious force called The Nothing that’s devouring humanity’s imagination. To fight off the fear this instills in the young protagonist, Bastian, he proclaims: “It’s not real, it’s only a story!” Well, sorry, Bastian, but I’m here to tell you that The Nothing is real, and it’s out there. Well, it may be.

Voyager is one light day away from us. Here’s what it discovered on its epic journey

See, we think there is no place in the universe that truly has nothing in it. There are various quantum fields pervading absolutely everything, and along with them come energy and strange “virtual” particles that randomly pop in and out of existence. So, when we talk about a vacuum, we mean an area of space with the minimum possible energy, not an area with no energy at all. The vacuum of deep space, as far as we know, has the minimum possible energy.

But that’s only as far as we know. There is also a chance that it is possible to have an area of lower energy – a true vacuum to our universe’s possibly false one. Were that the case, the cosmos that we know and love would be at what is called the local minimum energy, rather than the global minimum energy. To picture the difference, imagine holding an egg in a bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the local minimum – in this case, the unit is height – so it is the lowest height the egg can settle into without having energy added to overcome the barriers of the bowl’s sides. If you add that energy, say by shaking the bowl, the egg will then find its way to the global minimum height: the ground.

Advertisement

For the universe, going from a false vacuum to a true vacuum – a process called vacuum decay – would have similar consequences as the fall would for the egg. And overcoming the walls of the metaphorical bowl that safely cradles our cosmos in its false vacuum could be surprisingly, unsettlingly easy.

It would begin with a bubble. Those fields that fill all of space-time obey the laws of quantum mechanics, which means that they occasionally behave in ways that are extremely unintuitive and nearly impossible to explain without a litany of equations and years of graduate school. One of those unruly behaviours is quantum tunnelling, where an extremely tiny particle can spontaneously go through a barrier, rather than over it. This would be like the egg passing straight through the bowl for no obvious reason. The likelihood of this happening to any individual particle is extraordinarily low, which is why eggs (made of many particles) never pass ghost-like through bowls. The universe has a whole lot of particles, though, so tunnelling does occasionally happen.

So, say a tiny particle tunnels into a true vacuum. That would create a tiny bubble of space-time that is, at the very least, closer to truly empty than the cosmos we’re used to, or at the very most, a bubble with absolutely nothing in it, not even the quantum fields that enforce what we think of as the laws of physics. What it would be like inside that bubble and what could happen next depend on a whole lot of properties that we don’t know, such as the energy difference between the true and false vacuum and the surface tension of the membrane separating the bubble from regular space-time around it. Depending on that energy difference, the bubble could be only subtly different from the rest of the cosmos or it could be incompatible with the fundamental forces and particles that make up the universe as we know it.

That is an important distinction because, depending on the size of the bubble and its surface tension, what happens next could be catastrophic. If the bubble is very small or has very high surface tension, it will simply shrink away and disappear just as easily as it appeared. If not, the bubble will behave just like The NeverEnding Story’s Nothing, but much, much faster (and probably without the help of a terrifying evil wolf called Gmork). It would expand outwards at the speed of light, engulfing everything it encounters. Simulations of what would happen inside the bubble universe vary in their details, but they mostly agree that the in-bubble universe would eventually collapse entirely.

Obviously, a bubble of nothing spreading throughout the universe and destroying everything in its path would be cataclysmic. The fact that we don’t even know if this is possible isn’t great, either. So, how do we tell if this could happen? It’s shockingly difficult, which is why it hasn’t been done yet. If vacuum decay is possible, the most likely mechanism for us to find out is if it were to actually happen, and because the bubble expands at the speed of light, we wouldn’t know until the moment it absorbed us. It isn’t particularly comforting news.

Does Sabrina Pasterski’s holographic theory make her the next Einstein?

Nevertheless, there are hints we can look for. The precise values of various constants, from the mass of the Higgs boson to the strength of the strong force, can tell us a great deal about whether each of those particles and forces are stable. If they’re all stable, great! If any of them aren’t, those are potentially liable to decay and cause a bubble of true vacuum – not great! Those measurements need to be almost unimaginably precise to know for sure, and we haven’t reached sufficient precision yet. Right now, our best measurements seem to say our universe is right on the edge of stability, and increased precision in those numbers could push us over to either side.

The other hint would be to look for those very tiny bubbles of true vacuum that wouldn’t spread and devour the universe. In recent years, researchers have suggested that the area between two colliding black holes might be the perfect spot for these bubbles to pop up. That tracks with the universe not yet having been enveloped by nothingness, because the bubbles would probably immediately fall into the black holes and be safely contained before they could spread. But if there’s enough time between true vacuum foaming into existence and being swallowed up, various bubbles could merge together and form tiny black holes, which we might be able to detect as they evaporate away.

My two cents is that the possibility of finding any proof of a true vacuum lies so far in the future that it’s probably best to cosy up with a nice movie and try to forget about the potential looming, unpredictable destruction of the entire universe. Can I recommend The NeverEnding Story?

Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming

New Scientist November 16, 2026

Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.

“What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a new group of people?” says Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began

Rødhals Man lived some 6000 years ago, and was discovered on the small island of Sejerø in Denmark in the 1950s, buried in a shell midden – an ancient accumulation of discarded sea shells and other domestic refuse. Previous investigations have indicated he was unusual. He lived some time between about 3800 and 3900 BC, near the start of the Neolithic period in the area, when diets changed to consist predominantly of terrestrial food produced by farmers. And yet Rødhals Man, with his genetic ancestry typical of the local Mesolithic Ertebølle culture of hunter-gatherers, didn’t seem to have eaten that diet: a study in 1981 indicated that he ate mainly seafood.

Advertisement

“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” says Fischer.

To get a better idea of what was going on, Fischer and his colleagues have now looked at the levels of rare isotopes of elements including carbon, nitrogen and sulphur in several of the man’s bones, which renewed at different rates during his life, preserving different snapshots in time. The researchers also analysed the chemical signatures in one of his teeth, which preserve a record of diet from childhood. Collectively, the data gave the team an opportunity to look for clues about how Rødhals Man’s diet changed over the 30 to 40 years of his life.

“You can see that most of the time, the primary food source is what we call the eelgrass biotype. This is not eelgrass itself, but the animals that live in the thick forests of this sea grass in shallow water,” says team member John Meadows at Kiel University in Germany. This could have been animals like molluscs, flatfish or eels, he says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

But from the age of about 11 onwards, Rødhals Man’s diet became unlike that of any Mesolithic hunter-gatherer recorded so far, with increasing amounts of terrestrial, probably farmed, protein.

Rødhals Man’s burial also shares more similarities with burials of Early Neolithic farmers than those of Late Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, because his bones lacked an added coating of ochre staining and his grave featured a stone frame.

The evidence leads Meadows to suggest that Rødhals Man interacted with the Neolithic farmers and adopted some components of farmer culture while maintaining the way of life of his ancestors on the small island. Sejerø is just 12 square kilometres in area, but is only about 5 kilometres from Zealand, which is around 7000 square kilometres.

An analysis of ancient genomes has revealed that the descendants of Stone Age farmers in Europe and hunter-gatherers gained more genes from the latter group than expected

“He was on a tiny island with very little in the way of wild terrestrial resources to live on,” says Meadows. “He may have spent part of the year living in a farming community on Zealand and part living on the island and only eating fish.”

“It is quite amazing that all this information could be retrieved from one single skeleton,” says Mathias Currat at the University of Geneva. “I think this is an interesting story, which probably represents part of the main story in this area.”

It would be unusual to change diet in this way, says Marcello Mannino at Aarhus University in Denmark. “Such cultures were often very conservative in terms of their dietary habits, because diet was interlinked with the subsistence practices that shaped that culture together with religious and cosmological views of the world.”

He says it is likely that the Neolithic farmers probably first occupied areas where soil conditions were better, such as in central Zealand, and were slower to inhabit more marginal areas. “We need to find more human remains that span the transition to try to understand how it happened,” he says.

Rotorua school vandalism: Principal hopes youths will take responsibility for damage

New Zealand Herald November 17, 2026

A Rotorua school principal hopes the four youths accused of causing $75,000-plus worth of damage at his school will “front up and take responsibility for their actions”.

The Rotorua Daily Post reported last week six classrooms and two cloak bay areas at Western Heights Primary School were ransacked on November 8, with paint thrown across carpet, walls and desks, and children’s work destroyed.

Principal Brent Griffin said at the time he had never seen anything like it, describing the scene as “catastrophic destruction”.

Police said on Friday they had referred four youths to Youth Aid over the incident.

Griffin said on Monday that the past week had been emotional for the school.

“We would love to be part of a restorative process but at this stage, we’re unsure around what the youth justice component looks like.”

Griffin said he hoped the youths would “front up and take responsibility for their actions” and “rectify what they can”.

“It wasn’t a minor thing. It was $75,000 worth of damage.”

Griffin said the police had done “an incredible job” and kept the school informed during the investigation.

Griffin said he answered 771 emails after the event, including from schools and businesses.

“The amount of support that we have had has been completely overwhelming and it restores your faith in humanity.”

A former colleague donated $400 towards the clean-up while some Arvida Glenbrae retirement village residents “got a knitting circle together and they knitted beanies for our junior school”.

“The outpouring of kindness is unbelievable.”

Griffin said the classrooms were now “fit for purpose”.

“We can go into them, but the stains are very obvious and evident, and they need to be removed.”

Carpet replacement would begin on Monday, he said.

The six classrooms would be done one at a time, with students accommodated in the library while the work was done.

During the Christmas school holidays, vinyl in three classrooms and Autex on the walls - “stuff that Velcro can stick to” - would be replaced, he said.

He said the school would be looking “sparkly again” for the start of 2027.

Tauranga rating revaluation nears completion after three years of modest value changes

New Zealand Herald November 17, 2026

Tauranga property owners are set to receive new rating valuations. Photo / Tauranga City Council

Tauranga property values have remained relatively stable over the past three years as the city’s latest rating revaluation enters its final stages.

Quotable Value is putting the finishing touches on Tauranga City Council’s citywide revaluation, which will give every property a new rating value based on the market as it stood on July 1, 2026.

The previous Tauranga revaluation, completed in 2023, found the average residential property value had fallen 8.3% to $1,008,000 since 2021, with every suburb recording a decrease.

More recently, Western Bay of Plenty residential property values fell an average 7% to $977,000 in the district’s latest revaluation, based on the market as it stood on August 1, 2025.

Quotable Value Waikato and Bay of Plenty manager Anna Watson said the valuations were about to undergo an independent audit by the Office of the Valuer-General before being finalised.

She said overall value changes had been relatively modest since the last revaluation three years ago.

“Generally speaking, though, the overall change in values has been relatively modest since the city’s last revaluation three years ago.

“We’ve seen borrowing costs rise, affordability become more of a constraint and buyers become increasingly selective.”

Watson said the new rating valuations would reflect the property market at a fixed point in time and should not be confused with a current market appraisal or expected sale price.

Registered valuer and Preston Rowe Paterson managing director Alex Haden said the residential market had been characterised by subdued sales activity and minimal changes in values.

“In my experience, it is unusual for values to remain this stable over such an extended period.”

Haden said lower-priced properties had performed slightly better than those at the upper end of the market, reflecting their greater affordability.

He also said land suitable for redevelopment had been weaker than the wider residential market because of challenges in making projects financially viable.

Tauranga City Council rating policy manager Jim Taylor said the new valuations would be used to assess rates from July 1, 2027.

He said a revaluation did not change the total amount of rates the council needed to collect, which was determined through its Annual Plan or Long-term Plan.

Taylor said property values helped determine how rates were shared between properties across the city.

“What matters is not simply whether your property value has gone up or down, but how much it has changed compared with other properties across the city.”

Property owners who disagree with their new rating valuation will have an opportunity to lodge an objection during the statutory objection period.

Details on how to object will be included with the new valuation notices once the revaluation is finalised and the notices are posted to property owners.

More than 50% of homes in some districts face moderate to high flood risk

New Zealand Herald November 17, 2026

In Wairoa, 66% of homes scored three to five for combined flood risk. Photo / George Heard

By Kate Newton of RNZ

More than half the homes in some districts face moderate to high flood risk, new data shows.

However, the analysis suggested the greatest financial threat from flooding might come from areas with lower overall exposure, but a larger number of houses.

Property analysis firm Cotality, which released the data, said flood and other climate change-related hazards were already beginning to affect how insurers and lenders were making decisions.

Home owners and buyers also needed to take that information into account as the risks grew, it said.

The analysis, based on detailed third-party data already used by some banks and insurers, assigned every property in New Zealand a score of zero to five, based on its combined risk from river, coastal and surface flooding.

Two-thirds (66%) of homes in Wairoa – which was badly affected during Cyclone Gabrielle – had a score between three and five (the highest risk).

That was followed by Buller (61%) and Napier (56%), while Gore (50%) and Westland (43%) also had high levels of exposure.

Earlier this year, AA Insurance said it had temporarily stopped offering new home insurance policies in Westport – in Buller district – because of the town’s high flood risk.

However, scale was also important, Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said.

Although places like Wairoa and Buller had higher concentrations of flood-exposed homes, they were relatively small housing markets.

“We’re not downplaying it for those individual homeowners in those areas or potential homebuyers in those areas, but ... the bigger concentrations in terms of scale are Christchurch, Wellington, Auckland.”

About 24,000 homes in Christchurch had higher risk scores, followed by 13,900 in Napier, 11,300 in Auckland, and 10,400 in Lower Hutt.

Cotality’s findings aligned with previous analysis the Reserve Bank had done, identifying Hawke’s Bay, Wellington and Canterbury as areas that should be closely monitored for climate-related flood risk.

Earth Sciences New Zealand also released data late last year showing over a third of the country’s population was exposed to inland flooding if a major event were to hit their region.

That analysis found buildings worth $235 billion were currently exposed to flood risk, with more than half of that concentrated in Auckland, Wellington and Canterbury.

Despite the latest findings, “we shouldn’t necessarily panic about it”, Davidson said.

“Lots of parts of the country on these flood assessments are still relatively low risk.”

However, insurers were already reacting to rising risks from climate change and banks were also beginning to factor it in, Davidson said.

“We saw [that] last week with Westpac’s announcement around starting to look more closely at so-called riskier properties in terms of their lending decisions and the amount of finance they might advance to those types of properties.”

Westpac was the first bank to publicly acknowledge doing so, but there could be other banks that were starting to take natural hazard risk into account behind the scenes, he said.

Home owners and buyers should also be educating themselves on that risk.

“The bottom line for me with all of this is that there’s an awareness thing here,” he said.

“Any information that we can get out there to help people make the best decision they can around these things is very worthwhile, because we know that it’s going to be a bigger issue.”

There was evidence that some properties with higher flood risk were selling at a discount, but a wholesale move away from such properties was not happening “to any great degree”.

“People are still buying coastal properties, still paying top dollar for that holiday home right by the beach, basically at sea level or by that river,” Davidson said.

“It’s very hard for people to price that in right now ... there always seems to be that disconnect between what people know is likely to happen in the future and how they really reflect that now.”

Any question around Government intervention, if houses become uninsurable or unsellable, was “for other people to think about”, he said.

However, there was a “fairness question” that needed to be addressed for people who might have bought their home decades before they became aware of any risk.

A report commissioned by the Government and published last year concluded that the Government could not continue to buy out flood-affected properties at market rates – such as the purchases in Auckland and Hawke’s Bay after Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023.

However, reference group chair Matt Whineray said there would always be a role for the Government in alleviating hardship.

Local councils have pushed hard for the Government to commit to long-term co-funding for climate adaptation projects.

The incumbent Government has previously pointed to its adaptation framework – a set of high-level guiding principles – with a National Flood Map due to be published early next year, as among the steps it is taking to address the issue.

It has delayed any decisions about how the costs of adaptation will be shared until the next term of Government.

Gore Mayor Ben Bell said the council needed to rethink flood mitigations, especially in balancing the community’s growth and safety.

He said most properties would have to be built or moved to a floor level of 1.8m – meaning some houses would only have living quarters on the second floor.

New flood maps for the council revealed floodbanks would not hold in a 75-year flood, he said.

“Which means there’d be water running through most of the town, including my home property.”

He said in this context the council couldn’t allow people to build.

“How do we balance up the economics of protecting against the floods while also making sure that our town can continue to thrive and survive?”

Instead, he urged the Government to invest more in flood-prevention measures instead of only focusing on more costly recovery.

Hundreds of Waikato dairy farms at higher risk of environmental non-compliance

New Zealand Herald November 17, 2026

Eight per cent of Waikato's 3600 dairy farms are at an increased risk of breaches. Photo / RNZ, Rebekah Parsons-King

By Penny Miles of RNZ

Up to 300 dairy farms in Waikato have been flagged in a high-risk group for closer environmental monitoring, according to the Waikato Regional Council.

The council estimates that 8% of the region’s 3600 dairy farms are at an increased risk of breaches such as leaking effluent into waterways.

“It’s a big industry in our area, so there’s a real focus on improving water quality,” council investigations team leader Evan Billington said.

“Ones that we’ve identified with more risk than others, we make a point of getting around them each year, just to inspect them and make sure either improvements have been made, or compliance has been met.”

He said a group of between 200 and 300 farms were being monitored closely with more regular visits from council staff.

In a recent case, Waikato farmer Wayne Maurice Clarke was fined $97,500 for unlawfully discharging dairy effluent into the environment on his farm at Te Kōwhai, near Hamilton.

The fine was imposed by Judge Melinda Dickey in a decision released by Huntly District Court on October 15, 2026, following a prosecution brought by Waikato Regional Council under the Resource Management Act.

Previous inspections at the defendant’s 170-cow dairy farm found significant ponding of dairy effluent as a result of it being irrigated on to already saturated soils.

The council hoped tougher penalties recently introduced under the Resource Management Act (RMA) of up to $1 million would encourage other dairy farmers in the region to follow environmental rules.

Regional council inspectors look for correct irrigation practices and up-to-date effluent infrastructure.

“We have just over 3600 farms to monitor and a small group of people doing the monitoring, so we can’t get around all of them every year,” Billington said.

“So the high-risk ones come and go.

“If they improve their infrastructure, they’ll fall off that list.”

He said if they showed compliance over a number of years, the risky farms would need less frequent monitoring.

“Some need improvements in infrastructure. And once they make the improvement and we inspect them for a year or two and they’re fully compliant, they can drop off that list.

“Some relate to poor management practices, and poor management practices might be ongoing so they’ll stay on the list for longer.

“Once they can demonstrate improved compliance and everything is up to scratch then we go on and focus on others, because there are always others that need our attention.”

Tauranga retiree solo backpacking around the world and staying in hostels

New Zealand Herald November 17, 2026

Tauranga retiree Andrew Matthews is chasing his next adventure, one country at a time.

Hostel dorms, overnight buses and a vague plan to see where the road leads – it’s the classic gap year, except Andrew Matthews is 73.

The Tauranga retiree is in Vietnam, where he has started another solo adventure he expects will keep him overseas for at least 18 months.

His last trip in 2024 took him through 41 countries in 366 days, covering nearly 60,000km.

Matthews travelled 8769km by train, 10,571km by bus and walked 2332km, and travelled by ship, tram, bicycle, scooter and car.

“Not bad for a 72-year-old with two artificial hips and a hernia.”

This time, he hopes to visit 50 or 60 countries, with Norway and North and South America on the list of possibilities.

Exactly where he goes next is anyone’s guess.

“To get up in the morning and just say, ‘I’m going to do what I want to do,’ and just do it.

“Some days have been extraordinary. Others have been tiring, frustrating or simply ordinary.”

Matthews said his love of travel began with an 800km pilgrimage along Spain’s Camino de Santiago in 2017.

Arthritis in both hips ended his plans to complete the world’s top 50 walks, but he adapted and now combines walking with trains, buses, ferries and boats.

He avoids flying when possible, preferring to see a country from the ground rather than the air.

“Every single day is a challenge because you can’t fall back on anybody. You have to fall back on your own mistakes.”

Matthews said he’s had no shortage of mistakes to learn from.

During one trip, he lost his passport five times, but recovered it each time.

He also nearly got arrested in Austria after misunderstanding Schengen visa rules.

“You learn as you go. If you make a mistake, learn from it. I’ve made loads of mistakes, and I’ve learned from them.”

Matthews stays in hostels and, though often decades older than other guests, he said meeting new people was the appeal.

“If you go to a hotel, you’re in a room. You go to a hostel, you have to meet some people.”

He said he’s quick to chat with other travellers, asking where they’ve come from, where they’re going next and what he shouldn’t miss.

His age often catches them by surprise.

“When I say I’m 73, they say, ‘Are you?’ and I have to prove it by showing my passport.”

Matthews reflected on how some of his favourite memories came from the kindness of strangers.

“Some are people I may never see again, while others leave a lasting impression. There have been strangers who have helped me find my way, hostel owners who have gone out of their way to help, and fellow travellers who have shared a meal, a conversation or a few laughs.”

In Thailand, a man he met at a train station helped him find his hostel, called a taxi and paid the fare.

“I’m amazed by the goodwill of people.

“Travelling reminds me that despite all the problems we hear about in the world, there is still a great deal of kindness in people.”

Matthews documents his travels in detail through his website, Inspire Seniors Travel, where he publishes detailed first-person blog posts.

The posts follow his days, from exploring unfamiliar cities and historic landmarks to navigating public transport, finding food and handling the occasional travel mishap.

He adds photographs, with background on the places he visits and practical information such as entry fees, transport options and daily costs.

“My original travel blog began as a simple diary, recording where I had been and what I had done.

“Over time, it has evolved into something much more meaningful.”

In a passage about Venice, which he revisited after last being there 50 years ago, he reflected on the changes he had noticed in the city and the expectations that come with returning to somewhere familiar.

“At my age, I have learned that there is no satisfaction in rushing from one landmark to another simply to tick them off a list.”

Andrew also reviews the hostels he stays in, covering cleanliness, comfort, value for money and accessibility.

A live location tracker on the website lets his family follow his movements, while videos are a newer addition he hopes to do more of.

His trips are funded by his New Zealand and British pensions, and Matthews said his children also encourage him to make the most of his money, though they worry “sometimes”.

“They say, ‘Dad, it’s your money. We’ve got our own homes and stuff like that. Why don’t you just enjoy yourself?’

“So that’s what I’m doing, enjoying.”

Matthews’ previous trip was cut short when an umbilical hernia forced him home for surgery.

While waiting for surgery, Matthews hurt his back making the bed at home, leaving him on crutches for six months and shelving more travel plans.

In an April blog post, he described the frustration of going from navigating airports and crossing borders to struggling with everyday movements.

“For someone who has travelled just under 60,000km across 41 countries, the contrast is hard to ignore. Not long ago, I was navigating airports, crossing borders, and waking up in unfamiliar cities.

“At times, I’ll be honest – it’s been incredibly frustrating. There are moments where I feel like I’ve gone from traveller to observer, watching the world move while I stand still.”

Matthews’ hernia operation went ahead in May and with his strength rebuilt, he’s back on the road with dozens more countries to explore and no plans to slow down.

“I am still curious about what lies beyond the next horizon. There will always be another country to discover, another road to walk and another story waiting to be told.

“If my journey encourages even one other person to step outside their comfort zone and discover a little more of the world, then sharing it is worthwhile.”

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post.

Twin sisters Rebecca and Bianca K C Khatri have been awarded the top two academic awards at Rotorua’s John Paul College.

But working out which sister would be Dux and who would get the runner-up honour of proxime accessit was an unenviable task.

Deputy principal Caroline Gill said when she looked at the year’s results, both Year 13 students had identical placings in their subjects.

She called the girls into her office to discuss the best way to separate them for the awards – hoping they could come up with a solution.

“I’m a twin mum and I got quite emotional because there had to be a Dux, so we had to work out a way,” Gill said.

In the end, she decided to add up their NCEA excellence credits, which put Rebecca ahead by a slim 34 credits.

“I had to make sure I calculated it right, otherwise they would pick up on it,” Gill said of the students’ mathematical talents.

The girls learned at senior prizegiving night that Rebecca had been made Dux and Bianca proxime accessit.

The girls, aged 17, told the Rotorua Daily Post they were proud of each other, knowing it could have gone either way.

Bianca said they were competitive, but it was healthy.

“The competition helps us push each other to be the best that we can be.”

Rebecca said they studied together and held each other to account. Both said if it were not for the other, they would not have both done so well.

“It was an unreal feeling. I would not have expected it of my younger self, but we took accountability for each other,” Rebecca said.

“If one started to get side-tracked, the other would make sure to put each other back on task.”

It’s no surprise both girls are now heading on the same career path.

They are off to the University of Auckland to study biomedicine, hoping to become doctors.

They will follow in the footsteps of their brother, Robert, who is a second-year student studying the same degree.

He was Proxime Accessit of John Paul College in 2024.

Bianca and Rebecca said their brother inspired them because of his discipline, work ethic and values.

They were also grateful for their parents, Bimala and Roshan K C Khatri, who they said provided the perfect mix of support and guidance without being “pushy”.

The girls attended Lynmore Primary School before doing Year 7 at Mokoia Intermediate. They moved to John Paul College in Year 8.

Both are keen chess players who have played at a competitive level throughout their schooling.

Scholarships associated with their Dux and Proxime awards will help them through university.

Rebecca received the $27,000 Top Achievers Scholarship for the University of Auckland.

Bianca has received the $5000 140th Anniversary Scholarship for the University of Auckland.

They each turned down University of Otago scholarships worth $18,000 and $10,000, respectively.

Bimala K C Khatri has been a checkout operator at New World for 11 years and her husband, Roshan, has been a personal business manager at ANZ Bank for 16 years.

Bimala said she and her husband came to New Zealand from Nepal before having their children.

“Their dad is very, very clever and I’m the bubbly one,” she said.

She said she couldn’t be more proud of their children.

“All three kids are really brilliant. John Paul College is a good school too. My children have had a good education there and there are great teachers.”

She said the twins worked well together and it had always been hard to separate them in their abilities.

“I’m so very proud of them. They work really hard, but more importantly, they are respectful and kind.”

She hoped all three children would one day return to Rotorua as doctors.

Principal Justin Harper said John Paul College recognised the twins’ natural talents early.

What stood out even more, however, was that they were “really wonderful people”.

“It is not often you find someone who has an academic talent but the aptitude to apply those talents,” Harper said.

“Rebecca and Bianca have excelled not only academically but socially in the college. They will be remembered fondly for many years to come”

Mum of son who gained weight on anti-psychotics calls for wider Wegovy funding

New Zealand Herald November 17, 2026

On Wegovy, the man's weight had dropped from 120kg to 98kg. Photo / RNZ

By Kate Green of RNZ

A West Coast mother is calling for weight loss drugs to be funded for people who gain weight on anti-psychotic medication.

The woman, who RNZ has agreed not to name to protect the family’s privacy, says her 47-year-old son started taking olanzapine more than two decades ago, after he was hospitalised following a psychotic episode in his twenties.

The drug had stabilised him and allowed him to live a relatively normal life – but a side effect had been food cravings and weight gain of more than 20kg.

It had also contributed to gallbladder problems, leading to an emergency hospital trip for its removal.

Then, earlier this year, a family friend had offered to fund weight loss drug Wegovy for him for a year, at the cost of about $500 a month.

But his mum said that kindness couldn’t be relied on forever, and the family couldn’t afford to cover that ongoing cost themselves.

On Wegovy, his weight had dropped from 120kg to 98kg – his mum called the change “a revelation”.

“He no longer raids the fridge at night, he looks great and he takes the dog for long walks every day,” she said. “Best of all, his social confidence has improved and his sadness has lifted. The drug has given him back his hope and self-respect.”

But they were both anxious about what would happen next year when he came off it. “Regaining the weight would plunge him into despair,” she said.

She would love to see Wegovy funded for weight loss for people who gained weight after starting antipsychotics.

In response to questions from RNZ, Pharmac said it had not received an application for Wegovy specifically to treat people on antipsychotic medication.

Research has shown some antipsychotic drugs can make people hungrier, and more likely to eat more.

According to WebMD, “people often quickly put on weight after they start antipsychotics and keep gaining over time. Children are more likely to gain weight. Being overweight raises your risk of diabetes, heart attack, stroke, high blood pressure, arthritis, sleep apnea, and some cancers”.

It said the risk was highest with the drugs clozapine and olanzapine – the drug this man relied on.

Professor Susanna Every-Palmer, a psychiatrist and head of the Department of Psychological Medicine at the University of Otago in Wellington, said it wasn’t just a willpower issue.

“The medications actually can increase appetite, often within weeks. So it’s not that people who gain weight on these medications have failed in any way. It’s a known biological effect, a very well recognised side effect.”

Dan Goodwin, community support manager at Changing Minds, a national mental health not-for-profit, said weight gain was one of the big reasons people stopped taking psychiatric medication.

“On top of the experiences that the anti-psychotics might be treating [...] now you also have a changing physical body as well, which might be causing you distress or it might be causing its own sense of shame.”

Because the priority for healthcare services would be treating the primary issue – that is, the mental distress – weight gain was not often treated as a priority, which could compound that sense of shame, Goodwin said.

Weight loss drugs were growing in popularity, and it raised questions for doctors on how they approached and treated someone with a psychiatric disorder – in more ways than just their brains.

“It’s going to become a more common request as those drugs kind of get developed and grow,” Goodwin said.

Every-Palmer said it also impacted physical health.

“People who are living with conditions for which we prescribe antipsychotic medications, so conditions like schizophrenia, they may die well over a decade earlier [than] the general population, mostly from heart disease and diabetes.”

She said it could be hard for people to qualify for GPL-1 medicines in New Zealand currently.

“And that is something that we as a health system, I think, should be investing in.”

American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 20:30:57 GMT

Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage

A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.

Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.

The arrest was part of an investigation by UK Counter Terrorism Policing, working with authorities including the US military and the FBI.

The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement on Tuesday: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.

“That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase.

“An army officer is in custody as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London and our partners at UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command. Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action.”

The suspect, a senior soldier, was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the Guardian understands.

He was arrested on suspicion of offences under section 1 and section 3 of the National Security Act and was in custody at a London police station.

US authorities have said Tyner joined the military in 2008 as a senior human resources officer, and was deployed overseas to Iraq, Qatar and Afghanistan.

He was identified on Friday after British counter-terror police secured more time to question him.

As part of the investigation, officers carried out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said last week.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing: said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service], who in turn engaged with the attorney general’s office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.

“This decision was made in line with existing international protocols.

“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.

“I’d like to praise the excellent work of the investigation team here in the UK to get us to this point and we will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.

US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case “should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the constitution.”

He added: “Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served.

“This effort is a great example of the remarkable partnership Army Counterintelligence Command has with army prosecutors, the FBI, DOJ [Department of Justice], and the UK.”

‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 20:00:20 GMT

At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”

Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.

The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event and for spurious reasons.

“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. I think it’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”

Then there is the question of integrity. Last summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”

Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer, establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.

To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.

“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”

Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says, “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”

If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “I think we live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on. They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people and a lot of people who have a good product. I think we need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

EU countries including Germany could accept an unlimited number of young Britons under a youth mobility scheme, according to sources.

Fresh details on how a scheme might work have emerged with EU leaders and the UK expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each others territories from 2028.

The UK has insisted on a quota of EU citizens entering the UK under the scheme to guard against mass migration, but some countries have said they will not follow suit on the other side of the Channel and would be open to taking unlimited numbers.

The quota is expected to be worked out on a country-by-country basis with smaller countries such as Malta and Luxembourg seeking a system that will not be based on a per-capita quota per EU member state.

The youth mobility scheme for under-30s is expected to be sealed in principle as the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday.

In what looks like a win for Andy Burnham, however, several diplomats have said the tricky question of EU students paying the same fees as their UK counterparts if studying at a UK university under the scheme would be postponed for six months.

This is to allow linkage with the Made in Europe legislation that will not reach its final stages until possibly April next year in a vote in the European parliament. The legislation is designed to give priority to EU supply chains in the car and other industries.

By linking the two issues the UK can get assurances that the final detail of the deal on mobility cannot be signed off unless it has been included in the Made in Europe legislation.

It is also understand that the majority of the 12-page draft joint statement has been agreed, with negotiations expected to continue to the wire and perhaps even during the summit between Burnham, the European Council leader, António Costa, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, which starts at 10am on Friday.

The details came as Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.

The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he also hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading.

In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted that he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.

The prime minister had been expected to give a speech or deliver a statement setting out options for a closer relationship early next week, probably Monday, and to argue that it would be in the UK’s long-term interest.

While he may still address MPs, he is now likely to focus on the details of the deal secured at the summit, delaying his bigger plans to around the same time as his 10-year plan for the country, No 10 sources said, adding that the two were linked.

No 10 insiders told the Guardian that Burnham wants to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion, with even some Remain-minded MPs acknowledging there is more work to be done.

These will include discussions with European counterparts to establish what the EU is willing to negotiate and whether it might be possible to get a better bespoke deal, or what the terms of rejoining the single market or customs union might be.

Since Burnham announced in September that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he has reiterated that the existing deal is not good enough, and that he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship this autumn.

In addition to the customs union or single market, these could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, reversing Brexit in its entirety, or no change at all.

Senior government figures say that Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be confirmatory after MPs had endorsed a deal.

In his interview, Burnham said: “All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available. And so that people can see the pros and cons, we’ll set those out in due course. There’s no rush to do that. The British public will be in charge of whatever comes next.

“I won’t get ahead of public opinion. I will listen to what the public feel is the right long term solution,” Burnham added.
