Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 19:47:31 GMT

He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.

What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.

It is nothing less, Milburn suggests boldly, than rescuing an abandoned generation and giving their lives “shape and meaning”. It is about strategy, planning – making sure all kids are school ready by the age of five, as well as job ready by 18 – but it is also across the finer detail: he asks bosses at one point, for example, if they might at least bother to reply to young people’s job applications.

It is not dull, as employment policy goes: this is Milburn possibly at the peak of his persuasive powers, throwing it all at one last big legacy-defining job, joined by an advisory committee packed with old Blair-era policy comrades. This is not your modest, average independent policy review, he suggests at one stage, but “a broad-based manifesto for change” on a generational scale. It’s not a plan, he says, so much as a 278-page settlement, a recasting of the state, laws, and institutions.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

For the most part Milburn is well tuned to Labour voter ears. There are promises of full employment for the young and promises to change the way the labour market operates. There are calls to double the number of youth apprenticeships and roll out a dynamic new cohort of specialist career advisers. There is no shyness about the central role of the state in fixing markets that have let down young people so terribly.

Nor are the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to blame for their predicament, he concludes. This is not a snowflake generation, lazy and unambitious. Milburn acknowledges the central negative presence in their lives of poverty, inequality, intergenerational unfairness, the scourge of mental ill health and disability discrimination.

Which is why Milburn’s proposed welfare changes lurk like a dark heart. We have been told for months now that this is a government that, unlike its predecessor, does not do “crude cuts”. But this is a plan that proposes a young, out of work disability claimant on a £2,000 benefit income has that replaced with £339 a month. This, it concludes, is better for their longer-term life chances.

For Milburn it is all about the guarantee, the promise of work and training and “the gift of a future”. It’s short-term pain for long-term gain. Not that they have much choice: young people will be expected to work or train. If they don’t engage they will have their benefits sanctioned. The report picks at welfare reform like an itch, obsessively; given half a chance it says it would love to overhaul everyone else’s benefits too. At one point it describes disability benefits as the “weakest link in the chain”. About half of Neets do not claim any benefits at all.

Within 10 years, the plan would strip £3.6bn from young people’s net disability benefits. Past experience, says the poverty charity the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, shows disability benefit cuts deepen poverty, worsen mental health and do not increase the likelihood of finding a job. It is unclear if Labour backbenchers will revolt on benefits as they did last year, but they too may ask themselves why Milburn offers jobs and skills support at the expense of financial security. Why cannot it be both?

Using law to try to silence abuse victims is ‘ultimate form of gaslighting’, MPs told

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 19:36:11 GMT

Woman sued by alleged rapist tells justice committee that Slapp lawsuits present perpetrator as victim of wrongdoing

Attempts by perpetrators and alleged perpetrators of sexual abuse to silence their victims using the law are “the ultimate form of gaslighting”, MPs have heard.

Verity Nevitt, a co-founder of the Gemini Project, a survivor-led nonprofit organisation, told the House of Commons justice committee about the ordeal of being sued by the man she and her sister, Lucy, respectively accused of sexual abuse and rape.

At Tuesday’s session, held after the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault and the allegations of improper behaviour against David Walliams, which he denies, MPs heard that wealthy and powerful men silenced victims through injunctions, non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) and strategic lawsuits against public participation, known as Slapps. The latter are used to harass or intimidate opponents speaking out on matters of public interest.

Nevitt said: “When you experience rape or sexual assault, choice is taken from you, and being subject to a Slapp replicates those dynamics in the sense that you have no choice but to be subject to it … and I think that also means that these cases are quite attractive to someone who is coercive, controlling.

“I think Slapps allow a flipping of the script where the perpetrator is presented as a victim of wrongdoing, and then the victim/survivor is presented as the aggressor by being made a defendant. It’s an egregious reversal of reality, and it’s the ultimate form of gaslighting.”

Nevitt and her sister reported the man to police but, when the case was dropped, they decided to name him on social media to warn others, which led to him suing them.

They eventually reached an out-of-court agreement and, having waived their right to anonymity, the sisters could talk about the case without naming him.

Nevitt told MPs that in the case brought against her and her sister the truth “didn’t matter at all” – it was all about the costs. She said that after the first hearing, the solicitor took the sisters aside and told them they would have to find £100,000 to make it to the next hearing.

Jennifer Robinson, a barrister and co-author of Silenced Women: Why the Law Fails Women and How to Fight Back, told MPs that survivors who were sued faced huge costs.

“The chilling effect is actually much broader than simply women themselves who want to speak out,” she said. “It’s also having a chilling effect on journalists’ willingness and their newspapers’ willingness to report their stories, which is not in the public interest. We can’t tackle violence against women if we can’t talk about it.”

Harriet Wistrich, the chief executive of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said there was a good argument for “very severe cost capping” in such cases.

Rupert Cowper-Coles, a partner and head of media at RPC solicitors, told the committee the UK was a “major outlier amongst western democracies” because it did not have a general anti-Slapp law but one that only covered disclosures relating to economic crime.

Robinson said: “Why are we privileging the protection of public interest speech on economic crimes and not for crimes against women in the context of the crisis of violence against women that we have in society?”

Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 19:30:32 GMT

Youth unemployment review risks clash with unions and Labour left over workers’ rights and minimum wage

Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s youth unemployment report?

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights.

The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a “watershed moment” for young people.

But while ministers embraced his central recommendation of cutting benefit and sickness payments to pay for more concerted employment support, his recommendations on workers’ rights, national insurance and the minimum wage pose potentially awkward dilemmas for the government.

In the 278-page report, Milburn called for ministers to cut national insurance for companies that hire young workers, to apply a “cautionary principle” when abolishing exploitative zero-hours contracts and to slow the rise in the youth rates of the minimum wage.

“A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government: employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so,” he wrote. “That is the give and the get.”

Trade unions warned against some of his proposals, despite broadly welcoming Milburn’s push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to “crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full” in the face of lobbying from business groups.

“The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people’s employment prospects. It’s for the birds,” he said.

Burnham welcomed Milburn’s report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a “comprehensive vision” for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work.

He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver “a new settlement for young people”.

Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.

It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.

The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people’s disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim.

People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.

The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.

Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.

The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office.

Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals.

Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo.”

But while Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn’s recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts.

McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.”

On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying “caution” when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate.

And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: “There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences. I believe this is likely to be the case.”

Business leaders welcomed the recommendations, in particular the call to backtrack on Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions with a tax cut for under-25s, starting in retail and hospitality.

Maxine Bligh, the interim chief executive of the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, said: “Tackling the Neet [not in education, employment or training] crisis gives ministers the perfect opportunity to reconsider a guaranteed hours gamble that risks costing jobs and damaging the chances of young people accessing the labour market.”

Industry chiefs have intensified their lobbying against the government’s Employment Rights Act, with bosses finding a warm reception from Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said Labour was pressing ahead with an “unemployment act” that would hit youth jobs. “You cannot solve a youth jobs emergency without jobs, and this government has spent two years destroying them.”

Government analysis published this year showed estimated costs to employers could range from £350m to £2.9bn a year, with a central estimate of £1.1bn.

But unions and charities urged Burnham not to water down the plans, arguing that low-paid and insecure work had contributed significantly to Britain’s youth jobs crisis.

Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, said “crucial policies” on workers’ rights needed to be retained. “We are clear that the government must ensure that employment is fairly paid and secure, with workers being treated with dignity and respect.”

Banning zero-hours contracts was a promise at the heart of Labour’s election manifesto. Under Starmer, however, elements of the party’s plan to “make work pay” were watered down amid opposition from business.

Clare McNeil, the chief executive of the charity Timewise, said: “Where we disagree with Alan Milburn is in any suggestion that the new responsibilities in the Employment Rights Bill will stop employers hiring.”

Allies of the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, who had championed the government’s zero-hours plan as Starmer’s deputy, insisted that her proposals would not discourage employers from hiring young people. The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 19:08:54 GMT

This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

While cuts to some benefits are part of the package, this doesn’t look like a rerun of the Starmer government’s ignominious failure to cut £5bn from the welfare bill. Its fiscal impact claims to be largely neutral, with spending on employment support offset by savings. Higher workforce participation is not expected to significantly reduce working-age benefits for a decade. Instead, the plan is to face down demands by the Tories and Reform UK to cut welfare spending and a poisonous narrative about workshy “snowflakes”, by persuading voters that what young adults need is help. Of the hundreds of young people he met, said Mr Milburn, “I have not found a single one who wanted to be Neet”.

A Youth Opportunity Service will be the new system’s “engine room”, offering wraparound support, including with health issues, to those who need it. Legislation will ensure that access to an adviser, and a job or training place, are guaranteed. Mayors will be responsible for delivery, making the new Neets service a core element of the devolution project.

Mr Milburn says that jobs must be created for the scheme to succeed, and draws unfavourable comparisons between the UK and countries that spend more on employment support relative to benefits. While he stops short of demanding that employer national insurance rises should be reversed, there is implied criticism of earlier decisions taken without sufficient regard to their impact. Presumably, his unit will take charge of a proposed “youth opportunity test”, whereby every new policy is examined from this perspective.

Ministers should expect the principle of age-linked entitlements to be challenged. Mr Milburn makes a good case for treating young adults without significant work experience or higher education as a distinct group. But 18- to 24-year-olds are adults, and there are legitimate objections to drawing lines in this way. Nor can people be expected to take it on trust that the new opportunities and allowances will be an adequate replacement for what they lose when they are moved off existing benefits. The Department for Work and Pensions has frequently failed to assess need fairly in the past. And while the proposal for waiting-time limits for mental health support is welcome, it points to a challenging reordering of NHS priorities.

This is not the only commitment that will be difficult to deliver. The need for cross-department cooperation will stretch Whitehall to its limits. But the emphasis on young people’s long-term prospects is positive, as is the decisive rejection of welfare cuts to bolster fiscal credibility. Youth participation is an overlooked form of inclusion. Increasing it is a sound principle for a Labour government.

The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 19:08:05 GMT

Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

“The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis, ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation.

With US interest rates rising, the cost of borrowing dollars for developing nations is seeing more cash paid to creditors. Between 2021 and 2024, the debt of such countries increased by just 2%, but debt repayments rose by 28%. The UN’s latest figures show that in the global south, excluding China, external interest costs reached $125bn in 2024. The UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, was right when he said that developing countries faced a “downward loop”, where climate risks raise borrowing costs, disasters increase debt levels and mounting repayments leave governments with little to invest in resilience. This makes them more vulnerable to future shocks. Climate finance, he argues, “must help countries break free”.

But is the world failing to tackle climate change because governments lack the political will? Or because climate action, among other development objectives, is being pursued within a global economic system whose rules entrench the inequalities inherited from colonialism? That is the question posed by Fadhel Kaboub, an economist at Denison University, Ohio, and adviser to the UN. His answer is that those structures never truly disappeared, but have evolved into today’s rules governing international finance, trade, investment and taxation. The upshot is that the countries least responsible for global warming have the fewest resources to confront its consequences.

At Cop31, Dr Kaboub was among a group of experts arguing for the least developed countries to emulate Mark Carney’s middle-power strategy and employ the same logic of collective bargaining in a world of great-power rivalry. Poorer nations should seek not just strategic autonomy but economic sovereignty. The experts suggested that they pool resources and build regional common markets as well as green industries together. The aim was to negotiate as a bloc with western powers – and China – for technology transfer and investment without racking up further debt. Half a century after developing nations demanded a new international economic order, the climate crisis may be giving that unfinished struggle a new purpose.

Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 18:28:42 GMT

The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

The Neets review has taken on a life of its own. ITV has commissioned a four-part docudrama on the writing of the report. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Neets: The Musical will be opening just before Christmas. And Mud’s classic, That’s Neet, That’s Neet, I Really Love Your Tiger Feet is the hot favourite to be the UK’s entry for next year’s Eurovision. At long last, a song we can all get behind and that has a realistic chance of winning.

But Tuesday was the day. The day Big Al took centre stage at Google HQ to tell us he was about to tell us everything he had already told us. We just had to listen quietly and bathe in his reflected glory. And tick off all the review’s highlights as they were mentioned. Neets bingo. We were in danger of creating a lost generation. In fact we already might have done, as more than 10% of young people under 25 had been out of work, education or training for more than 20 years.

It wasn’t that young people were lazy snowflakes. They had been let down. Time now to invest in this generation, not write them off. To invest in their futures like other northern European countries do. You couldn’t get hundreds of thousands of people back to work just by cutting benefits. That was delusional. Rather, a culture shift was needed. A recalibration of the way the state engaged with an abandoned generation.

Almost seamlessly, the venue shifted to the Commons where Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, surrounded by Andy Burnham and most of the cabinet, was due to give his own 10-minute potted version of the Milburn review. First though, an intervention from the speaker, who wanted to put on record his concern that copies of the report hadn’t been laid before the house. Not that anyone needed a copy; we all knew it off by heart.

Pat then repeated pretty much everything Milburn had said an hour earlier. The only difference being that McFadden managed to sound a bit gloomier about the whole thing. Not because he wasn’t enthusiastic, but because he was. The more engaged and upbeat Pat is, the more depressed he sounds. It’s just the way he’s wired. Gloom is his natural state of being.

Even with McFadden’s rather downbeat delivery, this still felt like quite a moment. For the last two and a half years, many have criticised the government for its lack of vision. For lurching from one crisis to the next. Here, at last, was that vision. A major shift in the way the state would engage with a generation of young people who hitherto had been ignored or left on benefits. You couldn’t help feeling a bit sorry for Keir Starmer. He was the one who – albeit late in the day – had commissioned the review, but Burnham would get the credit. That’s showbiz for you.

While Labour benches were packed, barely a dozen Tory backbench MPs had bothered to come for what might be a seismic shift in policy. Maybe they are the snowflakes. Or maybe they really aren’t that bothered that so many young people feel they have no future. Or maybe they couldn’t face sitting through the truly hopeless response of the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately.

You really can’t blame so many Neets for feeling the odds are stacked against them when they see the rise and rise of Whately. Helen is everything the Tories believe Neets to be. Lazy, stupid. A woman without principle who has morphed into whatever shape is required to fit in with a Tory party sliding ever further to the right. If there were any justice, Whately would be one of the many people struggling to find a decent job. Or any job. Had she been born 25 years later, it would have been Helen claiming benefits.

Her reply was one of the most half-witted imaginable. You can just about forgive the nastiness. That comes with the Tory territory. So of course she was demanding that billions more be cut from benefits. Because that’s the only language they think Neets understand. What was too much was the stupidity. Only Whately could claim that Milburn was just following Tory policy in the same breath as declaring it was a Labour benefits bonanza.

The rest of the session passed with little incident. A few Labour backbenchers gently reminded Gloomy Pat that while they were fully behind most of the review they were concerned that some young people might lose out on benefits. A warning shot. This was a battle to be fought over later. Suella Braverman managed to take off her handcuffs for a few minutes – like most Reform MPs she is being paid a fortune to be chained to Katie Price – to ask about immigrants. No one paid her any attention.

Where this goes from here is anyone’s guess. Will the new jobs exist or become Milburn’s Potemkin village? It could be that in 10 years’ time, we will look back and see this as the moment society reshaped its attitudes to young people. Or it could just get forgotten, filed away under “too difficult”. A road to hell paved with good intentions. But hey! We will always have Eurovision. And Neets! Might even get transferred to Broadway.

UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:59:41 GMT

Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

Although no global “solidarity levies” have yet been put in place, a taskforce backed by the French government has suggested making a small charge on flights for the most frequent flyers and passengers in business class, and charges on crypto-currency transactions as potential ways of raising revenue.

Analysis last year by the Dutch environmental consultancy CE Delft, commissioned by the Global Solidarity Levies Task Force, showed that a levy on tickets that began at €10 on short-haul flights in economy, rising to €30 on long-haul flights, and €20 for short-haul business-class tickets, rising to €120 for long haul, would produce revenues of about €106bn a year.

However, these ideas have been hard to put into practice. A proposed levy on the carbon dioxide produced by international shipping, overseen by the International Maritime Organization, has been postponed after opposition from the US under Donald Trump.

The UK government told the Guardian it was “committed to leading developed nations in mobilising at least $300bn per year by 2035”.

“In that context, the UK supports looking beyond the traditional flows of donor financing, to exploring much wider and deeper types of financial flows, from emerging markets, from private actors, and through financial innovations that can channel much greater levels of climate finance.”

Signing the letter does not commit the UK to any immediate actions.

The government added that it was carefully considering the “solidarity levy” proposals. “However, tax is an important matter of domestic sovereignty, so we will need to consider whether proposals are in the national interest,” the Treasury said.

NGOs welcomed the move. David Hillman, co-convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said it was a “clear sign that the politics are shifting”.

“This is hard-won progress. But signing a statement is only the beginning,” he said. “The UK must now use its G20 presidency next year to turn words into action – putting taxes on polluting industries firmly on the agenda and building international support for measures that make the biggest polluters pay their fair share.”

Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “It’s good to see the UK finally looking at new ways to pay for the escalating costs of extreme weather. Right now, global funding for adaptation is just a 10th of what’s needed to survive worsening floods and heatwaves, and this Cop has barely moved the dial.

“With public finances as tight as they are, it’s madness to keep handing the bill to taxpayers and the people struck down when extreme weather hits. It’s time to make the polluters pay – starting with the fossil fuel giants swimming in record profits.

“As next year’s G20 host, the UK needs to turn this statement of intent into cold, hard cash.”

Developing countries have been disappointed at the Cop31 negotiations on climate finance so far, as no substantial amounts of new money are likely to be pledgedat the summit. Spain’s minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen, said: “The world cannot wait and neither can our societies. They are the ones demanding action and living through fires, heatwaves, floods, droughts. They are the ones paying the bill for dependence on fossil fuels.”

Sleep paralysis: when you’re awake, but can’t move – or even breathe

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:52:53 GMT

Readers recount their terrifying experiences of sleep paralysis in response to an article by Amy Fleming

I experienced sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations from childhood and into adulthood, with the episodes only waning in my 30s (Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis, 11 November). I never spoke about them to anyone.

I experienced hallucinations in the form of severe perspective distortion (oversized bed and rooms) and full hallucinations/dream states, auditory hallucinations (screaming and loud thumping) and, of course, paralysis. I didn’t know at what point I was asleep or if I had woken and could easily slip back into a hypnagogic state. I only became aware of this state as an adult, having been referred to a psychiatrist on an unrelated matter.

Some of the episodes were literally the stuff of nightmares. I have always had exceptionally vivid dreams and rarely do I go through a night without a dream waking me up (or so it seems). Once I understood what was happening, it was less terrifying and more fascinating, though the actual physical state cannot fail to be frightening.

It is such a strange state to experience, and while I am glad that the episodes are much less frequent and severe now, in a strange way I slightly miss the otherworldliness of it, and I would not ask to never have experienced it, even some of the most terrifying episodes. Perhaps most interesting is how quickly the fear dissipates once properly out of the state, though that can take some time. Name and address supplied

Sleep paralysis struck me years before I learned, at an exhibition at the Wellcome Institute, that this was not just me being weird in my sleep, but a proper thing with a name. And yes, it is absolutely petrifying. I still remember how relieved I was on the one hand and fascinated on the other by all the evidence of sleep paralysis through the centuries at this exhibition.

Since then, I have only seen one article about it, until now. Thank you, Amy Fleming, for finding words for something that is so difficult to put into words that I have never even tried to mention it to anyone. I find it equally helpful and super-interesting that the “monster” is being studied by neuroscientists. It is comforting to be able to say: “Look, this is not me making something up, this is real.” Barbara Geier London

Having suffered from sleep paralysis for most of my adult life, there were times when I would be scared to go to sleep. There is an aspect of it that is far more terrifying than “monsters”. When sleep paralysis occurs with me, not only can I not move, I can’t open my eyes or breathe either. My mind is awake, in utter dread, but my body is still asleep. I was diagnosed in the early 1980s with acute anxiety syndrome and hospitalised for three weeks, so maybe anxiety is a big factor. But GPs, psychologists and other doctors I encountered have no curiosity about sleep paralysis at all, and that’s scary too. Caroline Staley London

Your article reminded me of an old custom in the Alpine region: to ward off night-time disturbances caused by the Toggeli (a night spirit), Swiss farmers would fasten a Werchhechel (a tool for combing flax, studded with numerous long, pointed iron needles) to their chests. This served to physically ward off the nocturnal tormentor, which choked the sleeper’s breath and caused severe nightmares or sleep paralysis. Thomas Recher Ziefen, Switzerland

Have yourself a stress-free Christmas

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:52:41 GMT

Tara Padfield will be buying her marmalade and leaving the trees in the woods; Jen Arnall-Culliford says cooking in advance is key. Plus a letter from Alan Ravenscroft

I read Ammar Kalia’s article (Christmas is all in the preparation! Chefs on eight easy things to do now – so you can relax on the big day, 12 November) with a mixture of disbelief and mounting despair.

Apparently, the secret to a stress-free Christmas involves roasting a kilogram of chicken wings and simmering stock for hours, making marmalade from scratch, infusing gin with Sichuan peppercorns and, should we have a spare afternoon, heading into the woods to forage for Douglas fir needles. I had naively imagined that time-saving tips might actually save time.

Instead, we are encouraged to embark on an elaborate programme of culinary projects, requiring specialist ingredients, considerable effort and a seemingly inexhaustible supply of enthusiasm.

There is a fundamental difference between making Christmas easier and creating several weeks of additional work. I shall be buying my marmalade and enjoying Christmas without a jar of homemade mushroom oil in sight. Tara Padfield Ventnor, Isle of Wight

Every year we have a Christmas dinner that is cooked in advance and frozen. In our house that is usually chilli con carne, but we have done curries and other dishes. The main aim is to be able to do the bulk of the cooking on a weekend in late November or early December.

Then, on Christmas Eve, I simply get the tub out of the freezer and let it defrost, and I warm it up on the hob 30 minutes before lunch. We can then add lots of dips, toppings, nachos or whatever other tasty bits we fancy, but the effort is absolutely minimal. Instead of spending the day trying to create some idealised Christmas, we play a game, hang out and appreciate each other.

So yes, Christmas is all in the preparation, but making a special day doesn’t need to involve spice rubs or cocktails or whatever. It can also be manageable and affordable. Jen Arnall-Culliford Frome, Somerset

Jamie Oliver contends that gravy is the most important ingredient to ensure a first-class Christmas lunch (How I Christmas shop with Jamie Oliver: ‘The most important thing? Gravy’, 10 November). I feel he has ignored the two real heroes of the Christmas table: Christmas pudding is really just an excuse for serving lashings of brandy butter, and the turkey merely an excuse to serve a brimming bowl of that other Christmas stalwart, bread sauce (both delicious cold too, by the way). Let’s keep gravy in its place. Alan Ravenscroft London

Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.

Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday , after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there.

The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him.

Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications .

Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues.

The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions.

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:30:40 GMT

With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea

At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”

The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.

Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.

Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.

As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.

Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.

A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.

Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.

One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”

In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.

Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.

“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.

The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Spud-one-likes: is King Charles really a baked potato aficionado?

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:25:10 GMT

On a visit to Preston, the royal revealed his favourite classic filling. But with jacket potatoes as far as the eye could see, he surprisingly failed to order one ...

Name: Jacket potatoes.

Age: As everyone knows, potatoes originated in South America where Incas cooked them in a huatia, an oven dug in the earth. So quite ancient.

Mash-u Pichu? No, baked. But yeah, around those parts.

Still very popular today, especially among students. Everyone: students, royals …

Jersey Royals? Wrong type, too small.

King edwards? No! It’s not about the potato (though a king edward does bake well, light and fluffy, delicious with a big blob of butter). It’s about the baked potato lover.

A royal one? Correct. Guess who?

One of the little ones, Charlotte? William’s daughter? Nice try, and of course a charlotte is also a potato, a smaller one as it happens, good for salads, not so for baking. No, the royal jacket potato lover is in fact … Charles.

The actual king! Now guess what his favourite type of baked potato is.

Is it a tweed jacket potato? No. Think fillings.

Is it pheasant and cucumber? It isn’t.

Gentleman’s relish? Nope.

I give up. Cheese and beans.

Baked beans? Does he even know what they are? How do we know this? He was in Preston earlier this week and stopped by a popular food van called SpudBros.

Run by brothers and serving baked potatoes? Correct. And when one of them, Harley Nelson (the other is called Jacob) asked: “Do you like jacket potatoes, sir?” the king replied: “Of course.”

Naturally. The conversation then moved on to the fillings, his majesty professed to liking “all sorts of things”.

You’d think the Nelsons would have left it at that, out of deference. Oh no, they pressed and the king confessed: cheese and beans.

Presumably he ordered one, on the spot? He didn’t. “I’d never survive, I’d be asleep,” he is reported as telling them.

Hmm, I’m wondering if he does love jacket potatoes with cheese and beans, or whether he just knows they are something people put in them. Possibly treasonable.

So he left empty handed? No, they gave him a crocheted “positive potato”.

What the hell is one of those? To be honest, I have no idea, but they told him to give it to his grandchildren.

Charlotte maybe. Anything else to report from the encounter? The king also revealed that his favourite potato was the Red Duke of York …

Oh dear. Well the less said about that the better … Eh? Oh yes, I see.

Do say: “Mmmmmm.”

Don’t say: “Quick, start up a new upmarket chain with a royal appointment of approval, and call it Spud-One-Likes.”

‘It was probably the lowest point’ at Manchester United

Wayne Rooney has revealed there was a period in his Manchester United career where he contemplated taking his own life. The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, he was struggling with his mental health off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai.

He said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life.

“I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with,” Rooney said. “Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well.

“I got to a place where you’re contemplating suicide. You just didn’t want to be around anyone. I didn’t want to see people in the streets. I didn’t want to go into shops. I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else [I] really struggled with it.”

Rooney, United’s record goalscorer, said the issues he faced occurred at the height of his career. “You don’t want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it,” he said. “Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man if you like for doing that.

“I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I’ve just had a young son, I’ve just been married. It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn’t. It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.”

Rooney, who is currently featuring on the ITV show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, credits his wife, Coleen, with helping him turn the tide. “Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it.”

Rassie Erasmus’s tired ref-blaming act is wearing thin – South Africa deserve better

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:10:48 GMT

Springboks’ achievements are remarkable but their head coach lacks statesmanship, diplomacy and good grace in defeat

So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat.

To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of any doubt everyone respects the remarkable achievements both of Erasmus and his double World Cup-winning teams. It is the rest of the package, sadly, that is too often a major letdown.

At times the Boks’ patron saint is almost reminiscent of Donald Trump in a tracksuit: crass, petulant and seemingly immune to the damage inflicted on the “little people” who get in his way. How else to interpret his latest outburst after South Africa’s defeat by France when he suggested that alleged incidents of foul play not picked up by either the referee or the television match official amounted to “match-fixing” or “manipulation of the game”?

Dissatisfied coaches are a familiar ingredient of the game’s bubbling stew. And, yes, Erasmus technically has a point when he complains that several knee-drop tackles, recently classified as illegal, were missed in Paris. Rugby is a game of tiny margins and South Africa, as befits the world’s No 1 nation, hate losing more than most.

But there is a much bigger picture involved and Erasmus remains seemingly incapable of appreciating the insidious toxicity of finger-pointing and ref-shaming in defeat. Back in 2021, when he embarked on his 62-minute social media rant after the Boks had lost the opening Test of their series against the British & Irish Lions, he warned the Australian referee Nic Berry he would publicise 36 refereeing errors if the official failed to meet him. The disciplinary panel found him guilty on six charges, imposed a lengthy ban from all matchday activities, and described his video as “an attack on the impartiality and integrity of the match officials”.

Berry, who will be in charge of England’s game against New Zealand this weekend, duly attracted the online wrath of every keyboard warrior in South Africa and felt that “my reputation as a referee and a person will forever be tarnished.” It did not stop Erasmus from being banned for two more matches the next year after his social media posts precipitated an internet pile-on for the English referee Wayne Barnes, also after a South African loss to France.

Which is why Erasmus’s latest outpourings, aimed at Matteo Liperini, the television match official in Paris, on the subject of multiple missed knee-drop tackles, were always going to be costly. “I’m saying if he didn’t see it, it must be a technology problem,” suggested Erasmus. “If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?”

Only in the eyes of a practised agent provocateur. Erasmus attended World Rugby’s refereeing summit in Windsor this month when the mantra of penalising only “clear and obvious” indiscretions was repeatedly stressed, as was a desire to reduce the number of TMO referrals. Yes, there were some French tacklers who had knees on the ground as they hauled down Bok ball-carriers in the tumultuous final quarter in Paris but the refereeing team seemed to have decided they didn’t want a truly fabulous contest to be defined by some arbitrary late penalty.

It is possible to pore over any breakdown and find multiple things that could conceivably, by the letter of the law, be pounced upon. But, by the same token, none of it would have ultimately mattered had South Africa, with their scrum dominating, been minded to use any other instrument beyond the bludgeon.

Sign up to The Breakdown

The latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewed

after newsletter promotion

It would have spared us all the tiresome “Why always me?” whingeing that invariably resurfaces whenever northern hemisphere opponents or referees are involved. There were bound to be teething problems with the new hip-drop directive, hastily introduced from 1 November to bring rugby union into line with other contact sports. But to say that Ireland’s Sam Prendergast, cited for the offence after last weekend’s Fiji game, will escape punishment because double standards are at work? Talk about a victim complex.

Like all great conspiracy theorists, Erasmus is also only interested in selective facts that fit his preferred narrative. Of course he wants the refs to be vigilant when his team face Ireland this weekend; the strict letter of the law worked nicely for the Boks in Dublin last year. Of course he wants to spread the notion that South Africa may have been hard done by in the Stade de France and deserve more sympathy this Saturday. He is by no means the only coach to operate in that way but his sledgehammer subtlety is in a league of its own.

Maybe in past years he, and his staunch defenders, could have blamed it on English being his second language. Such excuses, however, are long since redundant. To repeat, South Africa are a remarkable sporting nation and their rugby players remain first among equals. They deserve to be fronted by someone with rather more class.

Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:59:54 GMT

The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job

The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments.

There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. The meek nature of Scotland’s collapse in the 4-0 loss to a second-string Switzerland was lamentable. The Belgian’s assessment, with overpraise a key theme, raised eyebrows.

Pocognoli’s team scored five goals in six Nations League games, four coming against North Macedonia. They drew blanks in three fixtures. The concession of 10 depicts a team soft against set pieces and in open play. Scotland have wingers who are not appropriately deployed because of dedication to a system. They have an obvious shortage of centre-backs yet Pocognoli picks three at a time. The midfield lacks balance. Not one player under Pocognoli’s watch is consistently excelling.

Pocognoli is obstinate in respect of his tactics. At club level this can work owing to daily work on a training pitch. Scotland are wedded to a 3-4-2-1 that fits too few of their players. There is no transfer window capacity to change that. Pocognoli’s insistence upon his “philosophy” sets off alarm bells. Although his English is strong, it is far from perfect, which raises questions about communication. Scotland do not look well drilled or clear in approach, which was plain in the unimpressive home win against North Macedonia even before the Switzerland debacle.

Unlike with Clarke, there is no detailed body of work to suggest Pocognoli can adapt or oversee improvement. He achieved great success in Belgium, winning the title at Union Saint-Gilloise, before a brief spell at Monaco. The Scottish FA’s deep faith in this 39-year-old, amid all manner of waffle about metrics and analytics, was on the basis of just over 100 games as a manager. It remains probable that the association erred in not sourcing a coach with dugout experience at a country of similar scale to Scotland. This always had the whiff of trying to be too smart by half.

The best Scotland sides are unapologetically horrible to play against, physical, energetic and direct. Shortcomings in skill are offset by attitude. Pocognoli’s version is the opposite on all fronts, ponderous and timid. The Tartan Army, hardly a ferociously demanding lot, have failed to demonstrate any excitement about Pocognoli.

This counts as no ode to Clarke. After seven years, change was required. It was the turn taken by the Scottish FA in implementing a new strategy that looks increasingly dubious.

Footballers are typically selfish beings. For now it suits the Scotland squad – and is fair – to state Pocognoli requires time and that they are behind him. Not only did the body language amid the unravelling in St Gallen suggest otherwise, those players are likely to adopt a different position if focus turns towards them. Scotland’s contingent is heavy on influential, experienced players.

There is no sense of the Scottish FA dispensing with Pocognoli at this point. Not only would such a move be premature, it would deliver an admission of failure that those running the governing body are never keen on providing. They enjoy the trappings and profile provided by the national team without anything like the adjacent accountability. They are assisted in this context by domestic football obsession within the country. There will be grumblings about Pocognoli for a brief period this week before the theme is placed into cold storage.

Next month’s Uefa 2028 qualifying draw, where Scotland will appear from pot three, carries intrigue and danger for Pocognoli. The assumption that Scotland will feature in the tournament is undermined by performances; England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are co-hosting and a maximum of two spots are open for any of those nations who do not qualify. Not playing in a competition where games will be staged in Glasgow would count as a humiliation for the Scottish FA.

If Scotland face competitive games rather than friendlies in March, which will be determined after the draw, Pocognoli needs stark improvement. Without it, his paymasters would then have a decision to make while looking to keep Euro 2028 dreams alive. The situation is already that acute.

Pocognoli was not part of the Scotland party that landed in Glasgow from Zurich on Tuesday. His family have remained in Belgium. Alone with his thoughts on his journey home, Pocognoli must have pondered the harshness of his new environment. He has the sternest of challenges to quieten legitimate background noise.

What is the polar vortex, why has it flipped and will it bring the UK snow?

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:16:06 GMT

We look at what is happening over the Arctic and what it might mean for winter weather in the northern hemisphere

The polar vortex has flipped direction, signalling the earliest “major sudden stratospheric warming” ever observed. We examine how it is likely to affect you and whether it will bring snow.

It is a circle of strong winds in the stratosphere, about six to 30 miles (10 to 50km) above the surface of the Earth, that usually blow in a west to east direction around the Arctic, creating an insulating ring between the cold air mass closer to the north pole and warmer air further south.

The vortex relocates or splits in two, which allows cold air from high altitudes and the pole to spill down over northern Europe, north America, Siberia, Japan and other parts of east Asia.

This part of the stratosphere is thought to have warmed by up to 50C in just a couple of days as a result of large atmospheric waves spreading up from the troposphere, the lowest and densest layer of Earth’s atmosphere.

Not always, but in this case, yes, for at least some parts of the northern hemisphere in the coming weeks.

The polar vortex is part of the climate system. Any disruption has knock-on effects. In the north Atlantic, for example, it upsets the jet stream and weather patterns for millions of people.

When the jet stream is weakened or wobbles, chilled air can move south out of the Arctic, often bringing colder, drier spells to northern Europe and north America, while southern Europe tends to become milder, wetter and windier.

Very possibly, but it’s not guaranteed. It depends where high pressure systems form. The UK Met Office released a yellow snow warning on Tuesday for the Midlands, the north east and west of England and south west Scotland.

Yes, sudden stratospheric warming famously led a few weeks later to “the beast from the east” snowstorms that affected the UK in 2018. In the US, it was associated with deadly winter storms in 2021. Similar phenomena were also observed in 2009-10 and 2013. These events usually occur much later in winter, but this year it has happened on 10 November, 18 days earlier than ever before.

The probability of colder-than-average weather tends to continue for between 30 and 40 days after sudden stratospheric warming.

This is a matter for debate, but scientists have found evidence that El Niño conditions, which start with warmer waters in the Pacific, influence planetary waves – known as Rossby waves – that spread across the lower atmosphere and can propagate upwards in the Arctic, raising the chance of sudden stratospheric warming.

Possibly, but the scientific jury is still out. Some researchers say a link is likely. Others are more cautious, noting that early sudden stratospheric warming falls within the bounds of natural variability. Even though this event comes at the end of a year of extreme weather, the bigger question is likely to be filed under “more study is needed”.

‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:00:15 GMT

Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial

When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country.

The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence.

Then he came across Project Search, a nationwide year-long transition-to-work programme that helps young people with learning disabilities or autism move into permanent paid employment.

It changed his life and now Bowman is thriving in his work as a personal trainer at Pure Gym.

“Getting actual experience in workplaces, understanding how they function, what would be expected of me and how to interact with people, it was exactly what I needed,” he said. “And having a job coach who does half the jump with you.”

Alan Milburn’s report on how to get the UK’s Neets into work has recommended an overhaul of welfare support for young people, including moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to a new “youth allowance”.

In return, eligible 18-to-24-year-olds will be guaranteed a fully funded, six-month job if they have been claiming universal credit for 12 months. Milburn said this was about prioritising “their longer-term life chances” over “immediate shorter-term finances”.

Interns and staff at the Project Search course run by Phoenix College in Tower Hamlets welcomed the bold commitment to get more young people into work, but there were concerns about cutting support and the quality of job opportunities being offered.

Bowman said he disagreed with the proposal to cut benefits like the personal independence payment (Pip) for young people to help push them into work.

“I think alongside any workplace initiatives, Pip is still absolutely a must-have. I would argue it’s more important to have if you’re going to be engaging in a structured programme – for me, things like noise-cancelling headphones are essential,” he said.

“I need that funding more to enter the world of work than I did when I was sat at home playing video games.”

Staff said getting young people, especially those with extra needs, into a long-term sustainable job wasn’t as simple as filling a vacancy – many students need holistic support and extra help even once they’re in work.

“We’ve been noticing a lot more interns coming in with serious mental health conditions and that requires extra help,” said Renato Marques, principal of Phoenix College. “But here, even for our very high-needs students, everything is geared towards getting them into a workplace.

“They learn the job doing the job. A lot of courses say they are preparing students for work, but they are not taking them into work.”

Rather than studying at a traditional campus, their interns learn in classrooms hosted in partner businesses – including a global law firm, a large distribution company and Queen Mary University of London – and they rotate through daily 9am to 3pm work placements.

Over the past six years, 68% of students ended up in employment at the end of the course – four times higher than the national average rate of disabled young people who are Neet.

All graduates also have access to a follow-on service they can use for advice in the first few years of their career.

For students with higher levels of need, the college developed a pre-supported internship combining two days of workplace experience – supported by an on-hand job coach – with extra training in social skills and independent travel.

Osman Osman, assistant principal for Project Search, said Milburn’s plan would only work with better paid and resourced careers advisers in schools, and high-quality work experience and job offers.

“You see careers advisers managing schools with a thousand kids, and they’re expected to meet with every single one, and it’s a very, very hard job to actually get those young people work-ready,” he said. “We spend a long time building our young people’s confidence and skillset in the field they’re interested in.

“And any job offer has to be meaningful placements because inset days, taster sessions or a week’s work experience often lead to no actual outcomes for young people.”

Tawhid Ahmed, 21, said finding work or apprenticeships after finishing school had been overwhelming – he now works at Phoenix College after building confidence and social skills on the course.

“I have a learning disability, and it was hard because I’ve been rejected for so many jobs. The fact that I was able to find Project Search really was a blessing,” he said. “Now I do admin and I have really good colleagues who help and support me. I want to help students face challenges that I’ve faced as well.”

Businesses are also a key part of the puzzle – Milburn’s proposals included a raft of incentives to encourage employers to take on more young people, including tax breaks.

“Employers might scoff at the review because there’s a lot of expectations placed on them,” said Cigdem Yilmaz, supported employment lead on the course. “We need an army of people, maybe that’s people like us, to be working with employers until we can get more young people on to the ground. Otherwise it’s just going to be more of the same.”

Max, a 22-year-old with autism, is being supported by the Youth Environmental Service (Yes), which works with environmental organisations to create accessible and entry-level employment in the west of England.

The organisation, which targets young people from diverse backgrounds and those with disabilities, provides access to paid work as well as peer support networks, a transferable skills programme and one-to-one coaching.

“That was really beneficial, especially for neurodivergent people, because it’s really nice to be put on a level playing field with everyone,” said Max, who is employed part-time by Bristol-based Make a Film.

The 22-year-old, who has a degree in plant science, said the traditional way to apply for jobs was not accessible for all and called for more opportunities that offered young people a clear career development.

“I really strongly believe that there are lots of young people who are really passionate, who really hold skills, really great valuable skills for the workplace. But there aren’t enough jobs that are entry level, which give opportunities for training to actually get into something that will set them off into a future career that they are passionate about,” he said.

Prof Neil Greenberg, the president of the Society of Occupational Medicine (SOM), which works to protect people in the workplace, emphasised the value of work in building self-esteem, routine and social support, for all young people.

“We shouldn’t be waiting until people are completely ready to put them into work. They need to get a flicker of work as soon as they can, because once people try it out and they get success, that builds more success,” he said.

Chris Goulden, the interim deputy chief executive of the Youth Futures Foundation, which supports young people into work – particularly those from diverse and marginalised backgrounds – said stereotypes of young people being lazy or unwilling to work were “untrue” and “unhelpful”.

“The number of jobs that most young people are applying for are in the hundreds, so I think it is an unhelpful stereotype and not born out of evidence that we have experienced,” he said.
