Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 15:58:47 GMT

The PM’s first big speech on the UK and Europe was cautious and disappointing. Don’t expect any great leaps towards a new deal

Ever since Andy Burnham became the British prime minister this summer, people all over Europe have been asking me one question: “Will the UK rejoin the EU?” Sometimes they add: “And if so, when?” None of the intermediate options between the current hard Brexit and Brejoin are of any interest at all to most other Europeans.

Measured against these great expectations, Burnham’s first big speech on Britain and Europe, delivered on Monday evening amid all the pomp and circumstance the City of London could furnish, must be considered a disappointment. It was both a cautious and a curiously old-fashioned speech.

Cautious in diagnosis: his bold statement that “we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years” was immediately followed by “the hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain”. (So a soft Brexit would be fine?) Cautious in prescription: beyond the welcome modest steps to be agreed at this Friday’s UK-EU summit (easier access for food and agricultural products, linking our carbon emissions markets, creating a youth mobility scheme), anything this government does during the term of the current parliament will stay within Keir Starmer’s “red lines” (no rejoining the customs union, single market or freedom of movement). Burnham will, however, explore “options for our long-term relationship” with the EU, “to inform decisions in the next parliament”. Unless we have an early election, that means not before 2029.

This caution is easily explained. Roughly half of his cabinet doesn’t want even to mention Brexit. Roughly half of his MPs are in constituencies that voted leave in 2016. The country at large thinks Brexit was a mistake but dreads the prospect of rerunning the debate and isn’t sure it would vote for rejoining if the UK didn’t have its previous opt-outs, including from the euro and the Schengen free travel area. For all the great expectations that were raised, Burnham himself had actually only said in interviews that he hoped Britain would rejoin the EU in his lifetime. He’s a robust 56-year-old, so that could take us to about 2060.

More surprising was how old-fashioned his speech was, albeit delivered with demotic verve. Here, for starters, was the weary old trope of Britain always having to “lead” in whatever it does (nine references to leading, if my count is correct). Then there’s the curious way in which Britain’s commitment to European defence and support for Ukraine is totally divorced from all the other dimensions of European security and strength, which self-evidently involve the EU. Instead, there’s a relentless narrow focus on what’s good for Britain economically. At the heart of his speech was what he called the “Makerfield test” – that is, what would deliver economic benefits for the hard-pressed people of his constituency of Makerfield, which in 2016 voted to leave the EU.

Oddest of all was the way he harked back to a 1948 speech in which Winston Churchill conjured Britain’s position at the intersection of three majestic circles. Gliding over the fact that the first circle Churchill mentioned was “the British Commonwealth and Empire”, Burnham talked at some length about the Commonwealth before coming to Europe. For obvious reasons (don’t offend the egomaniac in the White House!), he also glided over the fact that Churchill’s second circle was “the English-speaking world”, with its superpower being the US. Yet if we are highlighting, as Burnham did, how the world has changed since 2016, then the drastic change under Donald Trump in the US approach to its allies, including Britain, should be top of the list. Oh, and by the way, Churchill’s third circle was “United Europe”, which he talked of in visionary terms long before it ever existed. Now, with something called the European Union, much of Europe is at least halfway there.

Unlike in Churchill’s speech, in fact unlike in everything that great British and European leader said and did, here there was no sense of a wider European story in which Britain has always played an important part. Instead, Burnham spoke of Britain’s reset “with Europe”, as though Britain were not part of Europe and “Europe” only means the EU. The most European things in London’s Guildhall on Monday evening were the Polish vodka served by the Polish-South-African-British lord mayor of London, Bronek Masojada, and a few words in Dutch that he addressed to the prime minister’s wife, Marie-France van Heel.

But enough about the words. What of the actions to follow? I’m not sure how long these conversations with EU partners about “options” need to last. An hour or two might suffice. For the EU has repeatedly spelled out the current ones as it sees them. If you want a nice summary, look at the visual “staircase” of options prepared by the now sadly closing UK in a Changing Europe thinktank. But don’t get me wrong: continuing to explore all options until the next British election is the right thing to do, not least for one simple reason. After Europe’s megacycle of elections in 2026/27, an EU with, say, President Marine Le Pen in France, a coalition of centre-right and far-right parties in Spain, hard-right governments in Poland and Italy, and the AfD making the political running in Germany, may be a very different proposition.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Rationally speaking, I have no doubt that it would be much better for both Britain and Europe were the UK still to be a full member of the EU. Britain has many strengths that Europe needs: most of its best universities, leading AI startups, financial services, creative industries, supposedly super spooks (even if they don’t all resemble Robert Pattinson as James Bond). But the politics on both sides of the Channel will make this very difficult to achieve.

Meanwhile, Burnham’s tentative reopening of the issue has already led to the launch of not one but two anti-Brejoin pressure groups, one called Stay Out and the other mysteriously named Enough Official. Backed by some of the surviving old Brexit warhorses, they are already claiming that to rejoin the EU would cost Britain £750m a week. As in a nightmare, one glimpses the prospect of Boris Johnson, Michael Gove, Jacob Rees-Mogg and – gawd help us – Liz Truss tottering, like a gaggle of the undead, out of a red battlebus on the side of which is blazoned “Rejoining the EU would steal £750m a week from the NHS”.

Silver-tongued Gove, the Artful Dodger of British politics, the Iago of Brexit, now warns us that any move towards rejoining would “commit the country to another decade of fractious negotiations”. But that’s what we’re in for anyway, because both Britain and the EU will keep changing and therefore the relationship between the UK and its largest trading partner will inevitably be the subject of constant, difficult negotiations. And guess who gave us this dreary prospect? Gove, Johnson and all that gang. For all the criticisms I have made of his first big, not very European speech about “Europe”, give me Burnham any day.

Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7½ Chapters, is out now

Peter Storey, Arsenal Double winner and England international, dies aged 81

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 15:46:45 GMT

Storey made 501 appearances for Arsenal from 1965

He won 19 England caps and finished career at Fulham

Arsenal have paid tribute to Peter Storey, a key member of their 1971 Double-winning team, after the death of the former England midfielder at the age of 81.

Storey was part of the Bertie Mee team that secured the First Division title and FA Cup in a season that remains one of the most celebrated in Arsenal’s history and played 501 times for the club. That places him eighth on their appearances list.

Storey, who represented England on 19 occasions from 1971-73, earned respect for his uncompromising approach and versatility, also featuring at right-back.

Storey died in hospital after a short illness, surrounded by his family. Arsenal said: “Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of 1970-71 Double winner Peter Storey. All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.”

Born in Surrey, Storey began his career at Arsenal and made his debut shortly after his 20th birthday in 1965. He is fondly remembered by the club’s fans for scoring a stoppage-time penalty in the 1971 FA Cup semi-final against Stoke that forced a replay and kept the Double dream alive.

Storey left for Fulham in 1977 and retired eight months later when his contract was cancelled, going on to own a pub in north London. He was later convicted of several criminal offences, including financing a plot to counterfeit gold coins and smuggling pornography. He released an autobiography, True Storey: My Life and Crimes as a Football Hatchet Man, in September 2010.

Storey’s family said: “We are deeply grateful for the many kind messages, tributes and good wishes we have received. It has been a great comfort to see the affection and respect in which he was held by so many, both within the football community and beyond.”

Should JD Vance run for president? I say go for it, habibi!

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 15:21:32 GMT

Now the vice-president’s luck is turning, he seems reluctant to commit himself to the next presidential race – and I, for one, hate to see it

How do you think history will remember JD Vance? As the first vice-president to spark a vigorous debate about their eyeliner routine? As one of the last public figures to see Pope Francis alive? As the only politician in US history to have been the subject of a rumour about sexual relations with a couch (even though it was unfounded)?

I have no idea. But it seems increasingly unlikely he will be remembered as the 48th president of the US. After Maga’s midterm thrashing, Vance’s political future doesn’t look as bright as it used to. So much so that there has been a flurry of recent headlines debating whether or not Vance, once considered Donald Trump’s heir apparent, may slink away from a presidential run altogether.

At CNN, for example, “people close to [Vance]” report the VP is giving “serious consideration to not running for president in 2028”. One of the people with the misfortune of being close to Vance noted that he is 42, a mere baby, and can afford to sit out the next election. “He’s young enough that he can have a comeback should this environment make success impossible,” the unnamed source said. What “environment” would that be, eh? The one in which Vance and his boss managed to muck up the country so badly that even the world’s stupidest podcast bros have turned against them?

The US news website Axios dug up “two sources with knowledge of [Vance’s] plans”, who shared the very secret, very exciting revelation that Vance does not know what his plans are. “People familiar with Vance’s thinking say he’s genuinely undecided about running,” Axios added. If you can’t bear all the suspense, bad news: we may have to wait until late spring for a definitive answer. According to Axios, Vance is “wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him”.

That’s a valid concern, considering Vance doesn’t seem to be in the president’s good books. After the midterms, JD wrote a long, and quite sensible, social media post arguing the war in Iran was why Republicans had lost so badly. (Vance has always had just enough brain cells to see the war was a terrible idea and has repeatedly tried to distance himself from it, even while defending it in public.) Trump, who still hasn’t endorsed a successor, shrugged off that critique in a post-election 60 Minutes interview, saying he had no problem with it, and even made a similar statement to the Wall Street Journal. However, he also unceremoniously booted Vance from Iran negotiations.

Other Republicans were more direct with their criticism of Vance. “I don’t think the vice-president did himself any favours by sending out that email or tweet or whatever it was after the election,” senator John Kennedy said in an interview with CNN.

Vance is not an idiot. But he is also not the political genius one imagines he likes to think he is. The reason he went from writing about hillbillies to being one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history at super speed is less about his political instincts and more about the fact he had a little help from some billionaire friends. Chief among these was Peter Thiel, who hired Vance at his investment company in 2016, poured millions into Vance’s Senate campaign and brokered Vance’s first meeting with Trump. Elon Musk and Tucker Carlson also helped ingratiate Vance with Trump.

He has been exceptionally lucky. Now, however, his luck is turning. The Trump administration is lurching from failure to failure and Vance is inextricably tied to this dumpster fire. Even Fox News seems sick of him. “You guys have been in charge for the last two years,” Laura Ingraham said in an interview, when Vance deflected blame for Friday’s nationwide flight stoppage. “Why hasn’t it gotten fixed?” Oooh, I’ll answer that one, Laura! It’s because they’re incompetent.

While this may not be the very best month of the vice-president’s life, I’d urge him not to shelve his immediate presidential ambitions. Please run in 2028, JD, habibi! This is a fairly selfish ask, I admit, as I’m eager to see him squirm. Unless Trump miraculously manages to fix cost-of-living problems, I’m not sure any Republican could win in 2028. As vice-president, Vance is going to have an extra tough time. Watching him try to distance himself from Trump will involve mental gymnastics so elaborate, they’ll make Simone Biles look like an amateur. Still, I suspect the man will land on his feet. If Vance’s brilliant political career goes bung, he has plenty of practice at reinventing himself.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

The 45 best Secret Santa gifts in the UK for £15 or less – tried and tested for 2026

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 15:00:15 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

From grippy socks and posh condiments to beautiful stationery and accessories, these affordable Christmas presents are anything but naff

The best Christmas gifts for 2026

Secret Santa is an amazing concept to reduce the amount of gifts you feel obliged to buy, but I find it can result in quite a bit of tat. Resist the urge to buy a joke gift – often instant landfill – and use your budget to get your recipient something useful, or that feels quite treat-y.

I’m assuming for this guide that the rules of Secret Santa are that you know who your recipient is – they just don’t know who the gift is from. That is helpful as you can tailor it to their tastes and hobbies. If it’s blind both ways, food is always well received, and socks – while a Christmas cliche – are something everyone wants a new pair of (just get the best you can afford, not, as one of my family used to do, just restock my black school socks).

Here is my tried-and-tested guide to the best Secret Santa gifts under £15.

Knitted gloves

These will be a very welcome gift for the freezes and chills of winter. They’re extremely thick and soft, and come in a range of colours, but I love a cheery pop of red wherever I can.

Goat Rodeo Disco cucumber pickles, 500g

I’m addicted to pickles, and these are a brilliant – if offbeat – gift and a good alternative to a bottle of alcohol for those who don’t drink. I also use the pickle juice in my martini.

Glass straws

These are a fun gift that you may not buy yourself but would be happy to receive – six borosilicate glass straws in bright colours that are dishwasher safe (essential) and a great addition to a drinks cabinet.

Cowshed hand cream

I have a tube of hand cream in every bag and coat pocket, so I try out a lot. This one is a particular favourite: it’s rich, moisturising and not too sticky for popping on under your gloves. It smells delicious too, and the packaging is chic.

For more, read our guide to the best hand creams

Cheeseboard decoration

I love buying a few spendy decorations each year to build up the collection, so would be delighted to receive one as a gift: this mini cheeseboard decoration is kitsch and sweet. This gift is probably best if your Secret Santa is ahead of the big day – such as a work party – to give them time to display it.

Fleece-lined reflective neck warmer

I have a Proviz running jacket, and the way the hi-vis lights up when a car shines on it is amazing (without headlights on it, it’s a wearable grey, rather than lollipop-lady yellow, making it good for a commute). I’ve bought this reflective neck warmer for my daughter: the hi-vis is part of the design and will keep her warm while making her visible.

Spicy margarita salt, 130g

This is a delicious premixed salt and chilli seasoning to roll a cocktail glass in before serving, but also works stirred through guacamole to increase the spice factor or dusted over nachos. Cornish Sea Salt is a lovely company that harvests its salt eight metres from the British Atlantic coastline.

Aesop Resurrection hand sanitiser, 50ml

Everyone loves Aesop, and it makes even hand sanitiser feel premium. This smells delicious – woody and citrusy – and is great to have in your bag when travelling, particularly in winter. I’m never without a little bottle.

Resistance socks

For a fitness lover, these resistance socks are brilliant for the gym floor (not just pilates) when they need to ditch their trainers to do heavy lifts. They come in bright colours and are gender neutral.

Christmas honey, 227g

A jar of Black Bee’s Christmas Honey is a welcome gift to any pantry. Open the lid, and you see the beautiful, thick set honey, and the smell of vanilla and almonds immediately hits you: designed to be reminiscent of marzipan, which I love. Every jar is traceable to the individual beekeeper.

A trio of chocolate hedgehogs, 60g

This charming trio of little hedgehogs, handmade in Suffolk from 38% Valrhona milk chocolate, is presented in a retro-style box. They’re almost too good to eat, but certainly make a great little present.

Kilner jars, four pack

Well, actually, the gift I’m suggesting is a single Kilner jar that you fill with homemade granola and a handwritten note. I’ve recently discovered you can make granola in the air fryer in 15 minutes: just line a baking tray, add in oats, nuts, seeds, oil, spices such as cinnamon and ginger and a bit of honey. I used this Instagram reel for inspiration – but drizzled olive oil instead of butter. A thoughtful gift that will keep giving (for a few mornings, anyway).

Hebridean seaweed hand wash, 300ml

I love this family-run brand based in the Highlands, which makes everything by hand at its workshop near Fort William. The seaweed hand wash is a treat: it has a subtle smell, is naturally antibacterial and comes in handsome packaging. You can buy refills so that you don’t waste the bottle.

Bath salts, 400g

A hot bath is one of winter’s greatest pleasures. These sleep bath salts include magnesium and are great for sore muscles – either from the gym or just, you know, life.

Marmalade, 220g

I used to live yards away from the London Borough of Jam’s shop in east London, and it was a dangerous spot for my wallet. But it is objectively the best jam and marmalade money can buy. Plus the jar looks stylish on a shelf.

Personalised leather bookmark

A useful and chic gift that is personal – you can put their name on it – but that is universal enough that anyone would appreciate it. Handmade in Lincolnshire from high-quality, thick leather, I suggest tan or black, which will age well.

Caviar keyring

I love the size of this double-sided embroidered keyring – it holds my gym fob and means I can always find it in my bag. The kitsch caviar tin design makes me smile, and I’ve even been to the studio where Brighton-based artist Kate Jenkins designs and makes her fishy creations, so this is a well-endorsed gift.

The Traitors-themed sports socks

For The Traitors lover in the group, these 80% cotton sports socks are a fun gift (you can choose Traitor or Faithful). They’re made in England, comfy – with a padded toe and flat seam – and don’t slip down. I’m getting these for my Traitors-mad daughter.

Rib knit unisex beanie

Everyone appreciates a spare beanie to stuff in their pocket in the winter months, and this rib-knit number feels as soft as cashmere (though it’s an acrylic-nylon blend) and comes in three colours: cheery red would be my festive pick.

Tea towel

This tea towel for the charity Fine Cell Work – providing skills, training and paid work for people in prison – was designed by Cath Kidston to celebrate the theme of regrowth. It’s a lovely weight, made from 100% unbleached cotton, and will look handsome in any kitchen.

Ball of wool

I love the brand Herd because it uses British fleece from Bluefaced Leicester sheep in the north-west of England, which is then made into yarn within 150 miles of the farms. I love its jumpers and accessories, but for those craftier than me, it also sells its oh-so-soft wool by the ball.

Pearl star earrings

These faux pearl earrings from the National Gallery Shop are, I think, a huge find: they look way more expensive than they are, and they’re fun. Neutral enough to suit anyone – especially at Christmas – but with a distinct personality.

Kitpas rice bran wax crayons, set of six

These crayons are a fun gift: if you use them to draw, you can sweep a wet brush over the picture and turn it into a watercolour, but you can also write on mirrors and windows (or any other hard surface) and then wipe it away, making them perfect to whip out for festivities and parties. I’ve had a set for years that I love.

Sign up to The Filter

after newsletter promotion

Enamel mug

A classic enamel mug is great for camping. Having owned a couple of them for years, I’ve also found them good on long walks in the woods with a flask of hot chocolate. As far as I’ve tested, it’s indestructible.

SOS flower essence blend, 15ml

It’s hard to say how much is psychosomatic, but I’ve used this little SOS tincture a few times and found it gave me extra calm. So for anyone who needs a little boost, this could be just the gift.

Pugliese extra virgin olive oil, 250ml

For a keen home chef, a little bottle of premium Pugliese olive oil will go down well. I’ve drizzled this, made from olives grown on the Masseria Borzone estate, over a salad and used it for dipping bread in, and it has a delicious peppery taste. It comes in a smart, almost-sculptural black bottle.

Mini umbrella

The number of brollies I’ve lost on trains or in cafes means I never want to spend a fortune on them: this little one is so dinky it will fit in any sized bag and, cleverly, given the summer we had, is also UPF50, so you can use it as a parasol.

For more, read our guide to the best umbrellas

Real blush fermented tea, 75cl

I am always looking for delicious alcohol-free alternatives to try. This fermented tea feels treat-y thanks to the slight fizz, so it’s wine-adjacent, but crucially isn’t trying to be an alcohol-free wine. It’s also a pretty bottle anyone would be happy to receive.

Phone lanyard

A phone lanyard has slightly changed my life: no more digging around the bottom of my bag in a panic, and added peace of mind when I’m walking around texting, as it’s harder for anyone to snatch.

Ultimate baked bean box

I know a baked bean-lover (she’s actually nicknamed Bean) who would love this upgrade for her regular work-from-home lunch. Bold Bean Co has done the unthinkable and made beans feel premium, and its baked beans are delicious. The gift pack contains three flavours: rich tomato, smoky chilli, and masala. I’ve thoroughly tested the range: I get through a jar every few days.

For more, read Felicity Cloake’s guide to the best baked beans

Crochet kit

A cute present for the crafter: a crochet kit with two balls of wool, a crochet hook and a pattern to make a dramatic collar, using the filet crochet technique. It’s for an intermediate crocheter and should give them 10 hours of fun and a beautiful update for their wardrobe. I’ve used a Wool and the Gang pattern before and, even as a beginner knitter, it was easy to follow (there are online tutorials to help, too).

Scarf bag charm

One of those gifts that you didn’t know you needed, but is pretty: a vintage-inspired scarf affixed to a clip to attach to your bag. I have a necklace from the brand, and the whole range is charming.

Ceramic candle holder

I love lighting the house with candles in the winter months, and tall, plain white table candles are the cheapest way to do it: they look chic when in a lovely candle holder, and this characterful ceramic cube one is particularly charming.

Shinrin-Yoku cleansing bar, 160g

I am deeply in love with the evocative and beautiful products from Earl of East, which was founded by an east London couple obsessed with scent. This cleansing bar has a beautiful fragrance and looks more elevated than a normal bar of soap.

Neuhaus pralines, 50g

For anyone who appreciates a delicious Belgian praline, gift them this cute little box (no need to wrap it, it’s so nice) containing five Neuhaus pralines: incredibly rich and smooth chocolates that make you feel like Willy Wonka savouring each new taste.

Snowman Lego ornament

Lego isn’t just for kids – see the popularity of the big sets at Christmas for evidence (my husband is getting a Home Alone house, but shhh). This is a cute little project that will enable a bit of precious screen-free time.

Candle in a tin

Candles are easy crowd pleasers, unless they smell too synthetic or the label is either too fussy or cheap-looking. This is neither. It’s a candle made from a blend of soya and rapeseed oil wax, which is chosen for a cleaner, slower burn (up to 50 hours), and in a sleek-looking aluminium tin. I love neroli, which is fresh, zesty and uplifting, and the lid is helpful for keeping it covered when not in use (anyone else’s candles get dusty?). It’s a solid present to have in stock in case you need an emergency gift.

Flower frog

Trust me, this is the perfect gift for someone who likes flower arranging: you pop it in the bottom of any vase or pot and then stab the individual stems into it, making them stand up in the way you want. My mother-in-law bought me one years ago, and it transforms even a bunch of supermarket flowers into something that looks Instagram-ready.

Note block

For the stationery addict (hello, this is me), a fancy block of sticky notes from the cult stationery brand Mark+Fold would make an excellent gift. They come as a pack of three – yellow squares, white lines with pleasing tick-boxes, and green dots – and they’re designed to fit on to the wall planner, planner pad or diary, but equally work on their own. I love the geekiness of them.

Northern pasta, 360g

This pasta is beautifully made and packaged (and if you’re giving it to anyone from the north, they will doubly love the sentiment) and made from spelt grown on British regenerative farms, so it’s healthier and higher in fibre than cheap supermarket pasta. I love the radiatori for its big chunky ruffles – perfect for clinging on to homemade sausage pasta – while my kids love the dinkiness of the conchigliette (which is also great in soups). There are various gift bundles if you can stretch the budget, or just buy three bags for under a tenner.

Cross-body bag

This is a sell-out bag for a reason: it suits everyone and is extremely useful. I already have a slightly larger version, but this mini version can fit a phone, wallet, slim book and smallish water bottle (at a push). It has an adjustable strap so it fits neatly wherever you want and is unisex. There’s a wide range of colours, but black is relatively fail-safe.

PBJ chilled bar

Late Night Pudding has designed a range of bars for that after-dinner sweet craving I always have, dressed up in gorgeous, giftable packaging. PBJ chilled bar elevates a humble guilty pleasure into something more luxurious.

Dr Reju-All rejuvenating lip serum, 10ml

Anyone with a vague interest in beauty will love a Korean brand for their Secret Santa. Dr Reju-All’s lip serum is really very good: it has a gentle exfoliator to get rid of chapped lips and then uses PDRN to protect the skin barrier and moisturise. It doesn’t leave your lips too sticky, and it comes in a nice, grownup-looking tube.

For more, read our guide to the best lip balms

Innisfree super volcanic pore clay mask, 80g

This is a cult K-beauty clay mask that contains volcanic clusters from Jeju Island along with lactic acid to absorb excess sebum, cleanse impurities and gently exfoliate. It’s thick and gloopy – as you’d expect from a clay mask – and tightens your skin as it dries. A fun Friday night treat in a jar.

Breathe Deep roll-on

I really love Sweet Bee Organics – I use its magnesium butter on my kids nightly – and this new little roll-on is an excellent addition for anyone who needs to de-stress on the go. You swipe it on your wrists and then breathe in the eucalyptus, menthol, thyme and frankincense blend. I love it – not least because it encourages you to stop and take a beat and a breath.

‘Chloe’s policy’ aims to prevent repeat of case of Treasury worker who took her own life

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 15:00:14 GMT

Exclusive: Parents of Chloe Moffat urge employers to treat staff facing allegations in a kinder, more human way

The parents of a Treasury worker who took her own life last year have launched a policy that directs employers to treat staff in a kinder and more commonsense way, and are asking HR departments across the country to adopt it.

Chloe Moffat’s parents also said the government department plans to plant a memorial garden in her honour at its Horse Guards Road offices.

Moffat, a 26-year-old personal assistant, took her own life the day after she was called into a surprise disciplinary meeting about anonymous complaints alleging she had disclosed sensitive information at work, which she denied. A coroner found in August that the Treasury had “materially contributed” to her death.

She had been convinced she would lose her job, the coroner heard, despite that not being a likely outcome. Moffat’s managers declined to allow her to bring a colleague to the “informal” meeting, did not give her any advance notice of it and refused to tell her whether she was likely to lose her job. They also removed access to her director’s email and changed her work responsibilities.

She had worked at the Treasury for almost three years, loved her job and had an exemplary employment record, the coroner heard.

Her parents, Anne and David Moffat, have been working with the Global Kindness Institute, an NGO, to come up with “Chloe’s policy” for HR departments to adopt to prevent such tragic incidents from happening in future. They are calling on organisations across the country to help develop and take on the policy.

“All we want is for nobody else to go through this,” Anne Moffat said. “If it goes through HR departments, even people considering making allegations, everybody can hopefully follow the Chloe policy and ask if this is really necessary.

“So many people are so policy driven and so into disciplinaries and making people accountable when it may not be necessary. People aren’t being treated in a commonsense, human way.”

The policy calls on HR departments to consider the harms of disciplinary processes to those subjected to them, particularly when complaints are anonymous or unverified. It emphasises prioritising psychological safety and supporting those going through any disciplinary process, as well as minimising these processes in the first place by considering alternatives.

It also calls on HR departments to provide clarity to those going through disciplinary processes, including letting people know if their role is safe.

David Moffat said: “It’s a powerful leadership standard. If it raises the profile of the process that Chloe went through and avoids it happening to anyone else, that is good enough for me.”

The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report acknowledged the department’s role in her death and committed to safeguards. A review of the civil service by the Cabinet Office found that the conditions to which Moffat was subjected had been replicated in other disciplinary meetings.

Anne Moffat said: “If you think about what happened to Chloe, if HR had thought ‘we know that she was very well thought of, nothing else had ever happened, these were the first ever allegations, they were anonymous,’ was this process necessary?”

The prevention of future deaths report issued by the coroner last month found there was still a risk at the civil service due to its disciplinary procedures. The civil service has put in place multiple safeguards to address these issues.

This guidance includes allowing staff to have a supporter in disciplinary meetings, giving proper notice of any such meeting, and informing staff if a dismissal is not likely. The Treasury is also hiring an on-site occupational therapist to support staff wellbeing.

The Moffats met James Bowler, the permanent secretary at the Treasury, at the end of last month. David said: “We felt listened to, and as part of their response to the coroner as well we felt reassured that change was being implemented.

“If the changes they have put forward to the coroner had already been in place, we certainly feel that Chloe would be with us today. It was a very emotional meeting.”

Anne added: “It is the first time we felt that the Treasury had been compassionate to us and it wasn’t defensive or legal speak. They are looking at how to remember Chloe, and looking at the possibility of a memorial garden within the building and marking the garden with a plaque.”

David said: “We feel that Chloe is finally being acknowledged and remembered.”

A Treasury spokesperson said: “The Treasury’s deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.

“Our response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report sets out the action we have taken following this tragic case. An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline. org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping review – surreally awful prequel to the Katniss Everdeen era

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 14:00:14 GMT

Overwrought and boring, this nadir of a prequel to the Games’ death match saga is nothing but a cash grab for an exhausted franchise

Here is yet another iteration of the utterly exhausted, unbearably extended and now surreally boring Hunger Games franchise, based on the YA bestsellers by Suzanne Collins. This one has another of the series’ convoluted faux-mythic subtitles: Sunrise on the Reaping. What, “harvest dawn” not old-timey enough?

Well, “reaping” in fact refers to an annual process by which ordinary smudgy faced, raggedy clothed people are chosen at random for compulsory participation in this futurist dystopia’s brutal, televised survival contest to the death: a bread-and-circuses nightmare with which the rulers keep the populace in a cowed and pacified state. In this Darwinian process, competitors strategically team up with (and then betray) some players against others in the short term, to stay in the game.

The previous episode had an equally tiresome subtitle, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes – and these two films are a prequel to the Katniss Everdeen era with which we were first introduced to the series, although the actual process by which the Games came into being in the first place is still not dramatised. Joseph Zada is 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (played in later-set episodes as a grown man by Woody Harrelson), a cheeky kid who finds himself picked to play. He infuriates the chilling potentate President Snow (played by Ralph Fiennes and resembling George Washington) with a gesture of defiance at the opening ceremony and then with an apparent conspiracy to destroy the Games with explosives. The ruling class are once again a bafflingly bizarre pantomime gallery of grotesques, including Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close) and smarmy young TV presenter Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin). These characters are unconvincing and unfunny in their unreality, and a bewildering contrast to the Steinbeck-style realism of the rustbelt depression in which the ordinary folk live.

As ever, the “televisual” aspect of this is represented in the retro-style TV screens, but no one is ever shown actually watching these Games; Haymitch and his proletarian, quasi-hillbilly community don’t have TVs, but where is the middle class who are supposedly glued to their sets? Jesse Plemons is marginally less caricatured and tiresomely ridiculous as the organiser Plutarch Heavensbee, the younger version of the role earlier played by the late Philip Seymour Hoffman. But, really, this film has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is out on 19 November in Australia, and 20 November in the US and UK.

Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 13:32:44 GMT

I am at Cop31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices

Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.

Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.

Britain has a responsibility to lead, and we are determined to do so. I am proud of the progress we have made to cut emissions by 54% since 1990 and the action we are taking to achieve net zero by 2050. And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad. We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn. Britain exceeded its £3bn nature target and tripled annual adaptation funding from £500m to more than £1.5bn.

And the real measure of that investment is what it has achieved. Since 2011, UK climate finance has helped an estimated 159 million people across the world better adapt to the climate crisis, reduced or avoided 201m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and mobilised about £26bn in public and private finance.

So, what next? At Cop31, Britain will push for action. And what does that look like? A faster clean-energy transition, cuts to methane, protection for forests and oceans, and better access to finance. The drive for electrification, in particular, is a huge global opportunity. Investing in homegrown clean power is a win-win. It allows us to break our dependence on volatile fossil-fuel markets and protect families from price shocks, while reducing the carbon we use. And through the rollout of solar energy, batteries, clean heat and electric vehicles, communities in Britain will directly benefit from this energy transition through lower bills and a stake in the energy system of the future.

after newsletter promotion

Finally, the Climate Change Committee has warned that Britain must adapt for our changed climate – and we are doing exactly that. We also know that the climate crisis is now a national security issue and we must prepare for future threats. That’s why we are protecting homes from flooding and making them better able to withstand extreme weather. We’re building nine new reservoirs in England to secure our water supplies and restoring the natural systems that help protect communities from floods. I know we have more to do. Here in Britain and around the world, the longer governments wait, the more families will face the upheaval of losing homes to extreme weather and the more it will cost to put it right. The first duty of government is to protect people: cutting emissions and preparing for changes already under way.

I know these commitments feel remote, even when what we agree at Cop31 matters here at home. I understand why people question whether governments will maintain their resolve when politics gets difficult. On the doorstep, people want to see progress, not more promises. So I share here what I say there: I will keep pushing for greater ambition on climate and for results people can see: warmer homes, secure jobs, lower exposure to energy-price volatility and communities better protected from extreme weather.

We have too much to lose by stepping back, and everything to gain from leading. Our security, prosperity and the lives of generations to come depend on what we do now.

Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

Help! Why does my apple pie always have a soggy base?

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 13:00:47 GMT

Direct the heat and minimise the moisture to save your pastry from a saturated bottom, says our panel of pie pros

Why does the pastry base of my apple pie always come out soggy? What am I doing wrong? Sophie, by email “The very first thing I would say is that Sophie has got to look at her filling, and how wet it is,” says Calum Franklin, author of The Modern Pie Maker and all-round pie Yoda. “Apples contain quite a lot of water already, so you don’t generally need to add any extra liquid to the filling.” Instead, he’d simply cook the apples with sugar: “Just let them break down.”

That said, Sophie could always consider including some sort of barrier, too, says Dee Rettali, co-founder of Fortitude Bakehouse in London: “My mother was an amazing baker, and she always sprinkled a very fine crumble mix [just sugar and flour, no fat] on the bottom of her pie before putting in any fruit. That will then absorb most of the liquid.”

You need to let the dough rest first, mind, which Rettali does in the freezer until firm: “That will set you up for a good, longer bake, which obviously means you’re baking the bottom more.” Sophie will also need to consider how she gets the heat to her pie bottom, Rettali adds: “When I was a kid, we’d bake apple pies in ceramic dishes or in the lid of a Pyrex casserole dish, and you’d look at the bottom and think, well, that looks a bit raw. Now, I would never tell my mother she did it the wrong way, but when I became a pastry chef, the first thing I was taught was that if you’re making a pie, do it in a metal tin, because it conducts heat better.” If you have a perforated one to hand, so much the better: “That allows the steam to come out, meaning you get a nice, brown bottom.” This is also why she doesn’t bother making a hole in the top of her pies. Franklin, however, does go for a hole, then finishes proceedings with egg wash: “Pure egg yolk, though; no white, because that makes the pastry dull. Then I top that with some demerara sugar for crunch.”

On to the bake itself, and Rettali always pops her tin on a baking stone in the oven, because “it really conducts heat into the bottom of the pie”. Franklin, however, thinks that’s a “slightly unnecessary step”. The reason? “It puts a barrier between the base of the pie and the direct heat.” Instead, he simply slides the tin straight on to a rack in the oven: “It will just cook better.”

Gummy, undercooked pastry can also be avoided simply by baking the pie for a bit longer, Franklin says: “With the exception of my own cookbooks, of course, I never think pie recipes give the right cooking times. Always give yourself an extra 10 minutes.” After all, not every home oven is as hot as it says on the dial. And a large pie, Franklin adds, is going to take at least 40 minutes.

So how do you know it’s ready? “Look for a mahogany colour,” Franklin says. “That means it’s caramelised, it’s tasty and the likelihood is that the base is crisp.” Or, in other words, pie perfection.

Age instead of need drives Alan Milburn’s new reforms. Welcome to the two-tier welfare state

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:58:34 GMT

The long-awaited plan to address youth unemployment in the UK has positive aspects, but it will cause huge anxiety for young people with disabilities

Two things can be true at once. The government’s long-awaited plan to fix the youth unemployment crisis is a multibillion-pound generational reform package – and hundreds of thousands of young disabled people will be afraid that they’re about to lose the money they need to live on. Under Alan Milburn’s proposals – thought to already have the backing of Andy Burnham – young people aged between 18 and 24 would be barred from claiming the two main sickness and disability benefits: the health element of universal credit (UC), for people too ill or disabled to work, and personal independence payments (Pip), which pay for some of the extra costs of disability. While older unemployed disabled people get a “top-up” payment on UC, those under 25 will be given a new “youth allowance”: that’s just the standard benefit rate of just over £75 a week that healthy jobseekers get, alongside significant one-on-one employment support. Those living independently from their parents will get a higher rate of benefit as they seek work, as well as those whose health means they will never be able to have a job. Meanwhile, Pip would be replaced for under-25s with a new higher benefit rate called the “additional cost allowance” that will only be paid to a minority with “significant, well-established and ongoing” costs relating to their disability. That means many of the 453,000 young people who are currently claiming Pip would lose their entitlement to a monthly payment entirely. Instead, they will have to apply for money for a named specific purpose, such as travel expenses or a disability aid. This is in effect the creation of a two-tier welfare state, where the help you receive isn’t determined by your health but the date on your birth certificate. The £3.6bn in cuts would sever the link between need and entitlement that sits at the heart of the safety net – potentially leading to the perverse situation where two people with the same disability get unequal support simply because they’re a different age. After months of stories inflaming the narrative that feckless youngsters are feigning disability for cash, as a fashion statement or because of “social contagion”, Milburn will have felt under immense pressure to curb the youth benefits bill as a trade-off for his other large-scale spending plans. That pensioners receive roughly 55% of the welfare budget and young people (excluding children) just 2.5% is conveniently ignored. It’s true that young people today are facing unique circumstances and Milburn sets out a colossal pile of evidence to that end. And yet he fails to justify why under-25s should have a completely different benefits system from other adults, let alone one that involves giving the generation shut out of the housing and labour markets less financial support than their parents and grandparents. Nor is there much explanation as to why Pip – already up for reform in the Timms review, due to report this month – has been lumped in with an unemployment review, considering many young people who rely on it already have jobs. Even Milburn’s plan to extend child disability living allowance (the children’s version of Pip) from age 16 to 18 – in itself perfectly sensible – is framed as “preparing young people for work”. Not every pound the Treasury spends has to maximise productivity. Sometimes it’s about affording an accessible taxi to get to a friend’s birthday party. Removing Pip from these young people could have a devastating domino effect – not simply because of how much the money is relied on, but because it is a “gateway” benefit to other key support. When an 18-year-old loses Pip, do the changes mean their parent will also lose carer’s allowance? What about the Motability car they use to drive to their apprenticeship? None of this is covered in the review’s 241 pages and will have to be thrashed out by ministers if the recommendations are accepted. There is some reason to be relieved. On top of the longterm investment for employment, Milburn has pledged not to “reduce existing financial help before the replacement support and opportunity are in place”, although we must wait to see what that transition would look like in practice. The higher benefit rates will be welcome to those who have long buckled under the costs of their severe disabilities, as will the pledge to deliver it “immediately” by using information the state already holds (say, in the NHS or schools), rather than putting those with lifelong conditions through yet another assessment. But in Milburn’s own words, there will “intentionally” be a “very high bar” to qualify. That phrase will instil fear in those dreading the thought of not making the grade, not least those with significant disabilities who’ve been promised protection from cuts in the past, only for harsh criteria to judge them as “not disabled enough”. On paper, it’s smart to fix the system to target monthly support more effectively: one in five of Pip’s current 16- to 24-year-old caseload report little to no additional costs from their disability, as very real but “less expensive” conditions such as ADHD and anxiety increase for this group. But years of faulty benefit assessments mean it will be hard to trust that authorities can accurately work out who needs what.

The concept of young disabled people who don’t qualify for an entitlement having to ask local administrators for “permission” to buy something may appease the right, but it will fill claimants who have to justify every expense with trepidation. Meanwhile, there is little word on how to make the workplace more accessible. While employers will be incentivised to hire young people, an “opportunity guarantee” will remain hollow without roles suitable for those with significant health conditions. That a key reason young people are unemployed is poor mental health only makes it more obvious that the stress of losing their benefits will hardly make them feel more equipped to seek or stay in work. “Generational” reform may assuage the Labour backbenchers who have hung on for a year for Milburn’s plans. But it will be little comfort to the young people reading the headlines who are now scared they won’t make the cut to keep the benefits they need to pay the bills. For them, the wait is just beginning.

‘We are all in’: the Democrats trying to turn round the US’s reputation at Cop31

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:30:54 GMT

The 120-strong America Is All In group are trying to ensure that the US won’t remained sidelined at the climate talks for very much longer. Plus: wild oysters are back in Scotland and a super El Niño looms over Cop

Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The final week of Cop31 is in full swing, with just four days left to set a broad range of climate commitments into concrete action. I am on the ground at this year’s UN annual climate summit, where thousands of world leaders, businesses, nonprofits and scientists have converged in Antalya, Turkey, and there’s a lot left to do as the clock ticks down.

“Nearly 200 countries are working through 165 mandates,” executive secretary Simon Stiell told reporters at the midpoint on Saturday, pushing for a swift move to the hardest issues and championing compromise. “Each country has a view,” he said. “Every country has a voice.”

There have, of course, been some notable voices missing in Antalya. Although this Cop is the largest in history, with more than 92,000 participants registered, some of the heaviest hitters have left their seats empty. The UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make an appearance; China’s Xi Jinping opted out, and government heads from Canada, Japan and parts of Europe were absent last week.

Then, of course, there’s US president Donald Trump, who has repeatedly rebuked the summit and the challenging work being done within its walls. Last year, he told UN leaders that their governments would fail if they continued their work on the climate, which he called “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world”.

But just weeks after his party received a crushing defeat in the US midterm elections, Democrats emboldened by the landslide win set a different tone in Antalya this week. Roughly 120 delegates – Congressional lawmakers, governors, and local leaders among them – said the US wouldn’t remain sidelined for very much longer.

More on what they said, after today’s climate reads.

“America is not only back – we are all in,” California congressman Jared Huffman told reporters, noting that Democrats would soon likely hold the strongest majority in 50 years and would be able to challenge Trump’s anti-climate agenda.

Huffman is one of about 120 US delegates in attendance here in Antalya. They have maintained an American presence and championed climate progress at the talks, despite the president’s “drill baby, drill” approach of more fossil fuel extraction, deregulation and climate science crackdowns.

“While the Trump administration has shamefully abandoned international climate agreements and attacked climate and clean energy policies, state and federal climate leaders from the United States are here to show the world that they are committed to working with the global community,” Rachel Cleetus, climate program director for the Union of Concerned Scientists, said.

The delegation was led by California governor Gavin Newsom, a possible candidate for the 2028 presidential campaign who has been vocal about his state’s role in keeping climate agreements in the US alive.

“Trump is temporary. California’s partnerships around the world are not,” Newsom said in a statement about the work he and his colleagues were continuing this year at Cop. “States and local governments are where the promise of the Paris agreement becomes real, and California keeps its word.”

Delegates pointed to work at the subnational level to advance renewable energy and curb emissions as a path forward for the world’s second-biggest emitter to make progress, regardless of who is in the White House. Over the next decade, US state-level policies, market forces and falling technology costs can reduce carbon emissions up to 46% below 2005 levels, according to a new analysis from the University of Maryland Center for Global Sustainability and the America Is All In group that backed the Cop delegation.

That doesn’t mean they aren’t hopeful for a president who would officially re-enter the climate talks. Delegates are already laying the groundwork for the US return to the talks if Newsom or another Democrat moves into the White House. Either way, Huffman said, next year will be different thanks to this month’s landslide victory in the midterms.

“We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said. “Soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change – the United States will officially be back in as part of the negotiating effort at a future Cop.”

A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:00:37 GMT

Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna

In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side.

Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food.

In February 2019 the then mayor, Virginio Merola, asked his fellow citizens on Twitter to send him photos of spaghetti bolognese spotted abroad, and opened the collection with the chalkboard of a London restaurant. He told journalists it was “embarrassing to be known around the world for something that doesn’t exist”.

It wasn’t the first attempt at a clean-up. A few months earlier the Accademia Italiana della Cucina had formally registered with Bologna’s chamber of commerce a recipe for spaghetti in a tinned tuna sauce, billed as “Bolognese style”, which the press promptly hailed as the real spaghetti bolognese. In its eagerness to deny that spaghetti with ragù existed, the Accademia had officially handed the city a dish now cooked all over Italy, which seems to have begun around Rome in the early 1900s and has little or nothing to do with Bologna.

To understand how spaghetti bolognese became so famous, we need to step back. The first reason lies in the name itself. The city’s reputation travelled long before the pasta, which only appears in the 1890s. Bologna had been a byword across Europe for centuries, thanks to the cured meat that made it famous from the Renaissance onwards: mortadella.

In 1596 the pamphleteer Thomas Nashe mocked the poet Barnabe Barnes for strutting about court in “a codpisse as big as a Bolognian sawcedge”. His readers evidently knew exactly what a Bologna sausage looked like and needed no explanation. By 1660 Robert May’s The Accomplisht Cook was already giving a recipe for “Bolonia Sausages”, which English cookbooks went on copying for generations. Mortadella had always been made for export, but from the late 19th century, once the city’s charcutiers had learned to tin it, mortadella and the name of Bologna knew no borders.

The second reason is that Bolognese ragù was a small revolution. Neapolitan ragù, a century older, was made by braising a large joint of veal, whose juices dressed the pasta while the meat itself came to the table as the main course. The Bolognese version puts minced meat straight into the pasta course, which becomes richer and no longer depends on a long and costly braise. The thinking is much the same as the hamburger’s, which swaps a steak for mince to make something cheaper and more practical, but every bit as good.

Ragù entered the cookbooks in 1891, when Pellegrino Artusi published his “Maccheroni alla bolognese” in Science in the Kitchen and the Art of Eating Well, made with lean veal, pancetta, butter, onion, carrot and stock, and still no tomato. In this recipe, the true ancestor of ragù alla bolognese, the stars are dried durum wheat maccheroni, not yet tagliatelle. Spaghetti soon followed. They first appear in 1898, in an advertisement for the Hôtel Ville et Bologne in Turin offering “Spaghetti di Napoli alla bolognese”. Before ragù was ever paired with tagliatelle, it had already struck up a partnership with spaghetti.

In Bologna it was fresh pasta that kept ragù company for the rest of its history, but abroad, and in the United States above all, spaghetti bolognese took hold, for an obvious reason. Egg pasta was hard to come by, so when Julia Lovejoy Cuniberti translated Artusi’s recipe in 1917 she was already suggesting the sauce for “macaroni or spaghetti”. In 1952, at a fair held at the Royal Festival Hall in London, even the Queen Mother recognised spaghetti bolognese with interest, just before being welcomed at the British stand with a cup of tea.

Tagliatelle and spaghetti went their separate ways while the recipe was still taking its first steps, but that doesn’t mean spag bol has no right to exist. Perhaps one day the Bolognese will decide that having their city’s name known all over the world matters more than who gets to use it. Even then, tourists can rest assured that every time they order spaghetti bolognese, they will be corrected, kindly but firmly.

Luca Cesari is an Italian food historian and the author of A Brief History of Pasta. To order a copy, visit the Guardian bookshop.

They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:00:37 GMT

The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’

‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.”

On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers.”

Sat inches across from them, drummer Will Bradley breaks into a dry chuckle. “We are certainly not going to entertain.”

Life Without Buildings ended too soon, just before a post-punk revival in the early 00s that would have embraced their taut, innovative music, and years before the recent sprechgesang (spoken singing) movement – Dry Cleaning, Yard Act et al – that seemed to draw inspiration from Tompkins’ unique vocals, though her inspired flood of babble and rhythmic poetry has a disruptive, joyful magic that sets her far apart. In three years, they released one sublime studio album and a handful of singles, and played numerous shows, sometimes to packed rooms, often to just five to 10 people, before splitting in 2002 having achieved “only minor cult/niche success”, says Bradley.

Long after their trail went cold, however, this buried treasure of turn-of-the-millennium indie was rediscovered. In 2018, Frank Ocean played The Leanover, their signature track, on his Apple Music show. Then, one morning during lockdown, Beatrice Laus (AKA Beabadoobee) mimed along to the evocative first 11 seconds of The Leanover to entertain her followers on TikTok, who then shared themselves miming to those same 11 seconds (Beabadoobee’s initial TikTok has now been streamed almost half a million times). Two decades on, Life Without Buildings found their audience, who will finally get to see the group play this week, as they briefly reunite for four gigs marking Rough Trade’s 50th birthday celebrations.

“Robert, Will and I started playing music,” says bassist Chris Evans, of the group’s origins in late-90s Glasgow. “But that didn’t work out.” The trio were under the spell of experimental German electronic music, listening to lots of Underground Resistance, techno and post-rockers Disco Inferno. “We’d combine electronics with live guitar and drums,” says Gray. “And it always sounded bollocks.”

They reformatted as a guitar, bass and drums unit, though the music they played was far from traditional, often chasing the same riff for hours at a time. “But everything changed when Sue joined,” says Gray. Tompkins was a member of Elizabeth Go, a local art collective whose number included Cathy Wilkes, Victoria Morton, Sarah Tripp and Tompkins’ sister Hayley, at whose events she would perform from sheets of handwritten and typewritten paper. “She was brilliant,” says Bradley. “We all said, ‘This is it’. There was no doubt.”

They invited her to their practice space, playing song ideas at length, Tompkins selecting pieces she could work with as they pared their riffs back to the melodic bone. The music was “rock’n’roll, but like Television and the Modern Lovers were rock’n’roll, not Status Quo,” says Gray. “It was about doing the unexpected. We were conscious to not be boring.” Some songs took a direction they dubbed “Krautrock Keith Richards”, while others were “tumbling around, falling over themselves”. The Leanover was of this second category and was “the breakthrough. We recorded the demo in my bedroom, Sue with a cheap microphone, the rest of us squashed up on my bed watching her.”

During rehearsals, Tompkins would write on sheets of A4 that she’d later edit at her electric typewriter, which she operated like a musical instrument, creating rhythms within the music by tapping out words and staccato repeated letters she’d later speak/sing. She juxtaposed gnomic phrases and sentence fragments with rhythmic stutters and vocal tics, all seemingly improvised but actually painstakingly scripted. “Sue’s vocals built a structure that was rhythmic and melodic,” says Gray. “Frank Ocean must have recognised a flow he’d heard nowhere else. It’s like Dilla time,” the particular swing of hip-hop producer J Dilla: “Its own thing.”

Her repeating murmur of “if I lose you in the street”, which had enraptured Beabadoobee and her followers, was as haunting as it was impenetrable. “It veers between something meaningful, and not,” Tompkins says. “It’s about love and loss: it could be a child losing a toy, or a person losing a parent or a boyfriend or girlfriend. Even if it sounds nonsensical, it isn’t; there’s sense in it, it has meaning to me.”

Backed by New Town, one of their Krautrock Keith Richards numbers, The Leanover became their debut single on Rough Trade offshoot Tugboat in 2000. “The sum total of our ambitions was to get played on John Peel,” says Gray; the veteran DJ “never picked up on it”, but BBC Radio 1’s Steve Lamacq played New Town enough times for Tugboat to commission an album.

“I was apprehensive,” says Gray, “particularly because you hear stories about engineers being dicks, and what Sue was doing was so unconventional.” But when producer Andy Miller introduced himself by saying, deadpan, that he “taught dolphins to work as security guards”, the group knew they’d found someone following a kindred offbeat. Miller encouraged their invention in the studio; they recorded album closer Sorrow in one take, moments after it was written, its intimacy complementing the song’s fragile, fractured vibe. “Andy hadn’t sorted out the mic-placement or anything,” says Bradley, “but he ran tape anyway. You feel like you’re in the room with Sue, eavesdropping her talking.”

Any Other City arrived in February 2001, a 4/10 drubbing by NME equating it to “the scrape of fingernails on a blackboard”; it would fall to future generations to recognise the band’s idiosyncratic excellence. That month, the group opened for labelmates the Strokes at the Camden Barfly. It was the New Yorkers’ first London headline gig, the tiny room packed to bursting, and they were indeed as magnificent that night as legend remembers. However, they still didn’t possess the maverick, lightning-in-a-bottle magic of their support act, who played one of the most remarkable shows I’ve ever seen, a riot of joy and art that absolutely was entertaining. But Gray had a sense of “Rough Trade’s attention shifting”; certainly, over the months that followed, the Strokes’ accessible, familiar pop made indie rock suddenly bankable, a rising tide that would leave more experimental groups like Life Without Buildings untouched.

The following year, Belle and Sebastian took the group on tour across the UK: audiences heckled them and it was, Gray remembers, “fairly miserable”. They’d begun writing a second album, but Tompkins signalled she was done. “It was like I woke up and realised I was in a band,” she says. “And it was a lovely band. But if I was in a band I wouldn’t be able to do exhibitions; I’d be in the back of a transit van. It was very selfish,” she adds, as her bandmates shake their heads in amiable disagreement.

In the years since, Evans relocated to Brussels, where he works as an artist (currently exhibiting in Amsterdam and Vienna, and next year he’ll release a record with the poet Bianca Stone as Sudden Wealth), while art curator and critic Bradley is director of Oslo gallery Kunsthall. Tompkins and Gray remained in Glasgow, the singer mostly focusing on visual art (though she contributed vocals to Sleaford Mods’ No Touch earlier this year), while Gray has continued to make music, with a marvellous new album by his group Whin and a collaboration with Joseph Quimby of Rhins imminent. Life Without Buildings, however, remained firmly in the past, even as The Leanover began its remarkable second act.

“We’d all decided we were never going to go back to it,” says Bradley. “I really liked it as this half-forgotten, quite beautiful moment in the past. When we split, there was no soul-searching, no regret. When you do something you enjoy, but it’s only minorly successful, but you still build your identity around it, and your future, but you can’t pay the rent and you can’t build a life, and you’re becoming bitter … We’d realised there was a danger of spoiling the joy of it. And it couldn’t exist without that joy.”

Later that night at Mono, however – the musicians quickly slipping into the interlocking melodies and life-affirming rhythms of the songs, Tompkins reading from her reams of A4 and reinhabiting her enigmatic songs – everything that has been precious about Life Without Buildings remains intact and alive. Afterwards, hugging her bandmates outside the venue, in the July Glasgow rain, Tompkins seems giddy, like she just stepped off the greatest rollercoaster of her life.

“It wasn’t without elements of pure fear,” she says. “There was some of that tonight. But I get so energised when they’re playing. There’s something pure about music that is so joyful. I really wanted to enjoy it. And I really did.”

Life Without Buildings play St Luke’s, Glasgow, 17 November; and Koko, London, 19 and 20 November
