‘The landslide hit the side of my car. I heard screaming, and realised it was me’

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:00:36 GMT

Location: Agassiz, Canada

Disaster: Southern British Columbia floods, 2021

This is Chelsey Sharpe’s story

In 2021, Chelsey Sharpe was working part-time as a yoga instructor when a mudslide swept her car off the highway. Climate change made the heavy rains behind that mudslide and the 2021 floods across southern British Columbia more likely.

Around Remembrance Day, I was visiting one of my best friends in the Okanagan. The weekend was full of dance parties with my niece and nephew, authentic Mexican cuisine, fresh homemade churros, and games.

I didn’t really want to go home. I took my time leaving. I finally got on the road at about 2 or 3pm and, because of road closures, found myself on Highway 7 driving through Agassiz. I didn’t know why the roads were closed. I thought it was just weather. I didn’t take this route ever.

I remember stopping at a farmer’s market in Keremeos at about 4pm. The sun was starting to set. I made multiple stops to take pictures of the sunset and the sky. I wanted to capture the way the sun was reflecting on the clouds. It was oranges, pinks, and tons of different colours.

As I was approaching Princeton, rain started to set in. It was a steady patter on my windshield. I was listening to Snoop Dogg on Joe Rogan. Then my phone lost data. All I heard for a good hour was silence and the rain.

There was a ton of traffic when Highway 1 and Highway 3 were starting to merge near Hope. Traffic was crawling. Typically, this road trip takes four to five hours. I’d been on the road for about six hours at that point. I remember thinking: “When I get to Hope, I’m going to see if there is a motel that I can just pull in at and stay the night.”

When I was passing through Hope, the city was blacked out. There was no power anywhere. It was very eerie. You could see candlelight shining through the windows of homes and small businesses. It was not an option to stop there. My GPS said I would be home in about 90 minutes. I thought: “That’s OK. I’ll just keep going.”

At about 7pm, traffic was starting to pick up on the stretch between Hope and Agassiz. The cars around me helped illuminate some of the road, but it was really hard to see because it was so dark. I noticed a tree was starting to fall a little ways up the mountain. I thought: “At the speed that I’m going relative to where the tree is falling, if I try to slow down the tree will hit me.” I made a split decision to speed up.

I eased on the accelerator, because I thought if I could get past the tree then I’d be fine. My podcast started to kick back on, and I was like: “Oh, great. We have service again.”

A split second later my car was hit, almost like a freight train crashed into the passenger side. It was being pushed and careened. I was tumbling down and then, all of a sudden, I stopped moving. It must have lasted for a minute or less, but time stood still.

I was gripping my steering wheel as hard as I could, and I heard screams. I realised it was me screaming. In my screams, I heard the sound of a car horn blaring. I realised it was my car.

My car was leaning up slightly. I remember my headlights were shining, but I couldn’t see anything. I didn’t register that I was in a pile of debris. My car was surrounded with fallen trees, big boulders, and so much mud.

I realised: “Oh my God, this is an emergency.” Because I heard people outside my car, I started yelling: “Help! Help!” Then I started to clue in that anyone there at that moment would be in the same position that I was. They were also in need of help.

I had my phone with me and an old iPhone for music. I went into my centre console, pulled out my music phone, and held on to it just in case. Then, I pulled on the cord that my phone was plugged into. It came back empty. I reached down near my feet to where the cord came from. I stuck my hand into about a foot of muddy, dark water.

Even though my old iPhone didn’t have a sim card, it could still connect to emergency lines. I called 911. An operator put me through to an ambulance line. I explained: “I’ve been hit by a mudslide about an hour outside Hope, but I don’t know where I am.” The woman on the other line said: “Can you get out of your car?”

It’s funny how my brain was starting to turn back on as I realised I needed to get out of this situation. “I don’t know, maybe,” I said. I click the button to undo my seatbelt and it doesn’t work. I frantically start clicking it and, by some miracle, it comes out.

I looked up and noticed my sunroof had broken because a big tree fell on it. I got up and shimmied myself out around the tree and broken glass. I perched on top of this big tree trunk on my car. I looked around and it was very dark. There was some light from my vehicle because it was still running. We were in a body of water. I saw a patch of trees off to my left, but everywhere else around me was clear. The mudslide had taken out everything.

A vehicle with four UBC [University of British Columbia] students was behind my car. They must have been 19 or 20. A lot of them were in T-shirts. Some were barefoot. They were all huddled under one jacket. There was another car off to my right with the two women. We called out to each other. We confirmed we were all alive. Way off to the left, I saw a light coming from a pickup truck with a man and his wife. They were too far to see or hear.

I was watching the raindrops fall into the water and the water level slowly rise over the brake lights of my car. My car started to die. The lights shut off.

Time kept ticking away. There were very long stretches of darkness. At about 8.30, I was thinking: “We’ll be out of here by 10pm.” Then, 10pm rolled around. I remember thinking: “We’ll be out of here by midnight.”

A lot of the time on my car was spent shivering. I was wearing my moccasins, soccer pants and a white zip-up cotton hoodie that was soaking wet.

I was so tense from shivering, the muscles in my quads felt as if they were charley horsing [cramping]. I knew that when we breathe, our body relaxes on the exhale. I spent time taking very intentional deep breaths to stretch out my limbs and give my mind something to focus on. I remember trying to meditate, putting myself in the perspective of the forest. I told myself these trees are here all the time. The animals are here all the time. I was just passing through. But I got scared that I would fall in the water, so I would open my eyes.

My imagination was starting to play around. I thought of boats coming across the water. I thought of a helicopter coming and scooping us up. Some of these fantasies were not realistic. That was just my desperation wanting to get out and feeling as if I didn’t have what it took to get out of there on my own.

When I would call 911, my calls would sometimes get disconnected. At one point, I was put through to the Agassiz fire department, where I connected with the fire chief, Corey. I remember asking Corey at about 11.30pm if there was any way he could call my dad and merge our phone calls.

I took my best guess at his phone number. I said: “Hey, Dad, I just want you to know that I’m OK. I was hit by a mudslide a couple of hours ago. I’m sitting on top of my car right now, waiting for a search and rescue. Can you pick me up at some point tonight?” He was shocked. “Yes, of course,” he said. I remained on the phone with Corey consistently throughout the rest of the night.

At one point, one of the UBC students began to have an asthma attack and didn’t have access to his inhaler. Corey, via me, instructed one of the students to check his pulse, one of the students to count to 10. I relayed that information to Corey, who was monitoring the student’s vitals to make sure he was stable.

Eventually, 1am rolled around, and I remember seeing the beam of search and rescue lights far out in the distance. They were navigating fallen power lines and fallen trees. Over the next hour or two, rescue made their way closer to where we were. One of the guys yelled out: “Do you think you can make your way over to where we are, and then we can help you navigate back to the road?”

I said: “You want us to get in the swamp?” This was what I’d been avoiding for the last five hours.

I unzipped my sweater because it was soaking wet and weighing me down. I started to climb over the back of my car and the big tree that was there. I was perched on this tree trunk like a frog. When it was time to start moving, I was paralyzed by fear. I thought the swamp was going to suck me in.

I looked up, and one of the search and rescue crew had waded over to where we were. He reached his hand out to me, and I grabbed it. I felt the courage to get in the water. I had my hand on his shoulder until we were out of the waist-deep water.

The search and rescue team guided us through boulders and rocks. I remember seeing a crumpled up “Beware of Rockfall” sign in the debris.

All nine of us eventually completed the hour-long trek back to solid ground.

Once we were settled on a bus, I borrowed somebody’s phone to call my dad and let him know that we were out and going to Chilliwack general hospital. It was tricky for the team to navigate the roads to the hospital because there were so many hazards. When we got to the hospital at about 4am they triaged us. I had some soft-tissue damage. The couple that was in the truck were being assessed for a concussion.

After my dad got to the hospital at about 5am, I started to feel this horrible gut pain. I didn’t even register that I had to pee so badly. The fear and being in survival mode had shut down that part of my body.

We got on the road about 6am. My dad was bringing me back to my house, where I lived with my roommates Ruth and Ava. It was still raining a lot. I closed my eyes and fell asleep. My dad drove through a puddle on the passenger side, the side the slide hit me on. That jerked me awake. It felt like I was back in that moment. It was PTSD.

My dad dropped me home roughly 12 hours after the slide. I’m standing in the foyer, and Ruth walks out of her room. I’m wearing a hospital gown, my hair was in a bun, half out and caked in mud. She was like: “What happened?”

I took a shower and there was dirt all over the bathroom floor. I cuddled my cat and went to bed. I was in and out of sleep throughout that day. I remember Tuesday, I felt like I had internal bleeding or something. I called my dad and was like: “I think I need to go to the hospital. I am in so much pain.” Then, I started my cycle. It was regular cramps that you get around your cycle. Because I was safer, my system started to release all of the cortisol that embedded itself into my core, amplifying that pain times 10.

I started to go back and reassess every decision I had made that day. Had I not made stops, would I have made it through and gotten home that evening? There was another slide in Lillooet on Highway 99. A couple died and left behind a two-year-old daughter. I remember thinking, why? Who decides who gets to stay and who has to leave? These are questions that we ask and will never know.

For about a year after the mudslide happened, I would consistently have dreams about the end of the world. It was asteroids, earthquakes – scary situations I couldn’t do anything about. A lot of them involved floods. Sometimes I was thriving in the apocalypse, and sometimes I was struggling to survive. I experience a lot more anxiety. I do my best to deal with it because I don’t want fear to run the show.

I took time off work to take care of myself. I received help as soon as I could. It put me in a position to get my education in counselling. I am able to make a difference with people in their lives. I wouldn’t want to relive the slide, but I’m grateful for the lessons I’ve learned, for the perspective it’s given me, and for the way that it’s helped me realise that I need to live a life that feels aligned.

Even if you’re in a situation that feels out of control, when you change the way that you’re showing up inside of that circumstance, the outcome inevitably changes. My hope is that anyone who is reading this realises they are empowered inside of their own life, and they can make a big difference, even if we feel small.

Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 11:30:35 GMT

Former minister’s 278-page report calls for changes to employment regulations, education, healthcare and benefits

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Five months on from a first report detailing the growing crisis of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet), Alan Milburn has produced his recommendations on how to tackle it. Set out over 278 pages, they amount to, as he readily accepts, a major rethink of everything from employment regulations to education, healthcare and benefits.

Here is what he has said.

While this was in part covered by the first report, Milburn is at pains to begin the new volume with his belief that the issue of Neets is not a failure of the younger generation but a case of them being let down by a series of structural factors. “The young people I have met over the last year are not asking for an easier life. They are asking for a fair chance to build one,” he writes.

The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.”

At the centre of the proposed new system is a youth opportunity service (YOS), which would offer young people support in areas such as training and health – and would in return expect participation.

Currently, about 13.5% of people aged 16-24 in the UK are classified as Neet, the highest proportion in Europe outside Romania. This is not a new problem, the report notes, pointing out that the Neet rate has stayed above 10% for most of the past 25 years.

The aim over a decade-long transformational plan would be to match the records of the best-performing European nations on this metric, such as the Netherlands and Denmark. While Milburn talks playfully of aiming for “Neet zero”, he says this means an eventual consistent rate of about 5%.

He says the policies in his plan would get the Neet rate to about 6.8% by 2036.

Noting that youth employment has declined even as overall employment rose, Milburn says opportunities are limited by issues affecting young people – for example, a lack of connections to secure work experience or first jobs – and also employers, including the costs of taking on staff and regulatory complexities.

The report says this is worsened by a lack of government help. While Denmark spends about 1% of GDP on all-age hiring incentives and subsidies, in the UK it is about 0.1%.

The report sets out a series of recommendations, including:

Doubling the salary threshold for employer national insurance for entry-level jobs for young people in retail and hospitality, possibly then expanded to other sectors.

Extending the existing youth jobs grant, which gives up to £3,000 to employers who takes on a staff member on universal credit for at least six months, so it also applies to people not on benefits, with extra incentives for small employers and people facing barriers, such as those with disabilities or care leavers.

Avoid minimum pay rates being a barrier – for example, any moves to put young people’s minimum wages closer the adult rate should be judged “against the critical goal of protecting youth employment”.

This should be matched with increased simplicity for companies, with a single digital gateway leading to all the schemes set up to help young workers, and more clarity on help for workers with disabilities.

All this would be united in a so-called youth opportunity test, under which any future tax or regulatory policy changes would look at their effect on young workers, set out in a law.

The report notes that this is a long-term issue, with many of the indicators of future Neet status, such as low attainment and poor attendance, being clear during childhood. Milburn also says that while countries with low Neet rates take vocational skills seriously, in England “technical education has too often been regarded as for somebody else’s child”.

Among changes the report recommends are:

More investment in early years provision, such as family hubs, and individual support in school if a student is seen as being at “material risk of disengagement”.

Less use of school exclusion where possible. The report notes that the Netherlands has a permanent exclusion rate 73% lower than England’s.

More focus in school on preparedness for work, as well as passing exams.

More investment in further education and in apprenticeships, with greater financial incentives for employers who hire apprentices.

University courses “must be able to demonstrate clear value for learners, employers and the wider economy,” with funding withdrawn for poorly performing examples.

The report identifies health as central to the Neets issue, with more than half of young people in this position reporting a health condition.

Milburn says much of this is down to a health service “designed to diagnose and treat illness” rather than intervening earlier, and that is not aimed at helping people into work, with diagnoses and the fit note system creating a “binary” mindset.

It recommends:

Much quicker access to health and mental health assistance, long before a formal diagnosis, based around the new YOS system. If someone has a health issue, their YOS-designated adviser can point them towards advice and help, potentially including talking therapies.

A move away from GPs issuing fit notes, which would instead become the responsibility of other health experts such as occupational therapists or non-clinicians such as employment advisers.

The report is highly critical of what it calls a current system that can trap people in dependence. “It asks a young person what they cannot do before it asks them what, with the right support, they could. The welfare system for too many young people has become a trap when it ought to be a springboard.”

At the same time, it argues that crudely cutting rates or entitlement do not work, “fiscally nor morally”. It says: “If they leave young people destitute, then costs merely show up somewhere else on the state’s balance sheet in health, housing or criminal justice. Spending less is not the same as succeeding. The test is whether lives and trajectories change.”

Saying more must be invested in helping people on benefits, it recommends:

A new “opportunity guarantee” for a place in education, training or work for anyone aged 18 to 24, along with a “support guarantee” for the support required for them to do this. Based on significant investment, these must be in place before the changes begin, the report says.

Among the options under the guarantee are: a government-subsidised job with employers receiving £3,000 for each young person they recruit – more for smaller businesses or when the employee has extra needs; an FE place, or technical or university learning as appropriate; an apprenticeship; a work placement of up to 12 weeks; structured volunteering such as conservation, community gardening or a cadetship; help to create a business.

The “backstop” to all this would be a state-financed six-month job with an employer.

The creation of a new “youth allowance”, set at the under-25 rate of universal credit.

A new “health and disability fund” operated by the local YOS to help with extra costs, which are or might be time-limited.

An “additional cost allowance”, replacing personal independence payment for young people, when their disability-related extra costs “are significant, established and ongoing”. The report says eligibility “would be more closely targeted at those with demonstrable extra costs for functional needs that are long-term and enduring”, with an aim of enabling independence and participation.

A “severe and complex needs insurance”, a more generous long-term award without a qualifying period, for those with the most profound disabilities, and where it is clear they are unlikely ever to be able to work.

With this would come changes to “actively reward and enable participation”, for example allowing young people to keep more earnings before benefits are cut, and extra money for people who undertake civic service.

With this would come a responsibility to engage. Someone who persistently refuses to do so would lose their youth allowance benefit, but only after “multiple attempts to re-engage and understand what has gone wrong”.

While much of the media buildup to the report has been questions about whether the changes could result in benefits payments overall starting to fall in this parliament, Milburn makes it plain that this must be a longer-term process, with investment preceding savings.

The report says: “While the intention is to hit the ground running, the speed of change has to be sustained over time. This is a 10-year plan, not a one-year sprint … Short-termism has been a constant feature of our country’s approach to this issue over the last 50 years.”

This would involve an initial investment of £500m in 2027-28, taken from existing spending, which would then “ramp up”.

By 2036-37, the report says, annual investment would be about £5.8bn, covering the guarantees, hiring incentives and health, education and skills changes, offset by £3.6bn of savings and £2.4bn in increased tax revenues, covering lower welfare payments and more tax receipts.

I got scammed on Instagram – and it led to a truly disgusting dinner

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 11:00:35 GMT

Intrigued by an unusual recipe for spinach tacos, I followed the instructions, but was left with a soggy, inedible mess. It turns out there are a lot of made-up meals out there

I can’t tell you when my Instagram algorithm changed, from – this is embarrassing, but what the hell – buff guys trying to exercise and being interrupted by a Staffordshire bull terrier who wants to help them exercise, to cooking videos, but it has. I now get endless food content, following the same format: a millennial has 20 minutes to make dinner for his or her beloved (it’s very gender neutral), and launches into some unlikely techniques. He might shove a load of chicken into a cake tin, sprinkle mismatched spices all over, bake it, then slice it, as if it were a cake. Or she might cook tagliatelle in a pan of milk and salmon. This is not how it’s done, I think, as I watch all the way to the end, and then am astonished to be fed yet more weird food content.

Drawn with an almost zombified lack of free will, I got the yen to try it for myself. What would happen if you boiled a white cabbage whole, then roasted it in honey and miso? Well, I can tell you: the cabbage is very soft on the outside, and still uncooked on the inside, and this is why cooks, since time began, have been slicing a cabbage before they try to cook it.

I hit peak gullibility when I tried to imitate the spinach taco. Soak the spinach in water for three hours, she instructed; add nothing but salt; put it in a blender, and it’ll fry like a pancake. Newsflash – this does not work at all. How would that work? It’s just a load of waterlogged spinach. It didn’t even taste nice once I aborted the quest and just fried it in garlic the regular way. It had spent too long in water, and was off-puttingly spinachy.

Further research was called for, and it turns out the fake spinach taco is a well-known Instagram scam. I’ve learned nothing about vegetables that I haven’t known since the year 2000, but I think I am getting closer to the point of a scam: a lot of people just do it because they can.

Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 10:00:10 GMT

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood

‘Spit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones.

It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies, Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”.

The nurturing man, Hrdy says on a video call from her home in rural northern California, used to be laughed off as an “imaginary creature” by some of her colleagues. But “what we’re seeing in many developed countries is something very unusual for mammals that has astounded me as an evolutionary biologist – men completely committed to looking after babies with a tenderness that you think of as maternal”.

As well as higher levels of oxytocin, researchers have found lowered testosterone in fathers who care for babies – mirroring findings in other mammals and bird species. But neuroscientists have also learned something else. When they scanned the brains of men who were primary carers, neural circuits in the hypothalamus and amygdala were activated, rather than the much newer – in evolutionary terms – neocortex. What this suggested to Hrdy was that such men are drawing on a genetic inheritance shared with fish, frogs and other species in which paternal care features. Her hope is that the activation of such capacities could, over time, help to bring about a less belligerent world.

“This is the country where 40% of us elected a man who brags about never changing a diaper, and we’ve got Pete Hegseth [the secretary of defence], who says we need men with higher testosterone. Boy, do I have news for him. If you have normal testosterone and take supplements, your sperm count is going to go pishooo” – she demonstrates with a swooping downward gesture and laughs.

Hrdy (pronounced to rhyme with birdie) is primarily known for her work on women and monkeys. After earning a PhD in anthropology at Harvard in the 1970s, she became a leading figure in a cohort of scientists who challenged the male bias running through evolutionary theory. Given evolution’s foundational place in biology, it is hard to overstate how important this is. But while Hrdy is widely admired as an innovative thinker and communicator, she never gained anything like the name recognition of science writers such as Richard Dawkins, or the conservationists Jane Goodall and Dian Fossey.

Charles Darwin proposed that sexual selection was primarily a struggle between males. While he recognised that “coy” females had some agency as choosers – for example, between the spectacular nests built by male bowerbirds – his emphasis on male-male competition set up a sexist asymmetry whereby they were viewed as facing selection pressures from which females were exempt. George Eliot, the English novelist, was among the early critics of the idea that this pointed to male superiority. “You can see her on my bulletin board,” Hrdy says, moving her chair to reveal Eliot’s face. But it was a century before female scientists were in a position to counter evolutionary sexism with their own fieldwork, ideas and experiments.

“I don’t blame Darwin for being a Victorian; I am who I am, an 80-year-old grandmother who grew up in Texas,” Hrdy says. “I am a fifth-generation Texan with a Texas accent – and I think you are hearing it because I am getting animated.”

From the perspective of the present, it is obvious that Darwin was influenced by the racist, imperialist and sexist ideas of his time. But the revisions proposed by Hrdy and others were not well received. Her PhD research on infanticide committed by male hanuman langur monkeys in Rajasthan, India, for instance, was very controversial. “Growing up in south Texas in a very patriarchal environment, my family wanted to control my life and tell me who to marry, all that,” she says. “So yes, I was attracted to this topic of males behaving badly; it was the violence, but also the degree of control.”

Hrdy’s hypothesis was that habitat pressures and over­population lay behind infanticidal behaviour. But watching the monkeys, she realised that something else was going on. Langur infants were never killed by their fathers, always by males that were new to their troop. After an infant was killed, its mother would sexually solicit the killer. From this pattern, she deduced that males and females were seeking advantages: males eliminated the offspring of rivals in order to reproduce themselves; females, who were much smaller, could not “sexually boycott” the aggressors without compromising their own chances.

Sometimes a female would copulate with several males – an adaptive behaviour that reduced the risk to her infants, since males were unlikely to attack an infant that could be their own. Hrdy also observed older, low-status females, one of which managed to wrest a wounded baby back from the jaws of an invading male. “Think total warrior,” she wrote later, of this encounter, which supported the “grandmother hypothesis” that post-menopausal females have been selected to support younger kin – explaining why, in a handful of species including humans, females live for a long time after their fertility ends.

That females are agents with agendas, not passive vessels, was the broader argument. But when she presented her findings, one senior colleague walked out. “People were saying I was crazy and stuff,” she says. “By now, it has been vindicated: infanticide by males under exactly the conditions I predicted has been reported in more than 50 species of non-human primates. Hippos, wolves, lions, all these other animals do it; it’s not big news any more.”

Hrdy’s troubling specialism was not the only thing that made her unpopular. Harvard’s biology faculty was riven with conflict when she was there, with Edward O Wilson’s book Sociobiology: The New Synthesis being a focal point. Wilson was an entomologist specialising in ants – and one of Hrdy’s supervisors – who went on to become a crucial populariser of the concept of biodiversity. But in the 1970s, his focus was showing how evolutionary science could be used to explain social behaviour.

Crucial to this extension of Darwin’s theory was inclusive fitness – whereby relatives are motivated to support each other’s reproductive efforts (the grandmother hypothesis is an example) – and a view of altruism as an evolutionary adaptation conferring benefits (you scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours). Other scientists were engaged in similar research; Hrdy named her son after Nikolaas Tinbergen, who won a Nobel prize in 1973 for discoveries about the innate behaviour of birds. But Wilson pushed the argument furthest. By making the case that we cannot understand ourselves without reference to natural selection, he sought to meld the natural and social sciences into a new discipline: sociobiology.

Critics reacted fiercely against what they saw as a deterministic outlook that could be used to justify hierarchies and prejudices; in 1978, protesters poured iced water over him at an academic meeting. Hrdy, who believes that his chief antagonists were partly motivated by professional envy, remains “incredibly angry about the response to sociobiology”, which also made it hard for her to get a job.

When she finally received an offer, from the University of California, Davis, it was because they wanted to hire her husband, who studied infectious diseases. By this time, she had published a book with the sarcastic title The Woman That Never Evolved, which included a lengthy discussion of the female orgasm. But the book had another target: what Hrdy called the “feminist dream” of women’s “less egotistical, less competitive” natures. Her view has always been that such notions risk undermining rather than bolstering equal rights. What is needed, instead, is a clear-eyed view of the conditions that enhance women’s chances.

She expanded these ideas in Mother Nature (a show based on this book, called My Mother the Cannibal, will be performed in Vienna next year). By the time it came out in 1999, she had switched to writing full-time. Her experience is, she says, that “women can do two of the three things. There’s family; there’s research and teaching; and then there is the kind of writing I do, where you build an imaginary world and move into it. I have to do that because I am often using different starting assumptions than the ones that are in the literature.”

The book examined the diversity of breeding systems: gorillas, with their harems and alpha males; bonobos, with their dominant females; and titi monkeys, which are among the minority of primates with paternal care of infants and mainly monogamous pair-bonds. Building a bridge to human evolution, Hrdy drew on anthropological fieldwork with hunter-gatherers. As well as infanticide, she delved into such contentious topics as sex-selective abortion and foot-binding; she also continued her argument with feminist scholars who were hostile to evolution on political grounds. She warned repeatedly against taking social progress for granted. A lifelong advocate of reproductive rights, she had an abortion in her 20s and says she is “even more grateful now for the choice I had then”.

The history of ideas is part of every story she tells; she is generous in referencing others’ work. “It was a habit because my early work was controversial and I had to back it up, but it’s not just paranoia,” she says. “I think people should be credited and I am acutely aware that women’s ideas get usurped much more readily than men’s. I am grateful to my early critics who said I was crazy and making it up, because if my work had not been controversial I wouldn’t have gotten credit for it. I mean, who wanted to take credit for ideas that were that bad?”

Robert Trivers was a key influence, with his research on the way parental behaviours are shaped by reproductive roles. From Mary Jane West-Eberhard she gained insights into the two-way relationship between genes and the environment, including human culture, which makes “nature versus nurture” a misleading simplification. The primatologist Jeanne Altmann revealed female baboons as “dual-career mothers” struggling to reconcile roles as carers and food-gatherers – setting the scene for Hrdy’s highly original later work.

This concerns the centrality of care in human evolution and is rooted in the insight that climate shifts and population collapse about 1.8m to 12,000 years ago – in the Pleistocene epoch, or ice age – made cooperation essential as never before. Selection for traits (or genes) that enabled male mammals to reproduce was mirrored, in Hrdy’s account, by selection for traits that equipped females not only to become pregnant and give birth, but also to raise young with a chance of reaching maturity.

Selection also acted upon infants, favouring adaptations that made it more likely that group members would help to provision them: “I think that babies, because they had to ingratiate themselves with caretakers, developed neural systems that would allow them to think about what others were thinking. We communicate and cooperate in ways that other animals really never have before. We have this gift that we had to evolve in order to survive.”

Hrdy calls this behaviour “mind‑reading” and proposes that our capacity for empathy is the most human thing about us – although it carries risks as well as benefits, including our susceptibility to indoctrination. Her book on this topic, 2009’s Mothers and Others, was well received. But writing Father Time gave her sleepless nights and migraines. “I was worried, telling men about their inner fish, their inner frog; I didn’t think that was going to go over that well,” she says. Random House had the right of first refusal, but rejected a sample chapter overnight with the phrase “too many amphibians”. Princeton published it instead and the book has won high praise (a paperback edition came out this year).

Fifty years after the row over sociobiology blew up, Hrdy makes a point of calling herself a “card-carrying sociobiologist”, while others doing similar work prefer the term behavioural ecology, which carries less baggage. The controversy surrounding Wilson has been revived, since his death in 2021, by the discovery of supportive letters he wrote in 1989 to John Philippe Rushton, a Canadian evolutionary psychologist and advocate for “race science” and eugenics.

Like others who have defended Wilson, she views the correspondence as an error rather than evidence of covert prejudice: “Did he take the time to read the paper Rushton sent him closely enough? Probably not. Was he politically naive? Probably.”

One piece of evidence for this view is a letter Wilson wrote to the science periodical Nature in 1981, arguing that “no justification for racism is to be found in the truly scientific study of the biological basis of social behaviour”. After our conversation, Hrdy emails me an article by Prof Bert Hölldobler, a former colleague of Wilson’s, which cites a more recent source: in a 2004 edition of his book, On Human Nature, Wilson wrote that human races “do not in fact exist”. Hölldobler described Wilson’s recommendation of a manuscript by Rushton as “a serious misjudgment”.

Hrdy’s tentative optimism that the silos around academic disciplines are loosening and her hope that more paternal care could eventually lead to a less aggressive world coexist with alarm, especially at the actions of the Trump administration. She celebrated her 80th birthday with her three children and five grandchildren this summer: “As I get older and older, my sell-by date is approaching; of course I’m worrying more about the world they’re inheriting.” She and her husband planted 70,000 trees on their walnut farm and keep sheep, dogs and a llama. Last year, she gave a Ted Talk about the bleak prospect of robots caring for babies.

“I was never a good horseback rider because I lacked the courage to jump the big jumps,” she says when I ask what keeps her going. But over a lifetime she has found herself rebelling more often than she thought herself capable of. “It’s a raw topic,” she says. “It is curiosity that did it: I am driven to want to learn new things. I just am. I think my grandmother may have been as well – and my mother.”

The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 08:00:08 GMT

The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive

Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele.

The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide, I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; most recently, an omnivorous Malaysian restaurant with a walloping double-tofu laksa, which shut 24 hours before publication. But the process encouraged me to take a different viewpoint, instead focusing on the spots that had survived and the story they told.

Whether loudly thriving or doggedly trundling along, the bulk of the restaurants in this guide don’t necessarily fall under the umbrella of what may be dubbed “mainstream veganism”. No, these are places where vegan ingredients are used more naturally, not merely as sub-par swaps for meat and dairy. The dishes feature plant-based staples because they always have. It’s a story I’ve noticed across the country; the vegan restaurants doing best centre on cuisines with a historical precedent of plant-based cooking.

To talk about this form of vegan cooking, we have to address the other type first. I’m talking about corporate veganism, and its boom and bust. Examining this requires us to go back to the 2010s, when veganism turned from a crunchy fringe practice to the latest mainstream food trend. Overnight, menus were populated by ever meatier “dirty” junk food, like loaded fries, nuggets and stacked burgers. Avocado toast, too, was everywhere for me and my peers to fritter our totally-not-imaginary house deposits on.

Passionate plant-based restaurateurs followed this trend, but so did bad faith actors seeing a cash grab and ignoring the animal and environmental ethics at veganism’s core. And while I don’t want to downplay the role that restaurants like these played in getting people to try vegan eating for the first time, it’s telling that most of the big-name closures were places that once followed this model.

It takes a decidedly western viewpoint to see veganism as a novelty. This way of thinking (“veganism hadn’t appealed to me before now, therefore must not have existed”) overlooks the centuries-long history of plant-forward cooking in other parts of the world, where rice, beans and soy are staples. There are myriad reasons why different cultures have historically embraced plant-based eating, including religion, the price and availability of ingredients and recipes being passed down through families. Crucially, they all see vegan ingredients as foundational, rather than replacements for something missing.

Vittles’ vegan picks reflect this approach. There’s All Nations Vegan House, a Caribbean takeaway serving Rastafari Ital food, and Andu cafe, where Ethiopian dishes are piled atop a boat-like injera. We featured the lovingly prepared Thai and Lao street food at King Cookdaily and the Japanese miso-glazed aubergine and japchae (sweet potato starch noodles) at Itadakizen. From my own picks, I have to single out Persepolis, a vegetarian Iranian restaurant in Peckham, south London, for stacked flatbreads and rich rice dishes. That it was my local (and first meal out) when I moved to London nearly eight years ago only adds to that feeling of warmth, of home-cooked comfort.

Then there’s Tofu Vegan, which recently opened its seventh restaurant and which exemplifies this rich vegan history. At the core of every punchy dish, you’ll find vegetables or traditional Chinese mock meats made from seitan (a protein source consisting of wheat gluten that dates back hundreds of years). Nothing is forced in or hidden. Sure, my meat-eating boyfriend might have been convinced that he’d been served real fish on our first visit, but not as the result of some elaborate ruse to trick him into eating vegan. Rather than apologising for what it is not, the food speaks for itself.

Whether it’s Malaysian food at Soul Vegan in Edinburgh, Chinese at Lotus Plant Kitchen in south Manchester, or authentically vegan Portuguese fare at Plantuguese in Bristol, this trend can be observed across the country.

Social media’s obsession with the new means the exciting launches (or genuinely tragic closures) will always generate the most discussion. But for some, success looks a little different, and means maintaining an unwavering customer base year upon year, with reliably delicious home-cooking-style food.

So while these restaurants may use the term “vegan”, their food long predates the coining of the term in 1944. Veganism is more than a category of restaurants, or even diet; these places are what they are, not what they lack. In turn, I’ve come to see the British vegan dining scene in a similar manner. Lamenting the losses, of course, is natural. But at a certain point, we have to celebrate not just the places that remain, but what we may have missed along the way.

Isobel Lewis is a freelance culture and lifestyle journalist

I built a reputation as a ‘walker’ so I could cheat when it mattered most – and it worked

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 08:00:07 GMT

Cricket always celebrates sportsmanship and condemns cheating, but where exactly is the line between the two?

I once played in a one-day semi-final. We were in a very tight spot when I edged the ball to the keeper. I didn’t walk. The opposition couldn’t believe it. They crowded around me, furious, and I was getting plenty of abuse.

I managed to get a single and when I reached the other end the umpire said: “You didn’t nick that did you? You are a walker.” “Yep, that’s right,” I replied.

Then I carried on. We won the game. That was the end of it. This moment had been carefully created through deception. You could call it cheating. Over time, I had consciously built a reputation for walking when it was a thick edge, knowing there would be a moment I could use this later on. The umpires had seen me do it. So when a close call came along, that reputation gave me room to take a liberty. That was the level of thought I had put into it.

Later, I was talking to someone in the sport about cheating. He asked me to rate myself from zero to 10: zero meant never cheat, 10 meant cheat at every viable moment. I think I said three.

He told me he found that strange. I was someone who wanted to be the best at everything I did, but when it came to cheating I was only three out of 10. Surely there were only two answers, he said: zero or 10. How can you justify anything in between? From then on, I became a 10. I’m not proud of that. I’m not saying it is how I would choose to behave if I could go back. But when you play in environments where winning is everything, you make choices. You find ways to gain an advantage, and you learn which ones the game will tolerate.

That is why the recent furore around Australia has made me think about the contradictions in cricket. If a batter edges the ball and doesn’t walk, people often say it is the umpire’s job to decide. The batter has done nothing against the laws. The decision belongs to the umpire. But if a bowler or fielder tries to make the ball move more, or claim a catch, the reaction can be absolute outrage. Yes, altering the ball is not allowed, but it raises a question about how we talk about honesty and advantage.

I remember players – yes, multiple – who were geniuses at scratching the ball in their run and disguising it to look like natural damage. If the ball went over the boundary and landed on concrete, it might come back scuffed or it might not, but get it to said player and he would make sure it was. This is a deliberate practice by those who want to gain an advantage.

This is not new. Cricket has always had people looking for an edge. Some methods are celebrated as clever, others are treated as an offence against the game itself. Take the Mankad. The laws allow the bowler to run out a non-striker who leaves the crease early. The batter has gained an advantage by leaving before the ball is released; the bowler has the legal right to act. Yet when it happens, the anger can be extraordinary. The MCC is the guardian of the laws and the spirit of cricket. If the method were unacceptable, the law could be changed, but it hasn’t been – so why is it so emotive?

We have bigger bats, shorter boundaries and flat pitches. Batters are encouraged to hit the ball harder and further, while bowlers are often left looking for ways to make the contest more even. Why, then, is trying to make the ball more receptive to movement treated as beyond the pale?

There are performance dangers to doing it, and most professional cricketers know this. If you do pick at the ball there is the risk it gets soft and thus it becomes harder to take wickets. There is a period of 10-15 overs where you need to make it count. Otherwise you might be chasing leather. Is this not a skill?

Sign up to The Spin

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

When the lights come on and the pink ball goes round corners it is seen as a fascinating ebb and flow. Yet tamper with the ball – castigation. I am not advocating going against the law, but why do we need this law when the game is crying out for more balance between bat and ball?

I do think we need to be more honest about the culture of the game. There are a lot of weird contradictions. Players are constantly testing the boundaries: what the laws allow, what the umpire can see, what opponents will accept and what the culture says is fair.

My reputation as a walker in a crucial moment deceived the umpire. It was calculated and planned over months and I knew it was dishonest. I did it because I thought it might help us win. Accepted.

Perhaps that is the uncomfortable truth at the heart of all this. Cricket is full of contradictions about what is right and wrong and the line between the two seems to move depending on who is drawing it. We condemn some acts as cheating, while finding reasons to excuse others as instinct, gamesmanship or simply part of the contest.

The same contradictions run through society. We are quick to judge behaviour when it offends us, but more generous when it suits us or serves our interests. Maybe that is human nature. We call some advantages gamesmanship and others cheating. Often the difference is simply which ones we have decided to accept.

Don’t wait for a change in sexual consent law. Adults can act to stop age-gap abuse

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 06:00:05 GMT

The law is important, but so is the fact that people know when associates embark on inappropriate relationships. They bear responsibility too

Mia Latter was 16 and out clothes-shopping when Russell Brand stopped her on the street. He riffled through her bags to choose a dress he told her she should wear for the date he’d be taking her on. And so began a short relationship – if that’s the right word, given she was still at school and he was a 30-year-old MTV presenter, who she says publicly referred to her as “the child”. Towards the end, she claims, Brand orally raped her.

Lilly Creightmore was 18 when she says the then 32-year-old celebrity David Walliams asked her to dinner and then began pestering her for sex. There’s a hauntingly awkward photograph of her with him at a celebrity bash. Another time, at a house party, a fellow guest remembers her sitting on the floor alone, like a bored child. She now feels his behaviour was an abuse of power over someone vulnerable. Walliams’s lawyers say he denies grooming her or behaving inappropriately.

What would you have done if you were at that party, or passing Mia Latter and Brand in the street? Both girls were over the age of consent, and Creightmore legally an adult. But something about men chasing women young enough to be their daughters sets alarm bells ringing; so often it betrays a man seeking someone malleable, easily impressed or intimidated. It can be predatory, is unmistakably seedy, and if the girls are already vulnerable in other ways – as in the grooming gang cases of care leavers sexually exploited by older men – may well justify adult intervention.

But is an age gap in and of itself a crime? For that’s what the Close the Consent Gap campaign now gathering traction actually says: that 16- or 17-year-olds should be protected from sexual relationships with partners who are four or more years older than they are. And that’s not as simple as it sounds.

Is a four-year age gap automatically enough to make a 21-year-old a registered sex offender, with all the lifelong implications that holds? If a 19-year-old’s birthday falls a month before his 16-year-old girlfriend’s, is their relationship a sexual offence until she catches up? I’m not convinced.

Latter, meanwhile, suggested it should be an offence for men in their “30s, 40s and 50s” to sleep with anyone under 18, which seems more practical – but leaves open the question of whether an 18-year-old’s relationship with a 50-year-old, say, can ever really be one of equals.

Ministers have so far made carefully noncommittal noises, with the Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh arguing it would be “a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny”. Which is the sort of thing ministers say when they feel the emotional pull, but are wary of legislating in haste.

The urge to do something, after the heartbreaking stories of the last few weeks, is overwhelming. And raising the age of consent to 18 where one partner is an adult in a position of trust, like a teacher, has undeniably transformed safeguarding – including helping people see that teenage boys can be as vulnerable as girls.

But discussing it with friends at the weekend, all of us mothers of teenagers, we were split. Older teens must be free to make and learn from their own relationship mistakes at some point, if they’re ever to develop their own judgment. What we couldn’t agree on was when exactly that point comes, or how big an age gap exactly is too big. It’s less a number than a feeling, varying by each partner’s emotional readiness and life experience, and incredibly hard to codify in law.

What worries me about this well-intentioned campaign is the risk of failing to distinguish between a bad romance – the kind you wish your younger self hadn’t had, but from which you perhaps learned something about what a good one looks like – and an abusive relationship potentially already covered (as with Mia Latter’s alleged oral rape) by the law.

Would staggered ages of consent have stopped Brand? Sadly I doubt it, given the court heard that he indecently assaulted a grown woman at a radio station in front of four of his entourage, who did nothing to intervene. And though Close the Consent Gap argues that its proposals would make teenagers more confident in pressing sexual assault charges, since they wouldn’t have to prove they were coerced, it would also give adults who disapprove of a 17-year-old’s life choices or sexual orientation the power to report an otherwise happy relationship to the police. Better, perhaps, to treat age gaps as aggravating factors in sentencing, or else give them their rightful weight when considering pressing charges – rather as we treat other things, like alcohol, that can erode the ability to consent.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

These are difficult questions, and Haigh is right to argue against kneejerk decisions. But the one crystal-clear lesson of the last few weeks is that wherever the line ends up being drawn, the moral responsibility to protect what are still only baby adults begins wherever the law protecting older children leaves off. Brand denies Latter’s allegations, but everyone around him should have known that relationship was wrong, whatever the law said, just as Walliams’s peers should have seen the glaring red flags in a family entertainer pursuing teens. Young people are safest not when they’re infantilised, but when older adults quietly take responsibility for the behaviour of other adults around them. It shouldn’t take a change in the law to see that.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

The play that changed my life: ‘John Berger’s Pig Earth became something magical – they licked milk off bodies’

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:00:07 GMT

The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol by Complicité conjured the struggles of a French village with an intense rawness

There are many things you see that are impactful, but few you can genuinely say change your life. I saw Complicité’s The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol aged 16 on a school trip to Riverside Studios in London and it really reached me. I’d been educated in a very language, words-based way. Here the story was told – with such intensity! – through people’s bodies.

The world they were conjuring, from a story by John Berger in his book Pig Earth, was about this remote French village – a world of labour. And the strife and struggles of these characters was expressed through the physical work of the company.

It travels in time from the turn of the 20th century. There were Lucy’s three lives, the first being her real work life with Lilo Baur playing Lucy. Then her husband abandons her and she’s expelled from her community. And she then goes on a quest, which eventually leads her to love in the afterlife.

Physically they were unlike anyone I’d ever seen – Baur, Simon McBurney and Tim McMullan were not conventional-looking actors. It felt like somewhere between meeting a group of aliens and a kind of arthouse circus coming to town. You were completely lifted out of the norm and transported – it opened up very intense, deprived, raw experience into something magical.

I remember images more than story. There was an incredible sequence where the company told a love story within a cowshed. They played the cows, they played the lover, there was milk licked off bodies. It felt like something I’d never seen before. The actors were properly sweating doing it, reaching a sort of mystical level. It was amazing and made me realise just what theatre could do.

You didn’t judge these people. You weren’t ever allowed to, you had to go with them, whatever difficult turns their lives took.

I don’t make theatre like that. I don’t have the kind of physical storytelling language; I always look at it dreamily wishing I had that kind of training. My play Giant uses much more conventional, one-set, closed-time storytelling devices. But I hope that the audience experience something similar in terms of feeling compelled by something and made uncomfortable by it at the same time.

Giant can be seen in cinemas from 19 November

Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia named as biggest CO2 exporters in history

The Guardian Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:00:06 GMT

Analysis of fossil fuel exports since 1850 differs from most assessments – which look at countries where CO2 is released

Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the three biggest exporters of carbon dioxide in history, according to analysis of fossil fuels since 1850.

Russia tops the list of global exporters of fossil fuels, with its vast coal, oil and gas deposits. Accounting for the CO2 produced by burning these exports, Russia has been responsible for almost 70 gigatonnes, up to the end of 2025.

Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s biggest producers of oil and gas, comes next with about 60 gigatonnes of CO2 exported. The country has long been an obstructive force at the annual UN climate summits.

Australia is in third place, a long way behind the top two exporters, with responsibility for more than 25 gigatonnes of exported CO2, not far ahead of Venezuela. The revelation comes as Australia acts as president of this year’s UN climate summit, Cop31, which is now into its second week in Turkey. The country has yet to set an end point for the use or export of fossil fuels, which make up about two-fifths of its export economy.

Louise Hutchins, the convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said: “This analysis tells you a lot about what’s going wrong with climate negotiations. Here at Cop31, governments claim there’s not enough money to tackle the climate crisis, while Australia, Russia and Saudi Arabia, that have amassed fortunes from fossil fuels, continue to wield pivotal political power in this consensus-based process.

“Just look at Australia. Its contribution to global heating more than doubles when fossil fuel exports are counted. Yet it is co-presiding over the very negotiations where climate finance talks are once again in stalemate.

“Responsibility is on the wealthy, the powerful and the profiteers. Those who made fortunes from fossil fuels must pay for the damage.”

The analysis of historical exports of fossil fuels, conducted by Carbon Brief and seen by the Guardian, apportions responsibility for CO2 emissions based on the country extracting the fossil fuels, in contrast to most analyses, which look to the countries where the CO2 is released.

Calculating where the fossil fuels came from casts the global economy, and historical responsibilities for emissions, in a new light. Exporting countries can be relatively low on the list of global greenhouse gas emitters, because those calculations are based on fossil fuel use.

The analysis also shows that the US and China – the world’s two biggest current emitters of greenhouse gases – still bear greater responsibility for historical emissions than Russia, Saudi or Australia, because as well as importing vast quantities of fossil fuels, they have also burned their own supplies.

The Cop28 UN conference outcome in Dubai in 2023 called on all countries to contribute to a global fossil fuel transition, but set no timetable or workplan for doing so. At Cop31, on Monday afternoon, Australia issued a first draft of a potential outcome from the summit, which contained a call for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”.

However, many countries – including Saudi Arabia – have hardened their negotiating positions since Dubai, and the absence of the US under Donald Trump takes pressure away from them to find compromises. Many observers think the reference to the “immediate transition away” is unlikely to survive unscathed through the several more drafts of the cover decision text that are likely.

Saudi, Russia and allies in the Arab group and others are even opposing the idea of having a cover text, which could stymie negotiations further.

Climate Analytics, a thinktank, published separate analysis on Tuesday showing that Australia, despite presiding over Cop31, appeared to have no plans to curtail its own fossil fuel extraction.

Coalmines are still being permitted that would remain in operation until 2088, long after all countries are supposed to have reached net zero greenhouse gas emissions, around mid-century.

“It’s abundantly clear Australia is not ‘doing its part’ as the prime minister claimed here in Turkey last week,” said the Climate Analytics CEO, Bill Hare. “There is a deep contradiction in a government position that champions climate ambition abroad but plans for continued fossil fuel exports, with approvals for coalmines and gasfields that lock in production for decades.”

Addressing these contradictions is politically difficult for the Australian government. Anthony Albanese, the prime minister, attended Cop31 last week, but at home he is under pressure from a resurgent One Nation party that is riding high in the polls, and which spurns net zero and denies climate science.

A representative for the Saudi ministry of energy told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia accounted for approximately 1% of historical global CO₂ emissions within its borders. “Saudi Arabia exports oil to countries around the world to meet their energy needs. These countries decide how the oil is used, which technologies are employed, and how the resulting emissions are managed. It would therefore be misleading to place responsibility for those emissions on the exporting country while overlooking the role of those who consume the fuel.”

They added: “This does not absolve energy producers of their role in reducing emissions. Saudi Arabia is actively pursuing that role. Peer-reviewed research published in Science has identified Saudi crude among the lowest in upstream carbon intensity, while International Energy Agency data indicate comparatively low methane intensity in Saudi oil and gas operations.’”

Australia and Russia were approached for comment.

Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth, said: “It’s time for the deadly tango between the producers of fossil fuels, and those locked into dependency on oil and gas, to have its last dance. We must turn off the tap on fossil fuels and push richer nations to commit to a fair, fast and fully funded phaseout. That means real public finance, and access to the technology that can make it possible, for the countries bearing the brunt of climate breakdown.”

U. S. Loses Its Measles Elimination Status, a Historic Setback for American Health

The New York Times November 17, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

The nation was once regarded as a global leader for reining in the highly contagious virus. Now, large outbreaks that sicken thousands could become routine.

By Teddy Rosenbluth

Measles has come roaring back in the United States, as vaccination rates have fallen and cases of the once-extinguished virus have soared. That backslide has now cost the nation its measles elimination status, after the virus spread uninterrupted for more than a year.

“It’s a giant stain on our reputation,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “Everyone ought to be just utterly disgusted by the willing return back to an age of death and high cost.”

The announcement, made Tuesday by the Pan American Health Organization, ushers in a new era in which major outbreaks could routinely disrupt communities around the nation, sickening thousands of children. It also marks a highly embarrassing reversal for a country that showed the rest of the world it was possible to rein in the wildly contagious virus when it won elimination status in 2000.

State health officials have reported more than 7,700 cases of measles, including 10 deaths, since the resurgence first kicked off in a Mennonite community in Texas in January 2025. Hundreds have been hospitalized, many of them unvaccinated children. Infections have also risen among pregnant women and newborns, who are at increased risk of death and other dire health consequences.

“Losing measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of the Pan American Health Organization, in a news conference announcing the decision. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at the risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death.”

The organization announced on Tuesday that Bolivia and Mexico had also lost their measles elimination status, posing another setback for North America’s handle on the highly contagious virus. Canada officially lost its measles elimination status last year.

“None of this had to happen,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, a vaccine scientist and pediatrician at the Baylor College of Medicine. “That’s what’s so tragic.”

The circumstances that have allowed measles to take root again in the United States have been brewing for years, public health experts said. Vaccination rates, which began falling during the Covid-19 pandemic, have continued to drop, and now sit well below the 95 percent needed to establish herd immunity.

In some communities, including many of the insular religious groups hit hardest by measles outbreaks, an even smaller share of children are vaccinated.

But experts said under the leadership of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., federal health officials did too little to control outbreaks early on. And they criticized Mr. Kennedy himself for at times directly undermining efforts to improve vaccination rates, by promoting unproven treatments for measles and undermining confidence in childhood vaccines.

“I don’t think it’s an accident that this is happening under the current administration,” said Dr. William Moss, an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health who has studied measles for more than 25 years.

By Blacki Migliozzi/The New York Times

Grace Davis Jamison, a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in a statement that the department would continue working to “stop transmission, close vaccination gaps, strengthen outbreak response and protect Americans from measles.”

Ms. Jamison said that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention convened a meeting this year to develop a national strategy to regain elimination status. (Losing measles elimination status does not carry any formal penalty.)

“We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Dr. Erica Schwartz, the director of the C. D. C., said in a statement.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

In an X post published Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Kennedy added that his department would continue to “support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip health care providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.”

Regaining elimination status is likely to be a monumental task, one that experts said may require a vast public education campaign, investment in on-the-ground immunization efforts and a push to strengthen school vaccination requirements, which several states have loosened in recent years.

Even if the C. D. C. and cash-strapped state public health departments make that kind of investment, it will probably be “many years before we get the situation back under control,” said Dr. David Kimberlin, a pediatric infectious disease expert at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

While there were measles cases in the United States between 2000 and 2025, there were fewer than 200 cases most years, and many of them tied to international travel. When the virus did strike an unvaccinated community, the outbreaks did not continue for longer than a year, allowing the country to maintain its status.

That meant that many doctors around the country had never seen a case of measles before last year, when more children started arriving at hospitals gasping for breath or experiencing life-threatening brain swelling.

Many of those infected since 2025 have been young children, and several of the deaths have been in infants too young to be vaccinated.

“We are going to see a growing number of children, as well as young adults, dying from measles,” said Dr. Daniel Salas, who helps lead immunization efforts at the Pan American Health Organization.

That is not to mention the long-term health repercussions that are now “baked into our future,” said Dr. Cameron Wolfe, professor of infectious diseases at the Duke University School of Medicine. Even patients who appear to have recovered from measles may fall ill with an entirely different infection months or years later, because the virus weakens the immune system and leaves it more vulnerable to other threats.

In the next decade, experts also expect to see at least a few cases of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a devastating neurological condition that can occur after a measles infection and that slowly degrades the brain’s ability to access memory, control movement and, ultimately, breathe. It is nearly always fatal.

The resurgence of measles will have far broader consequences for American society. Already this year, hundreds of unvaccinated children have missed weeks of in-person classes this year while local health departments scrambled to stem the spread of the virus.

Since 2025, measles has cost the country roughly $125 million in medical care, lost productivity and public health resources, according to one estimate.

Public health experts are hopeful that the country will eventually reverse course, but some fear it will happen only after Americans see death and disability caused by measles in their own communities.

“Short of that, I’m not sure how to change the direction of this ship,” Dr. Kimberlin said. “That would take a lot of small coffins in the ground.”

I first started reporting on measles back in early 2025, when I flew out to a small town on the Western edge of Texas to write about an outbreak that had at that point infected just a few dozen people. Since then, measles has exploded into a national problem that has sickened thousands. For the better part of two years, my colleagues and I have shuttled around outbreaks all over the country trying to understand how this preventable disease had gained a foothold. Today, the U. S. has finally lost its elimination status, a monumental step back for the nation’s public health.

Teddy Rosenbluth is a Times reporter covering health news, with a special focus on medical misinformation.

Measles Is Officially Back in the United States. What Now?

The New York Times November 17, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

It may take years for the country to regain elimination status. In the meantime, communities will need to adopt numerous strategies to protect people.

By Apoorva Mandavilli and Dani Blum

The United States has returned to a time, until recently unimaginable, when measles is a persistent threat, not just a sporadic one that can easily be snuffed out.

Even with rigorous effort, it is likely to take years to regain measles elimination status, which the country officially lost on Tuesday. In the meantime, Americans will need to embrace strategies, some well worn and some new, to contend with this forgotten menace, more than a dozen experts said in interviews.
